cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
“Security policy management” is one shelf holding two different products: network security policy management (NSPM) firewall rulebases, segmentation intent, change automation and written-policy lifecycle the documents people sign and auditors demand.

Our roster spans both, so this countdown declares the lane on every entry and ranks within the honest frame: rulebase engines first by estate scale, document platforms by attestation truth. Tufin takes 1; AlgoSec and FireMon complete the NSPM podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: Tufin policy orchestration at the largest hybrid-estate scale.

• NSPM podium: Tufin (scale), AlgoSec (application-centric analysis), FireMon (real-time rulebase audit).

• Lane rule: rulebase automation and document attestation share nothing but the word “policy” declare the lane before the shortlist.

• Status note: Skybox Security’s corporate situation requires verification before any contract capability discussion below assumes that homework.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based evaluation; no lab testing, no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data.

NSPM criteria: rulebase-analysis depth, change-automation safety, multi-vendor/hybrid coverage. Written-policy criteria: lifecycle workflow, attestation tracking, framework mapping. Both: pricing clarity. Weights: lane-core capability 35%, automation safety 20%, coverage/mapping 20%, ergonomics 15%, pricing 10%.

The 2026 Policy Management Power Rankings

Editorial research-based scores, not lab results. Lanes ranked within their own frame.

1. Tufin — Best Hybrid-Estate Orchestration

Snapshot: Tiered platform | Multi-vendor firewall + cloud security groups | Segmentation intent enforced continuously

Why it earns 1: Tufin runs policy where the estates are largest: thousand-device multi-vendor firewall fleets plus cloud security groups orchestrated from one intent layer, with change automation that carries enterprise change-volume and segmentation policy enforced continuously rather than diagrammed annually. The scale ceiling of the category.

Pros: Hybrid orchestration scale; segmentation intent; change pipelines.

Cons: Platform weight below enterprise scale.

Bottom line: The big-estate policy engine.

2. AlgoSec — Best Application-Centric Analysis

Snapshot: Device/module licensing | Connectivity flows mapped to business apps | Risk-checked change automation

Why it ranks here: AlgoSec translates firewall sprawl into application language: flows discovered and mapped to the business apps they serve, so cleanup conversations happen in terms owners accept and decommissioned apps take their rules with them.

Change automation rides the same app-aware model.

Pros: App-centric mapping; business-legible cleanup; automation safety.

Cons: App-discovery depth takes tuning investment.

Bottom line: NSPM that speaks application.

3. FireMon — Best Real-Time Rulebase Audit

Snapshot: Device-based tiers | Live change detection | Cleanup analytics

Why it ranks here: FireMon watches rulebases as they drift: real-time change detection, compliance-drift alerts, and cleanup analytics surfacing the unused, shadowed, and risky rules that bloat every mature estate.

The continuous-audit pick for multi-vendor fleets that change daily.

Pros: Real-time monitoring; cleanup economics; compliance mapping.

Cons: Orchestration ceiling versus the scale leader.

Bottom line: The always-on rulebase auditor.

4. RedSeal — Best Hybrid Network Exposure Analysis

Snapshot: Enterprise-focused platform | Network topology modeling + security configuration analysis | Attack-path and exposure visibility across complex network environments

Why it ranks here: RedSeal helps organizations understand how network configurations, vulnerabilities, and connectivity combine to create security exposures.

Its network modeling and risk analysis capabilities help identify vulnerable paths, prioritize remediation, and assess the security impact of network changes.

It is a strong alternative to Skybox for organizations focused on network exposure context and attack-path analysis, although it is not a direct replacement for every firewall policy management workflow.

Pros: Network topology modeling; exposure management and attack-path analysis; vulnerability context; risk-based remediation prioritization.

Cons: Less focused on direct firewall rule lifecycle automation and change orchestration; enterprise-oriented deployment and implementation may require additional effort.

Bottom line: A strong Skybox alternative for network exposure modeling and risk prioritization, particularly in complex hybrid environments.

5. ManageEngine — Best Value NSPM Essentials

Snapshot: Per-device tiers | Firewall Analyzer rule cleanup | Compliance reports

Why it ranks here: ManageEngine Firewall Analyzer delivers the NSPM essentials rule analysis, config audit, compliance reporting at ManageEngine’s famously accessible pricing. The right weight for mid-market estates below the enterprise platforms’ complexity line.

Pros: Entry economics; essential coverage; low operational bar.

Cons: Orchestration and automation ceilings.

Bottom line: NSPM essentials without the enterprise invoice.

6. LogicGate — Best No-Code Policy Workflow

Snapshot: Application subscriptions | Risk Cloud policy lifecycle | Owner-built workflows

Why it ranks here: LogicGate’s Risk Cloud handles the document lane with no-code flexibility: policy creation, review cycles, exception workflows, and attestation campaigns built by the team that runs them.

The written-policy lifecycle inside a broader risk platform teams can remodel themselves.

Pros: No-code lifecycle; exception workflow; platform breadth.

Cons: Dedicated policy-tool depth in attestation chasing.

Bottom line: The policy workflow you redesign yourself.

7. Hyperproof — Best Many-Framework Policy Mapping

Snapshot: Platform tiers | One policy, every framework mapped | Evidence linkage

Why it ranks here: Hyperproof treats policies as mapped assets: one document linked to every requirement it satisfies across many frameworks simultaneously, with evidence attached and crosswalks maintained.

The compliance-ops answer for estates juggling five certifications on one policy set.

Pros: Crosswalk architecture; evidence linkage; ops workflow.

Cons: Network-policy lane untouched, by design.

Bottom line: One policy, every framework it serves.

8. Secureframe — Best Cert-Integrated Policy Library

Snapshot: Platform tiers | Auditor-ready policy library | Acceptance tracking

Why it ranks here: Secureframe ships the document lane as part of certification readiness: auditor-shaped policy templates, employee acceptance tracked against the HRIS, and evidence tied to the cert program.

Policies that arrive audit-shaped rather than drafted from blank pages.

Pros: Template quality; acceptance automation; cert integration.

Cons: Standalone policy programs outside cert context.

Bottom line: Policies born audit-ready.

9. ZenGRC (Reciprocity) — Best Lean Lifecycle Platform

Snapshot: Subscription tiers | Versioned policy lifecycle | Control mapping

Why it ranks here: ZenGRC manages written policy inside its lean compliance platform: version control, review cycles, control mapping, attestations the document lane handled at lean-team weight without heavyweight GRC implementation.

Pros: Lean lifecycle; control mapping; fast onboarding.

Cons: Attestation-chase depth versus dedicated tools.

Bottom line: Policy lifecycle at lean-GRC weight.

10. Netwrix — Best Endpoint-Enforced Policy

Snapshot: Per-user/module licensing | PolicyPak lineage | Settings enforced on devices

Why it ranks here: Netwrix closes the document lane’s credibility gap: the PolicyPak lineage enforces written rules as endpoint settings browser configs, application controls, least-privilege defaults so the signed document and the device state actually match.

Policy that reaches the desktop.

Pros: Endpoint enforcement; attestation tracking; Windows-estate depth.

Cons: Scope centers on Windows-estate enforcement.

Bottom line: The signature and the setting, reconciled.

Full Comparison Table

Yes/No Capability Table

Buying Advice: Declare the Lane, Then Pilot the Ugly Part

The shortlist writes itself once the lane is declared. NSPM buyers: inventory device count and vendor mix (multi-vendor fleets need Tufin/AlgoSec/FireMon-class orchestration), pilot on your ugliest rulebase and count the unused and shadowed rules surfaced cleanup findings typically fund the license before automation ever runs and gate change automation behind risk simulation with six months of clean history before production trust.

Written-policy buyers: test the attestation chase end-to-end (who hasn’t signed, automated reminders, auditor export in one click), demand framework mapping against certifications you actually hold, tie acceptance to the HRIS joiner flow, and weigh enforcement reality a Netwrix-class bridge between signed documents and device settings closes the gap auditors increasingly probe.

Both lanes: run the Skybox status verification before any evaluation effort, and route outputs rulebase drift or attestation gaps into the audit trail where findings get owned and dated.

FAQs

What are the best security policy management tools in 2026?

Network lane: Tufin, AlgoSec, FireMon, ManageEngine, with Skybox status-gated. Written lane: LogicGate, Hyperproof, Secureframe, ZenGRC, and Netwrix for endpoint-enforced policy.

NSPM or written-policy tooling — which do we need?

Firewall and segmentation estates need NSPM; audit and certification programs need document lifecycle most enterprises eventually run one of each, bought separately against different criteria (compliance management software solutions).

What does safe change automation look like?

Requests simulated against risk and compliance before any push, approvals routed, implementations verified post-change automation with a pre-flight check, never blind push.

What’s the fastest NSPM payback?

Rulebase cleanup: the unused, shadowed, and duplicate rules surfaced in a pilot typically justify the license on risk and performance grounds alone.

How do we prove policy attestation to auditors?

Version-controlled documents, timestamped acceptance records, exception registers, and one-click evidence export plus enforcement reconciliation where device settings should match signed policy.

Verdict

One shelf, two products, ten tools ranked in their honest lanes.

Tufin for the biggest fleets, AlgoSec for application language, FireMon for the live audit, ManageEngine for the value tier, Skybox behind a status gate; LogicGate, Hyperproof, Secureframe, and ZenGRC running the document lifecycle, Netwrix making signatures real on devices declare the lane, pilot the ugly rulebase or the attestation chase, and let policy prove itself instead of describing itself.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Audit management software is graded by a brutal metric: the spreadsheet-reversion point the moment auditors flee the platform back to Excel.

The 2026 rankings reward fieldwork ergonomics, evidence automation that pulls control tests from systems rather than people, and the committee-pack mile where most tools quietly fail. AuditBoard takes 1; ServiceNow and Workiva complete the podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: AuditBoard the adoption benchmark the profession measures everything against.

• Podium: AuditBoard (floor-vote winner), ServiceNow (workflow-routed findings), Workiva (filing-grade reporting fusion).

• Class split: audit-born specialists (AuditBoard, TeamMate) versus GRC-suite modules (ServiceNow, Archer, MetricStream) versus reporting-grade platforms (Workiva, Diligent) daily ownership decides.

• 2026 theme: AI drafting entered the workpaper narrative generation and summarization are real, with reviewer sign-off as the non-negotiable gate.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based evaluation; no lab testing, no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data.

Criteria: fieldwork ergonomics (workpapers, review chains), evidence/control-test automation, SOX depth, committee-grade reporting, time-to-value, and pricing clarity.

Weights: fieldwork ergonomics 25%, evidence automation 20%, SOX depth 20%, reporting 20%, time-to-value 15%.

The 2026 Audit Management Power Rankings

*Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

1. Onspring — Best Configurable No-Code Audit Platform

Snapshot: Subscription platform | No-code internal-audit workflows | Workpapers, findings, remediation, and reporting

Why it earns 1: Onspring gives audit teams the flexibility to build and adapt audit programs without relying heavily on developers, while still covering planning, fieldwork, workpapers, review chains, findings, evidence, and remediation.

Its strength is combining audit usability with no-code configurability, so teams can shape workflows around their own methodology instead of forcing auditors into a rigid process.

Pros: No-code flexibility; strong fieldwork workflow; workpaper management; findings and remediation tracking; configurable reporting.

Cons: Less market scale and brand recognition than the largest audit platforms; complex configurations still need disciplined administration.

Bottom line: The audit platform teams can reshape without rebuilding from scratch.

2. ServiceNow — Best Workflow-Routed Findings

Snapshot: Now Platform modules | Findings tied to CMDB assets | Remediation the business must answer

Why it ranks here: ServiceNow’s audit module solves the back half of every engagement: findings routed as workflows to owners who can’t ignore tickets, tied to CMDB assets and change records, with remediation status visible without chasing.

Fieldwork depth trails the specialists; finding-closure velocity doesn’t.

Pros: Remediation routing; asset linkage; estate adoption gravity.

Cons: Workpaper ergonomics versus audit-born rivals.

Bottom line: The findings that actually get fixed.

3. Caseware — Best Audit-to-Financial-Reporting Integration

Snapshot: Platform subscriptions | Audit workpapers + financial statements | Connected reporting and review workflows

Why it ranks here: Caseware connects audit fieldwork directly with financial reporting, allowing workpapers, risk assessments, procedures, review notes, and financial statements to live inside one connected environment.

Its advantage is strongest where audit results ultimately need to flow into formal financial reporting, disclosure review, and filing workflows without repeatedly moving data between separate systems.

Pros: Strong audit methodology; connected workpapers; integrated financial statements; review and sign-off workflows; reporting automation.

Cons: More accounting and financial-audit oriented than broad enterprise GRC platforms; less suited to organizations focused mainly on operational or cyber audit.

Bottom line: Audit workpapers and financial reporting connected from fieldwork to final statement.

4. Wolters Kluwer (TeamMate) — Best Methodology Incumbent

Snapshot: Per-auditor licensing | TeamMate+ web generation | Global install base

Why it ranks here: TeamMate carries decades of internal-audit methodology workpaper discipline, review hierarchies, the vocabulary the profession trained on modernized to web scale in TeamMate+.

The installed base makes it the shared language of audit shops worldwide; adoption-era momentum is the honest contest it fights.

Pros: Methodology depth; workpaper rigor; global ubiquity.

Cons: Winning hearts against the adoption leader.

Bottom line: The incumbent methodology, webified.

5. Diligent — Best Committee-Channel Integration

Snapshot: Suite subscriptions | HighBond lineage + board portals | ACL analytics heritage

Why it ranks here: Diligent owns the destination: board portals most large enterprises already run, with audit modules feeding committee packs without reformatting theater and ACL-era analytics underneath. When the hardest audience sits upstairs, the channel is the feature.

Pros: Board-channel ownership; analytics lineage; governance fusion.

Cons: Fieldwork depth consistency across acquired modules.

Bottom line: The shortest path to the committee.

6. MetricStream — Best Regulated-Enterprise Module

Snapshot: Platform licensing | Banking-grade audit integration | Federated architecture

Why it ranks here: MetricStream’s audit module inherits the platform’s regulated depth: audit integrated with operational risk and compliance at examiner-ready rigor, federated across entities and geographies. Heavyweight implementation reality included the institutional pick.

Pros: Regulated depth; risk integration; federated scale.

Cons: Implementation weight; adoption ergonomics.

Bottom line: Audit inside the enterprise waterfront.

7. Hyperproof — Best Compliance-Ops Crossover

Snapshot: Platform tiers | Controls mapped across frameworks | Continuous evidence collection

Why it ranks here: Hyperproof crosses from compliance operations into audit: controls managed once and mapped to every framework, continuous evidence collection feeding both certification and internal audit, and workflow built for distributed teams.

Strongest where audit and compliance share an evidence backbone.

Pros: Crosswalk architecture; evidence reuse; ops workflow.

Cons: Classic internal-audit fieldwork depth versus specialists.

Bottom line: One evidence engine, two programs.

8. Archer — Best Configurable Register Module

Snapshot: Use-case licensing | Audit encoded into enterprise registers | Methodology freehand

Why it ranks here: Archer models audit into the same configurable registers as enterprise risk: whatever methodology your shop runs, encoded exactly with the administrator staffing that freedom demands.

The integrated choice for estates already running Archer’s registers.

Pros: Configurability; register integration; program pedigree.

Cons: Staffing tax; modern ergonomics race.

Bottom line: Your methodology, encoded staff it.

9. Ideagen — Best Safety-Sector Specialist

Snapshot: Module subscriptions | Aviation/healthcare/manufacturing templates | Document-control lineage

Why it ranks here: Ideagen serves audits where the stakes are physical: aviation, healthcare, and manufacturing compliance against exacting operational standards, with sector templates and document-control DNA. The specialist lane the generalists don’t walk.

Pros: Sector templates; safety-regime fluency; document control.

Cons: General internal-audit breadth versus leaders.

Bottom line: Audit for the safety-critical floor.

10. Netwrix — Best IT-Audit Evidence Lane

Snapshot: Per-user/module licensing | IT-change and access auditing | Evidence-generation focus

Why it ranks here scoped honestly: Netwrix enters from the evidence side: IT auditing of changes, access, and configurations across AD, file systems, and databases the system-generated evidence IT audits consume rather than engagement-workflow management. The evidence lane, ranked as one.

Pros: IT-evidence depth; change/access auditing; value pricing.

Cons: Not an engagement-workflow platform.

Bottom line: The evidence feed, not the fieldwork desk.

Full Comparison Table

Yes/No Capability Table

Buying Advice: Pilot the Reversion Point

Run the only pilot that predicts success: working auditors on a real engagement slice one workpaper chain, one review cycle, one finding through remediation and watch for where they reach for Excel, because that reversion point is the product’s true boundary and no demo reveals it.

Grade evidence automation against your control population (what share of SOX tests can run from system data and consider the Netwrix-class evidence lane as a feed regardless of platform choice), demand the committee pack generated live from fieldwork data, and settle the archive question before migration: prior-year workpapers move with review chains intact or stay read-only half-migrations poison the first busy season.

Price per-auditor versus module models at your real headcount, require AI-drafted narratives to carry mandatory reviewer sign-off, and wire findings into remediation workflow the business answers an audit platform whose findings age in its own database has only moved the spreadsheet problem.

FAQs

What is the best audit management software in 2026? AuditBoard leads on adoption, ServiceNow routes findings the business must answer, Workiva owns the filing-grade mile, TeamMate holds the methodology lineage, with Diligent, MetricStream, Hyperproof, Archer, Ideagen, and Netwrix (IT-evidence lane) by class.

Audit platform or GRC suite module? Audit-led programs buy fieldwork-first platforms; risk-led programs extend their GRC suite the deciding question is who owns daily use, auditors or the risk function.

What should evidence automation actually cover? System-pulled control tests (access reviews, configuration checks), document-request workflows with chasing built in, and continuous feeds from compliance tooling graded against your real control population.

Is AI in audit software trustworthy? For narrative drafting, workpaper summarization, and risk-assessment assists, yes with reviewer sign-off mandatory and sampling-based quality checks on output.

How long should implementation take? Weeks for adoption-class platforms, quarters for enterprise suites put a first-engagement-live date in the contract either way.

Verdict

Ten platforms, one brutal metric: where do the auditors flee to Excel? AuditBoard set the adoption bar, ServiceNow closes the findings, Workiva files the result, TeamMate keeps the methodology, Diligent feeds the committee, and the estate modules serve their estates pilot on real fieldwork, automate the evidence, archive cleanly, and make the committee pack a query instead of a weekend.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Security ratings grade organizations from the attacker’s side of the fence exposed services, patch cadence, breach signals and the grades now move real money: insurance pricing, vendor gates, board narratives.

Two honesty notes shape this countdown: NormShield is Black Kite’s former name (one company, counted once), and Mastercard announced RiskRecon’s wind-down, making it a migration note rather than a pick so we rank nine services honestly.

SecurityScorecard takes 1; BitSight and Black Kite complete the podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: SecurityScorecard the operational rating teams actually work from weekly.

• Podium: SecurityScorecard (working-meeting clarity), BitSight (evidence-grade correlation), Black Kite (the dollar-lens rating).

• Honest count: nine, not ten one rebrand consolidated, one wind-down flagged.

• 2026 theme: attribution accuracy mis-mapped assets remain the category’s chronic complaint, and testing it with your own estate is the only pilot that matters.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based evaluation; no lab testing, no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data.

Criteria: signal quality and attribution accuracy, loss-correlation evidence, dispute-workflow fairness, actionability of findings, portfolio ergonomics, and pricing clarity.

Weights: attribution/signal 25%, correlation evidence 20%, actionability 20%, dispute fairness 15%, portfolio scale 10%, pricing 10%.

The 2026 Security Ratings Power Rankings

*Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

1. SecurityScorecard — Best Operational Rating

Snapshot: Portfolio tiers; free self-view A–F grades + factor drill-downs | Breach alerting cadence

Why it earns 1: SecurityScorecard made ratings a working instrument: letter grades executives parse instantly, factor-level drill-downs practitioners act on the same day, breach alerts at operational cadence, and the free self-view that seeded the market’s broadest visibility motion. The rating that drives Tuesday’s vendor call, not just the quarterly slide.

Pros: Grade clarity; factor actionability; alert cadence; free self-assessment.

Cons: Attribution hygiene needs your validation pass, as everywhere in the category.

Bottom line: The score built for working meetings.

2. BitSight — Best Evidence-Grade Correlation

Snapshot: Portfolio subscriptions | Decade-deep loss-correlated dataset | Fourth-party discovery

Why it ranks here: BitSight’s moat is published evidence: externally observed telemetry correlated against real incident history over a decade the dataset insurers price with and boards cite. Fourth-party mapping and governance-grade reporting complete the institutional pick.

Pros: Correlation receipts; insurer currency; fourth-party graph.

Cons: Operational-cadence ergonomics trail the leader.

Bottom line: The rating with the longest receipts.

3. Black Kite (formerly NormShield) — Best Financial-Impact Lens

Snapshot: Per-vendor/portfolio tiers | Triple-lens scoring | Open FAIR-based impact math

Why it ranks here: One company, two sheet names, counted once: Black Kite grades three ways technical rating, FAIR-based financial impact, compliance correlation plus a ransomware-susceptibility index, giving vendor conversations a dollar figure alongside the letter. The methodology-transparency pick.

Pros: Dollar-lens scoring; methodology openness; ransomware index.

Cons: Brand gravity versus the two giants.

Bottom line: The rating that also speaks CFO.

4. UpGuard — Best Value Bundle with Leak Detection

Snapshot: Tiered subscriptions | Ratings + data-leak detection + lean TPRM | Mid-market economics

Why it ranks here: UpGuard pairs continuous ratings with the finding other raters skip: leak detection surfacing exposed credentials, buckets, and documents tied to you or your vendors. Bundled with lean questionnaire workflow at mid-market pricing, it’s the sensible-scale package.

Pros: Leak-detection differentiator; bundle value; accessible tiers.

Cons: Enterprise portfolio ergonomics versus leaders.

Bottom line: The rating that also finds your leaked bucket.

5. Panorays — Best Workflow-Fused Rating

Snapshot: Per-vendor tiers | Rating + adaptive questionnaires in one pass | Cycle-speed focus

Why it ranks here: Panorays treats the rating as half the assessment: external scores fused with questionnaires that adapt to each vendor’s footprint, collapsing review cycles to days. The rating as an engine inside vendor-risk workflow rather than a standalone dashboard.

Pros: Native workflow fusion; adaptive assessments; speed.

Cons: Standalone-ratings depth versus the dedicated graphs.

Bottom line: The score with a workflow welded on.

6. Whistic — Best Security-Assessment Exchange Companion

Snapshot: Platform subscription | Shared security profiles + Trust Center Exchange | Assessments, evidence, and vendor risk workflows

Why it ranks here scoped honestly: Whistic sits on the assessment-exchange side of third-party risk, helping organizations reuse vendor security profiles, questionnaires, certifications, and supporting evidence instead of collecting the same material repeatedly.

It works best as a ratings-adjacent TPRM companion, combining standardized assessments with continuous vendor review and workflow automation rather than acting as a primary external security-rating originator.

Pros: Shared assessment exchange; reusable security profiles; evidence collection; workflow automation; standardized questionnaires.

Cons: Not a primary outside-in ratings provider; strongest value comes from assessment and trust workflows.

Bottom line: Reusable vendor assessments that reduce questionnaire fatigue across the ecosystem.

7. BlueVoyant TPRM — Best Managed Third-Party Risk Companion

Snapshot: Managed platform + service | Continuous external monitoring + assessments | Analyst validation and vendor remediation

Why it ranks here — scoped honestly: BlueVoyant approaches third-party risk from a managed monitoring and assessment model, combining external cyber-risk signals with questionnaires, analyst review, validation, and remediation support.

Its strength is helping teams move from finding vendor risk to validating and addressing it, making it a strong companion to security-rating programs that need more operational follow-through.

Pros: Continuous monitoring; managed assessments; analyst validation; remediation support; vendor engagement.

Cons: More service-led than pure self-service rating platforms; not primarily a standalone ratings originator.

Bottom line: Managed third-party risk operations that turn vendor findings into validated action.

8. SecurityStudio — Best SMB/Inside-Out Complement

Snapshot: Accessible tiers | S2Score self-and-vendor assessment | SMB/MSP channel fit

Why it ranks here: SecurityStudio grades from the inside out: S2Score risk assessments for your own organization and simplified vendor scoring sized for SMBs and the MSPs serving them the accessible complement to external graphs, not a competitor to them.

Pros: SMB economics; self-assessment lens; MSP channel.

Cons: Not an external-telemetry rating; scale ceilings.

Bottom line: The small-estate scoring on-ramp.

9. Mastercard (RiskRecon) — Wind-Down: Migration Note

Snapshot: Sunset path | Respected assessment-grade lineage | Transition planning required

Why it ranks last and why it’s still listed: RiskRecon built genuinely respected assessment-grade ratings, but Mastercard’s announced wind-down converts every evaluation into a migration plan: existing customers should map portfolios to successor platforms and export history; new buyers should choose from the eight entries above. Listed for the installed base’s sake, ranked as what remains.

Pros: (Legacy) assessment detail; action-plan reporting lineage.

Cons: Announced sunset decides everything.

Bottom line: Plan the exit, not the purchase.

Full Comparison Table

Yes/No Capability Table

articles.description:
Microsoft has released security updates for a Windows Active Directory vulnerability that allows an authorized attacker to execute code over a network. Tracked as CVE-2026-119948, the flaw was disclosed on November 10, 2026, and affects multiple Windows desktop and server versions. Microsoft rates it Important, with a CVSS 3.1 base score of 7.5. The CVE […]

The post Windows Active Directory RCE Vulnerability Allows Attacker to Execute Code Over a Network appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Microsoft has released security updates for a Windows Active Directory vulnerability that allows an authorized attacker to execute code over a network.

Tracked as CVE-2026-119948, the flaw was disclosed on November 10, 2026, and affects multiple Windows desktop and server versions. Microsoft rates it Important, with a CVSS 3.1 base score of 7.5.

The CVE record identifies the weakness as a stack-based buffer overflow. Exploitation requires low privileges and no user interaction, but the attack complexity is high. This means the flaw is not described as an unauthenticated attack that works against every reachable Windows system.

A stack-based buffer overflow occurs when a program writes more data to stack memory than is allocated for it. This can overwrite adjacent data and, under certain conditions, alter the program’s execution. In this instance, Microsoft confirms that the result may include the ability to execute remote code.

Microsoft has not disclosed the affected function, the exact network request needed, or a working attack method in the supplied advisory.

Its explanation of the high complexity rating says specific conditions must exist, such as particular protocol settings or configurations. Administrators should therefore avoid assuming that network access and valid credentials alone guarantee successful exploitation.

Windows Active Directory RCE Vulnerability

The CVSS assessment lists high potential impact on confidentiality, integrity, and availability. A successful attack could therefore affect protected information, change data, or disrupt the vulnerable system. However, the published record does not establish that exploitation automatically grants SYSTEM privileges or control of an entire domain.

At release, Microsoft reported no known exploitation and no prior public disclosure. It assessed exploitation as less likely and listed exploit code maturity as unproven. An anonymous researcher received credit for reporting the vulnerability.

The affected products include Windows Server 2016, 2019, 2022, and 2025, including listed Server Core installations. Windows 10 versions 1607, 1809, 21H2, and 22H2 are also included, alongside Windows 11 versions 23H2 through 26H2. Architecture coverage varies by release.

The supplied update list maps Windows Server 2022 to KB5131090, Server 2019 to KB5131085, and Server 2016 to KB5131291. Windows 11 version 23H2 uses KB5131087, while version 26H1 uses KB5132059. Administrators should check the package for each system rather than applying one update across all releases.

The disclosure follows earlier reporting on Active Directory security feature bypass vulnerabilities and a separate Active Directory Domain Services privilege escalation flaw. These are distinct issues, not evidence of an exploit chain involving the new RCE.

Microsoft also disclosed CVE-2026-105559, an Important Active Directory denial-of-service vulnerability with a 6.5 base score. The supplied advisory describes a network attack requiring low privileges, low complexity, and no user interaction.

Organizations should review both advisories, deploy the applicable official updates, and verify installation across affected systems.

articles.description:

The bug is tracked as CVE-2026-121529 and carries a CVSS score of 9.1. Fortinet published the advisory on November 10, 2026. The issue is […]

The post Critical Fortinet2Shell Vulnerability Enables RCE Attacks in FortiClient with FortiPAM Enabled appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Fortinet has warned about a critical flaw in FortiClient that lets a remote attacker run code on a user’s computer. The attacker only needs the user to visit a malicious website. The bug is tracked as CVE-2026-121529 and carries a CVSS score of 9.1. Fortinet published the advisory on November 10, 2026.

The issue is an origin validation error, classified as CWE-346. Researcher Kevin Joensen from Baldur Security discovered it during internal research and humorously dubbed it “Fortinet2Shell.” He noted that the root cause is a CORS misconfiguration.

CORS, which stands for Cross-Origin Resource Sharing, is a security rule browsers use to determine which websites can interact with other services. In this context, the settings are too permissive. As a result, a web page controlled by an attacker can send requests to a local service running on a victim’s machine, causing that service to execute code provided by the attacker.

Fortinet categorizes the issue under the API component and rates it as unauthenticated, meaning that an attacker does not need to log in. According to the CVSS vector, the victim must take a single action, such as opening a compromised page. This is the reason why the score is 9.1 rather than higher.

Critical Fortinet2Shell Vulnerability

Joensen confirmed reliable code execution, with the flaw affecting FortiClient Mac, Windows, and Windows PAM, while the 8.0 branch and FortiClient Mac 7.2 remain unaffected.

The affected builds are:

  • FortiClient Mac 7.4.0 through 7.4.7
  • FortiClient Windows 7.4.0 through 7.4.7
  • FortiClient Windows 7.2.0 through 7.2.14
  • FortiClient Windows PAM 7.4.0 through 7.4.7
  • FortiClient Windows PAM 7.2.0 through 7.2.14

The fix is to upgrade to 7.4.8 or later on the 7.4 branch. On the 7.2 branch, upgrade to 7.2.15 or later. Fortinet says no virtual patch exists, so updating the software is the only real fix.

Joensen says checking the version is the first step. On Windows, two more signs may point to a vulnerable setup. One is a service listening on TCP port 9191.

The other is a running FortiVRS.exe process. Admins can look for both across their fleet. These signs only suggest exposure. They do not show that anyone has attacked the machine.

Fortinet has indicated that this vulnerability is not currently known to be exploited. However, the technical details are now publicly available, and the method of attack is straightforward. Web-based vulnerabilities like this can be easily replicated once the weak point is understood. Teams should take action without delay.

FortiClient is widely used for VPN access and endpoint protection, so many staff laptops run it. FortiPAM is Fortinet’s tool for managing privileged accounts. A bug that lets a website reach code running on a machine with that access could give an attacker a strong first foothold.

Fortinet products have been a frequent target this year. Cyber Security News has covered the critical FortiClient EMS flaw that was exploited in the wild and a public exploit for a FortiSIEM bug. Those cases show how fast attackers move once a fix ships.

Update all FortiClient installations to patched versions, prioritize systems running on port 9191 or containing FortiVRS.exe, warn users against unknown links, and review web filtering rules during patch deployment, as detailed in Fortinet’s advisory.

A new hacking toolkit called GhostFrame gives criminals a single control panel for taking over VMware ESXi servers and the virtual machines that run on them.

Researchers at Recorded Future’s Insikt Group found the framework while tracking a group named TAG-218, whose activity overlaps with Settra ransomware. The tool can also pull Windows passwords out of hosted machines without ever running a program inside them.

The key point is where GhostFrame works. ESXi is a hypervisor, the layer that runs many virtual machines on one physical server. If a criminal controls that layer, they can reach every system on it.

Security tools inside each virtual machine often cannot see what is happening below them. Insikt Group’s report says the framework does not exploit a bug to get in. The operator must already have root access to the ESXi host.

GhostFrame Stays on the Server

The framework has a web panel with two sections, “Sessions” and “Builder.” The builder creates an ESXi implant named vmhostd-core. Once it runs, it copies itself to /opt/vmhostd-core and edits the boot script /etc/rc.local.d/local.sh so it starts again after every reboot.

The script also turns off the ESXi firewall and the execInstalledOnly setting, which normally blocks unsigned programs. It repeats this about every five seconds, so an administrator who turns the protections back on loses them again almost at once.

The implant calls /sbin/auto-backup.sh to save its changes across restarts. It also renames itself vmhostd, which looks like VMware’s real vmware-hostd service, to hide in plain sight.

The implant tries six network ports at the same time to reach its command server: 53, 2222, 3389, 4444, 8443 and 9443. It keeps the first connection that works and drops the rest. If nothing connects within thirty seconds, it waits between five and twelve seconds and tries again. That pattern can show up as six nearly simultaneous connection requests from one ESXi host to one address, which gives defenders a useful clue to hunt for.

After connecting, the implant loads code straight into memory and runs it, so nothing is written to disk. If it cannot get memory for that, it falls back to a plain /bin/sh reverse shell.

GhostFrame lets an operator list virtual machines, change their power state, and create or delete snapshots. It can switch on VNC remote screen access and send the screen view through its own servers to the panel. It can also expose the ESXi HTML Host Client, which is the management website for the hypervisor. A SOCKS5 proxy tool named gfsox lets operators send traffic through the host to reach internal systems that are hidden from the internet.

The credential theft features matter most. A component called sdkmon changes the ESXi service setup and captures the usernames and passwords of later ESXi logins.

GhostFrame also includes VMkatz, an open-source tool. It pulls secrets from VM memory snapshots, virtual disk images, or a scan of every VM on a datastore. The data it can recover includes NTLM hashes, WDigest credentials, Kerberos tickets, SAM and LSA secrets, and NTDS.dit data. In short, a criminal can steal Windows passwords from the outside, with no malware installed in the guest.

Link to Settra Ransomware and VPN Break-Ins

Insikt Group watched TAG-218 servers go after VPN devices in the US and Europe from late August to October 2026. The targets were mostly SonicWall, Palo Alto Networks, and Fortinet products.

Four of those victims later appeared on the Settra leak site. The same servers connected to two GhostFrame command servers and a MeshCentral server used to maintain access. On October 12, 2026, a Fortinet VPN device was seen contacting both GhostFrame and MeshCentral.

Huntress had already tied MeshCentral to Settra. Its report shows the group installing MeshAgent for lasting access, using a vulnerable driver, clearing Windows logs, and blocking recovery. Our earlier coverage of the Settra ransomware and its MeshAgent tricks covers those steps in more detail.

The timing matches the recent abuse of CVE-2026-0257, a flaw in Palo Alto Networks GlobalProtect that lets someone open a VPN session without valid credentials or MFA. Unit 42’s updated guidance says intruders moved from the VPN to the virtualization layer in one case.

They turned off execInstalledOnly and used a custom tool to dump domain controller credentials straight from a virtual disk. That skips security software inside the guest. We reported on how hackers used this Palo Alto VPN flaw to steal credentials from VMware disks, and the GhostFrame findings fit the same pattern. Fixes for the Palo Alto flaw have been out since May 2026.

Start by locking down who can reach ESXi. Allow management access only from trusted systems and look into any unexpected root logins or setting changes. Watch for edits to /etc/rc.local.d/local.sh, new files under /opt, and the repeated firewall and execInstalledOnly changes.

Look at network logs for the burst of six connection attempts to one address. Patch VPN devices quickly and review the earlier reporting on ransomware groups targeting VMware ESXi for more hardening ideas.

Insikt Group does not know if GhostFrame is limited to Settra or how it is shared. Still, it says it is highly likely that other money-driven criminals will use GhostFrame or similar ESXi tools. Treat your hypervisors as high-value systems and give them the same close watch you give domain controllers.

The post Critical Fortinet Flaws Expose FortiManager and FortiAnalyzer to Remote Code Execution Without Login appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Fortinet has disclosed critical security flaws affecting FortiManager, FortiAnalyzer, and FortiOS, including weaknesses that could let attackers execute code without logging in.

Published on November 10, 2026, the disclosures cover management APIs, device communication services, routing, and specific high availability setups. Attack requirements differ, making enabled features and network access central to assessing exposure.

Critical Fortinet Flaws Patched

The highest-rated issue, CVE-2026-126170, carries a CVSS score of 9.8. Tracked as FG-IR-26-219, it involves JSON injection in the JSON-RPC API used by FortiManager and FortiAnalyzer. When the JSON API is enabled, crafted requests could allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code or commands. Systems using the API for automation need close review.

Another critical flaw, CVE-2026-126261, affects FortiManager’s FGFM service. Rated 9.0 and tracked as FG-IR-26-275, the authorization weakness allows attackers who can reach the FGFM port to send crafted packets and potentially execute code. The problem occurs before the registration password is verified, placing the service itself within the attack path.

CVE-2026-126262, tracked as FG-IR-26-276 and rated 9.3, exposes FortiAnalyzer and FortiManager systems with FortiAnalyzer features enabled to SQL injection through OFTP. An attacker does not need to log in, and successful exploitation could lead to code execution. This makes access to the log transfer service an important part of exposure checks.

The disclosures follow the October security releases previously covered in Cyber Security News’ Fortinet patch warning. Fortinet released updates before publishing the detailed advisories, giving customers time to upgrade. However, administrators should not assume that installing one October build resolves every November finding, because fixes vary by vulnerability and software branch.

Fortinet’s FGFM advisory lists FortiManager 8.0.0, 7.6.0 through 7.6.7, 7.4.0 through 7.4.5, and 7.2.0 through 7.2.8 as affected by CVE-2026-126261. Fixed releases are 8.0.1, 7.6.8, 7.4.6, and 7.2.9, respectively. Fortinet marks this issue as not known to have been exploited when published.

CVE-2026-126260, tracked as FG-IR-26-274, adds a separate OFTP risk. Rated 9.0, this pre-authentication server-side request forgery flaw affects FortiAnalyzer and FortiManager with FortiAnalyzer features enabled. It should not be confused with confirmed remote code execution. Its impact involves causing the server to make requests, while the SQL injection issue provides a different attack path.

These weaknesses also show why protecting the browser login page is not enough. FGFM uses TCP port 541, while OFTP uses TCP port 514. Administrative login restrictions do not directly protect those services. Earlier FortiManager compromise reporting showed how access to a central management appliance could expose sensitive information linked to hundreds of managed firewalls.

Routing and Access Controls Also Affected

The broader release includes CVE-2026-126254, a 9.6-rated numeric truncation flaw in FortiOS BGP handling that requires traffic from a configured iBGP neighbor. CVE-2026-126253, rated 9.3, concerns an OSPF authentication bypass that could permit forged routing advertisements. These are routing risks, not interchangeable examples of management server code execution.

CVE-2026-126229, rated 9.1, could allow an authenticated administrator to access other virtual domains, or VDOMs, outside their permitted scope. Separately, CVE-2026-126259 carries a 9.0 rating and allows command execution with super-admin privileges in specific FortiOS setups involving FGSP with standalone configuration synchronization, or affected autoscale configurations. Neither issue should be described as affecting every deployment equally.

Fortinet’s security release guidance urges customers to prioritize exposed systems, back up configurations, and monitor unauthorized changes. For CVE-2026-126170, the 8.0 branch requires particular attention because 8.0.3 was listed as forthcoming. Disabling unused JSON API access with set rpc-permit none reduces exposure while administrators verify the latest advisory and plan the appropriate update.

The post Critical Fortinet Flaws Expose FortiManager and FortiAnalyzer to Remote Code Execution Without Login appeared first on Cyber Security News.

articles.description:
Microsoft has confirmed that hackers are exploiting an Outlook zero-day that can expose Windows authentication information when a user opens a malicious file. Tracked as CVE-2026-124194, the spoofing vulnerability was patched on November 10, 2026. Microsoft marks it “Exploitation Detected” and says it was not publicly disclosed before the update. The flaw carries a CVSS […]

The post Microsoft Confirms Hackers Are Exploiting Outlook 0-Day to Steal Windows Authentication Hashes appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Microsoft has confirmed that hackers are exploiting an Outlook zero-day that can expose Windows authentication information when a user opens a malicious file.

Tracked as CVE-2026-124194, the spoofing vulnerability was patched on November 10, 2026. Microsoft marks it “Exploitation Detected” and says it was not publicly disclosed before the update.

The flaw carries a CVSS score of 6.5 and a Moderate severity rating. However, confirmed attacks make it a patching priority. Microsoft’s Exploitability Index states that “Exploitation Detected” means the company knows of actual exploitation, not just that attackers could develop a working exploit.

Outlook 0-Day Vulnerability

An attacker does not need an account or prior access to the target’s system. Instead, they send a specially crafted message file and convince the recipient to open it in an affected Outlook version. Successful exploitation requires both user interaction and network connectivity.

Opening the file can cause Outlook to connect to a network location controlled by the attacker without showing its usual external-content warning. Microsoft classifies the underlying weakness as CWE-356, where a product’s interface fails to warn users about unsafe actions. The missing warning removes an important chance to stop the connection.

Microsoft explicitly states that the Preview Pane is not an attack vector. Simply previewing a message does not meet the documented exploitation requirements. That separates this flaw from earlier Outlook attacks covered in Cybersecuritynews.com’s report on Russian hackers exploiting Outlook, which involved a different vulnerability requiring no user action.

According to Microsoft’s advisory, successful exploitation discloses the user’s NTLMv2 hash, potentially allowing an attacker to authenticate as that user. This is authentication-data theft, not evidence that the flaw directly runs malicious code. Microsoft rates confidentiality impact as High, with no direct integrity or availability impact.

NTLM-related leaks can support follow-on attacks, depending on the receiving service’s protections. Microsoft’s earlier Outlook investigation documented authentication relay and offline password cracking as possible uses of captured Net-NTLMv2 data.

Cybersecuritynews.com’s coverage of compromised Ubiquiti routers shows how attackers previously used external infrastructure for credential theft. Those historical details do not establish attribution for this new campaign.

Affected Versions

Affected products include Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise and Office LTSC 2021 and 2024, across 32-bit and 64-bit editions. Microsoft lists fixed builds 16.0.14334.21048 for LTSC 2021 and 16.0.17932.21140 for LTSC 2024. Administrators should deploy the applicable Office security updates promptly.

As added protection, Microsoft recommends blocking unnecessary outbound SMB traffic on TCP port 445 to the internet. This limits external SMB exposure but does not replace installing the Outlook fix.

This update addresses 63 critical vulnerabilities, 1,029 […]

The post Microsoft November 2026 Patch Tuesday Fixes 1,093 Vulnerabilities, Including Outlook Zero-Day appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Microsoft has released its November 2026 Patch Tuesday updates, fixing 1,093 newly released vulnerabilities across Windows, Office, SQL Server, SharePoint, Exchange Server, Azure services, and developer tools.

The release includes one actively exploited zero-day in Microsoft Outlook that can leak a user’s NTLMv2 authentication hash to an attacker. This update addresses 63 critical vulnerabilities, 1,029 important issues, and one moderate flaw among the newly released entries.

Note: For our Patch Tuesday coverage, we count only vulnerabilities released by Microsoft on Patch Tuesday itself, excluding fixes issued earlier in the month.

Outlook 0-Day Vulnerability

CVE-2026-124194 is an actively exploited Microsoft Outlook spoofing vulnerability that can expose a user’s NTLMv2 authentication hash. Microsoft rates it Moderate, with a CVSS score of 6.5, and identifies the underlying weakness as missing warnings about unsafe actions, tracked as CWE-356.

According to Microsoft’s advisory, an unauthenticated attacker can send a specially crafted message file and trick the recipient into opening it in Outlook. Opening the file can make Outlook connect to an attacker-controlled network location without showing the usual external-content warning. This connection can disclose authentication information that could be used to impersonate the victim.

Exploitation requires the user to open the malicious file and have network connectivity. The Preview Pane is not an attack vector. Microsoft confirms that attacks have occurred, but the advisory does not identify the attackers, victims, or scale of exploitation.

Affected products include 32-bit and 64-bit editions of Office LTSC 2021, Office LTSC 2024, and Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise. Administrators should prioritize the applicable security updates because exploitation is already underway, despite the Moderate severity rating.

The same release lists CVE-2026-124227 and CVE-2026-124228 as Important-rated Outlook code execution issues, neither of which is marked as exploited.

Critical Windows, Office, and Server Flaws

Of the 63 Critical flaws, 48 are remote code execution bugs, and 15 are elevation of privilege issues. Excel alone has 12 Critical fixes, while Word has four and PowerPoint has one.

Outlook also receives three Critical code execution fixes, tracked as CVE-2026-111309, CVE-2026-110068, and CVE-2026-110043, none of which is marked as exploited.

On the Windows side, Hyper-V has eight Critical privilege escalation flaws, which matter for cloud and virtual server hosts. Message Queuing has five Critical code execution bugs across its core and Queue Manager parts.

Other key server fixes include CVE-2026-113825 in the SMB Server transport driver, CVE-2026-113859 in TCP/IP, CVE-2026-118207 in Exchange Server, and CVE-2026-119958 in LDAP. Microsoft also patched Critical flaws in Schannel, CredSSP, IIS, Print Spooler, Active Directory Domain Services, and Remote Procedure Call Runtime.

Cloud and security products are not left out. Azure OpenAI (CVE-2026-119990) and Azure Managed Grafana (CVE-2026-114160) each received a Critical privilege escalation fix, while Microsoft Defender received a Critical code execution fix tracked as CVE-2026-122194.

Microsoft provides a comprehensive Security Update Guide that outlines all identified vulnerabilities, complete with detailed references and resources for further exploration. This guide serves as a crucial tool for understanding potential security risks and implementing necessary updates to protect systems effectively.

The exploited Outlook flaw deserves early attention despite its Moderate rating. Earlier reporting on the exploited Windows Shell zero-day provides another example of why exploitation status matters alongside severity.

Other Patch Tuesday Updates

  1. Ivanti Patches New Security Flaws Affecting Endpoint Manager, EPMM, Sentry, CSA, and Workspace Manager
  2. Barracuda Confirms Active Exploitation of Email Gateway Flaws Allowing Root Access
  3. SAP Security Patch Day – Critical SAP NetWeaver, Dispatcher and Gateway Vulnerabilities Patched
  4. Progress WS_FTP Server Fixes 7 Security Flaws Allowing Credential Theft, Path Traversal, and Remote Attacks
  5. Apple Fixes 9 Security Vulnerabilities in iOS 27.2.1, Including Bluetooth Pairing and iMessage Flaws
  6. Google Chrome 0-Day Vulnerability in the Wild to Execute Malicious Code Remotely
  7. Notepad++ 8.9.9 Released With Fixes for 6 Vulnerabilities Allowing Plugin Command Execution

The claim remains unverified, and the material does not establish that Toyota’s systems were breached or that files were encrypted. The listing […]

The post BYOD Ransomware Group Allegedly Claims Toyota Data Breach appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
The BYOD ransomware group has allegedly claimed a Toyota data breach, saying it obtained personal information and access involving kiosk devices. A supplied screenshot shows a Toyota listing updated on November 10, 2026.

The claim remains unverified, and the material does not establish that Toyota’s systems were breached or that files were encrypted.

The listing names full names, email addresses, physical addresses, phone numbers, and dates of birth among the allegedly exposed information. It also mentions “Kiosk Devices,” but provides no explanation of their location, purpose, or ownership.

The screenshot does not show how many people, records, or devices may be affected by the alleged incident.

Toyota Data Breach Claim

BYOD says much of the environment was isolated but claims it found remaining access paths. Its wording suggests an alleged way around network restrictions, rather than proof of a specific security flaw. No entry point, stolen account, software weakness, or technical evidence supporting that statement appears in the visible portion of the listing.

The distinction matters because access to one device does not establish access across an entire company. The screenshot does not identify a Toyota business unit, country, dealer, or service provider.

It also does not show whether the claimed kiosk access involved stored records, remote control, or device details alone. These remain important unanswered questions.

Toyota has appeared in earlier breach reporting, including Cyber Security News coverage of a separate 240 GB data leak claim in August 2024. That report concerned ZeroSevenGroup, not BYOD.

It should not be treated as evidence supporting the latest allegation or used to assign an attack method to this listing.

Independent tracking provides some background on the name. Breachsense tracks BYOD as a ransomware group and records activity beginning in October 2026.

However, a tracking entry does not verify every victim claim. The supplied Toyota screenshot is evidence of an allegation, not independent confirmation that the listed information was stolen.

Toyota’s own disclosures show why incidents must be assessed separately. In a May 2023 notice, the company described potential customer information exposure caused by cloud settings.

Toyota said it blocked outside access and introduced ongoing configuration checks. That disclosure described a different incident and offers no confirmation of BYOD’s current claim.

The broader technical issue is checking whether security controls work across connected systems. Cyber Security News has examined cloud misconfiguration detection and fixes, a related concern when reviewing exposed services.

Still, nothing in the BYOD screenshot establishes that a cloud setting caused the alleged Toyota breach. Naming a likely cause now would be speculation.

The visible listing provides no ransom amount, payment deadline, encryption evidence, or clear account of business disruption. It also does not establish whether the information is new, complete, or linked to Toyota directly. Those gaps prevent a reliable estimate of the alleged breach’s size, impact, and relevance to customers or employees.

articles.description:

Disclosed during the November 10, 2026, Security Patch Day, the vulnerabilities carry maximum CVSS scores of 10.0 and affect core components used across business applications. Onapsis Research Labs discovered and reported both […]

The post Hackers Can Exploit SAP PROXYGATE and ICM2SHELL Flaws for Unauthorized Full System Access appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
SAP has released fixes for PROXYGATE and ICM2SHELL, critical security flaws that could let attackers take control of SAP systems without signing in.

Disclosed during the November 10, 2026, Security Patch Day, the vulnerabilities carry maximum CVSS scores of 10.0 and affect core components used across business applications. Onapsis Research Labs discovered and reported both issues.

The flaws allow attackers with network access to run operating system commands under the <sid>adm account, which owns the SAP installation.

This gives them control over the affected SAP environment, though it does not automatically mean root access to the underlying server. Business data, stored credentials, application settings, and system availability could all be at risk.

PROXYGATE Targets SAP Gateway Trust

PROXYGATE, tracked as CVE-2026-89103, affects the SAP Gateway, a component that handles communication between SAP systems and external programs. Unlike problems caused by weak gateway rules, this kernel vulnerability can remain exploitable even when administrators have secured the commonly checked secinfo and reginfo access control lists.

The weakness lies in how the gateway decides whether a request comes from a trusted internal server. When its proxy policy allows the connection, crafted requests can make an outside attacker appear internal. The gateway then accepts requests that its existing rules permit for trusted systems, potentially starting commands chosen by the attacker.

Exposure depends on the less commonly reviewed prxyinfo proxy access list and related settings. A restrictive policy blocks exploitation from untrusted networks, while permissive or missing rules can leave systems exposed.

The affected gateway runs across ABAP, AS Java, dual-stack, and standalone deployments, widening the scope beyond a single application type.

ICM2SHELL Affects Web Traffic Handling

According to the Onapsis ICM2SHELL advisory, the second flaw involves memory corruption in shared SAP kernel code that processes WebSocket traffic. CVE-2026-76964 affects Internet Communication Manager, while CVE-2026-89126 affects SAP Web Dispatcher, including its SAP HANA XS component. Cybersecurity News’s November SAP patch coverage also identifies the critical ICM issue.

Attackers who can reach an affected HTTP or HTTPS port could corrupt process memory, execute commands, or crash the service. WebSocket support is enabled by default, even where organizations do not actively use it.

Some SAP S/4HANA services accept WebSocket connections without authentication, removing the need for stolen credentials or user interaction.

Onapsis reported no observed exploitation of either vulnerability at publication. That does not establish that all environments are safe. Earlier, unrelated SAP attacks show the potential business impact, including the NetWeaver compromise used to deploy Auto-Color malware. Those incidents are separate from PROXYGATE and ICM2SHELL.

The PROXYGATE technical advisory warns that patching alone may not resolve exposure. Most affected kernel releases require the relevant update plus gw/acl_mode_proxy = 1. Administrators must also restrict permissive prxyinfo rules. Unsupported kernels need an upgrade to a maintained, compatible release, and changes must cover every application server.

SAP addresses ICM2SHELL through Security Notes 3778530 and 3778556. Teams should prioritize exposed Web Dispatcher and ICM services, then verify fixes across their SAP estate.

Gateway access should be limited to hosts that need it. Network restrictions reduce exposure, but they do not replace complete patching and required configuration changes.

articles.description:
Railway has revealed how an attacker used AI agents, a build system flaw, and cloud access mistakes to steal customer secrets and generate an estimated $740,000 in unauthorized charges. Its November 10 report describes an attack that crossed several internal systems while engineers worked to close multiple entry points. The findings expand on the earlier […]

The post Railway Reveals How Hackers Used AI Agents to Steal API Keys and Rack Up $740,000 in Charges appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Railway has revealed how an attacker used AI agents, a build system flaw, and cloud access mistakes to steal customer secrets and generate an estimated $740,000 in unauthorized charges. Its November 10 report describes an attack that crossed several internal systems while engineers worked to close multiple entry points.

The findings expand on the earlier Railway security incident disclosure. Up to 1.85% of workspaces, roughly 100,000, could have had environment variables decrypted. This is an upper limit, not a confirmed count of workspaces with stolen keys, because available logs identify affected environments rather than individual secrets.

The first successful exploit occurred at 07:28 UTC on October 20. A previously unknown flaw let the attacker partially escape the build system’s file isolation and read files on its host machine. Those files exposed a credential that build servers used to access internal services and push completed images.

That credential carried more trust than intended. Railway’s Temporal task system accepted it, allowing the attacker to read stored histories from 353 builds, including secrets. Access to cached repository snapshots also exposed Railway’s internal codebase, giving AI agents a map to search for weaknesses and test several routes at once.

Railway said the attacker used models with safety limits removed through an agent framework similar to ARTEX. Engineers detected unusual registry API calls at 13:58 UTC and later replaced the stolen credential. However, the copied codebase helped the attacker find another route after Railway blocked the initial entry point.

Cloud Trust Error Exposed Encrypted Secrets

According to Railway’s detailed incident report, an incorrect OpenID Connect, or OIDC, trust configuration exposed a short-lived cloud credential at 03:26 UTC on October 21. The attacker used it to retrieve internal credentials and an SSH private key, then entered a machine responsible for coordinating customer workloads.

That machine had network access to the production database and another credential able to authorize secret decryption. The attacker retrieved encrypted variables and used Railway’s key management service to decrypt some values. This was credential abuse, not evidence of broken encryption. Database queries specifically searched for AI provider key names.

Railway believes stolen keys reached services that relay or resell AI access, potentially supporting model distillation. However, it has not established whether the intruder operated those services. Wiz’s “Black October” investigation documents the wider credential theft pattern but does not independently attribute the Railway breach.

The stolen data included linked-account tokens for 1,852 users, which Railway reset. Investigators found no Railway account logins using stolen credentials and no evidence of customer database access. The resulting charges reflect LLMjacking attacks, where criminals use stolen credentials to consume paid AI services at victims’ expense. Railway estimated unauthorized spending reached approximately $740,000.

Railway revoked credentials, rebuilt internal systems, and restored builds for every plan by October 22. Its preliminary report outlined immediate recovery steps. Customers should rotate potentially exposed secrets, review provider usage, and report fraudulent charges.

Railway says it is working with providers on refunds and will cover breach-related charges where providers decline reimbursement, rather than leaving affected customers to absorb those losses.

The post Notion Confirms AI Chat Transcripts Exposed in Fireworks AI Breach, Affecting Customer Workspaces appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Notion has confirmed that a security incident at Fireworks AI exposed Notion AI chat transcripts linked to fewer than 1% of its customer workspaces.

Insights, a feature that helps teams understand their AI usage, used the affected conversations. Notion said its own systems were not breached and no other Notion features were affected.

The company has contacted affected customers and provided instructions for reviewing the impacted data securely inside their workspaces.

Customers who have not received a notification have not been identified as affected and need no action right now. However, Notion’s investigation remains open, and it will contact additional customers if it finds further exposure.

Notion AI Chat Transcripts Exposed

Fireworks first alerted Notion on the evening of November 2, 2026, after attackers accessed a small dataset. Notion’s initial review found only synthetic testing data, not customer information.

By the morning of November 3, Notion had disconnected its systems from Fireworks, deleted all data held there, and stopped communication with the provider.

The findings changed on November 6, when Fireworks warned that attackers might have accessed customer data. Notion launched another investigation, and Fireworks confirmed the new dataset on November 8.

That review identified customer chat transcripts processed for Insights, changing the company’s earlier assessment that no customer data was involved.

The disclosure follows the wider Fireworks AI data breach, which involved customer records, datasets, and incomplete model weights. Those broader findings should not be confused with Notion’s confirmed exposure, which concerns Insights chat transcripts.

Notion has not said that every data category affected at Fireworks was also exposed for its customers.

According to Notion’s security advisory, transcripts from the vast majority of affected workspaces were “unattributable.” They lacked labels identifying the author or workspace and did not contain tool call results.

Beyond the conversation text itself, Notion said there was no information linking these chats to users, workspaces, or companies.

That distinction does not mean the conversations were free of sensitive details. Information typed into a chat could still identify a person or business.

Separate coverage of exposed AI chat messages shows why conversation content matters even when the underlying AI model has not been compromised. These incidents have different causes, but both show the privacy risks surrounding stored chats.

Notion used Fireworks for Insights classification jobs and to run open-weight models inside its product. It has disabled Insights during the investigation and stopped serving those models through Fireworks.

Its AI settings documentation confirms that Insights is temporarily paused, with use cases and conversation counts unavailable.

Affected customers should treat the identified transcripts as exposed. Notion recommends changing passwords, API keys, and other credentials pasted into Notion AI during the incident timeframe.

Reviewing the supplied data is important because missing account labels cannot protect secrets written directly into a conversation. Further incident updates are available through Fireworks’ security bulletins.

The post Ivanti Patches New Security Flaws Affecting Endpoint Manager, EPMM, Sentry, CSA, and Workspace Manager appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Ivanti has released security updates for Endpoint Manager, Endpoint Manager Mobile, Sentry, Cloud Services Application, and User Workspace Manager.

The November 2026 disclosures cover flaws that could allow remote code execution, changes to trusted certificates, data exposure, and service disruption. Two critical vulnerabilities in Endpoint Manager and CSA present the highest risks.

Ivanti said it was not aware of customers being exploited through these vulnerabilities before public disclosure. The issues were reported through its responsible disclosure program.

However, the lack of reported attacks does not remove the need to patch, particularly where attackers can reach affected services without logging in.

Multiple Ivanti Security Flaws

The most severe issue, CVE-2026-121653, carries a CVSS score of 9.8. This SQL injection vulnerability affects the Endpoint Manager Core before version 2024 SU8 and allows remote attackers to execute code without authentication. Earlier Endpoint Manager SQL injection flaws also exposed management servers to code execution flaws.

Endpoint Manager also fixes CVE-2026-18128, rated 6.8. Sensitive information travels in cleartext through the agent, allowing an attacker positioned between communicating systems to read and change HTTP traffic.

Both vulnerabilities affect EPM 2024 SU7 and earlier, with fixes available in 2024 SU8 through the Ivanti License System.

CSA’s critical flaw, CVE-2026-121683, scores 9.4 and affects version 5.0.8 only. Missing authentication lets remote attackers add or delete arbitrary trusted EPM Core certificate entries. This is separate from previously reported Ivanti CSA authentication and code execution vulnerabilities, which required different updates.

According to the supplied CSA advisory, version 5.0.8.1 fixes the issue. Versions 5.0.7 and earlier are not affected by this specific flaw.

A dual network interface configuration following Ivanti’s guidance limits exposure to the internal interface and prevents external exploitation, but administrators should still install the update.

The EPMM advisory lists six vulnerabilities. CVE-2026-105425, rated 7.2, allows remote attackers with administrator privileges to execute code through operating system command injection.

The same vulnerability also affects Sentry, making it important for organizations running both products to update each deployment.

Other EPMM issues allow administrators to change Linux kernel settings as root, disable Apache HTTPS services, delete arbitrary files, or expose protected personal information.

These are CVE-2026-105426, CVE-2026-105427, CVE-2026-107404, and CVE-2026-83528. A separate local flaw, CVE-2026-107405, can cause denial of service. Listed fixed releases include 12.11.0.0, 12.10.0.1, and 12.9.0.3.

The Sentry advisory also describes CVE-2026-105669, an argument injection flaw that lets remote administrators execute existing disk binaries. CVE-2026-123179 allows a local authenticated attacker to disrupt service through the Tomcat shutdown listener.

CVE-2026-123181 lets remote administrators create arbitrary files and directories with root privileges. Fixed versions include 11.0.0, 10.8.3, and 10.7.4.

User Workspace Manager addresses CVE-2026-105813, a medium-severity cleartext storage flaw. A local authenticated attacker could retrieve another local user’s session.

Ivanti directs customers to install UWM 2026.4, available through its licensing system, according to the supplied Workspace Manager advisory.

Security teams should prioritize the unauthenticated EPM and CSA vulnerabilities, then schedule the remaining updates based on exposure and access controls.

Ivanti has not supplied vulnerability-specific indicators of compromise because no public exploitation is known. Administrators should confirm installed versions after patching and avoid treating restricted administrative access as a replacement for updates.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Barracuda has confirmed active exploitation of security flaws affecting its Email Security Gateway (ESG), warning that attackers could combine two vulnerabilities to gain root access without logging in. In a November 9, 2026, update issued at 9:00 p.m. EST, the company said exploitation had affected a small number of organizations.

The flaws, tracked as CVE-2026-116606 and CVE-2026-111560, involve an authorization bypass and command injection. Successful exploitation requires access to the appliance’s administrative interface.

This condition makes exposed management pages a key concern, although Barracuda says organizations with interfaces kept off the public internet are less exposed to this attack path.

The confirmation changes the risk picture from the initial November 2 disclosure. Cybersecurity News previously covered the Barracuda security flaws and available patches before the vendor reported active attacks. Barracuda’s latest advisory does not identify the attackers, affected organizations, malware, or the exact number of victims.

Barracuda Email Gateway Flaws

CVE-2026-116606 is a pre-authentication authorization bypass affecting ESG, with a CVSS score of 9.3. On November 5, Barracuda corrected its advisory to clarify that attackers do not need valid credentials.

They must, however, be able to reach the administrative user interface. Network access and authenticated access are therefore separate requirements.

CVE-2026-111560 is a command injection flaw with a CVSS score of 8.6. On its own, it requires administrative access. Combining it with the authorization bypass could remove that login barrier and provide root access to the device.

ESG is the only listed product affected by both vulnerabilities, so the unauthenticated chain should not be assumed to affect every listed product.

According to Barracuda’s updated security advisory, both flaws carry a vendor severity rating of High. Its public guidance confirms the combined root-access risk but does not provide exploit requests or a detailed attack sequence.

This limits what defenders can conclude about the methods used in the observed incidents. ESG customers need patch BNSF-40425 for versions 9.4.017 and later, or BNSF-40430 for earlier versions. The command injection flaw also affects Load Balancer Application Delivery Controller and Web Application Firewall, patched through BNADC-16586.

Message Archiver requires BNMA-32468, WAF Control Center requires BNWF-60060, and Web Security Gateway requires BNYF-24789. These products serve different roles, making accurate device inventories important when checking patch coverage.

For readers reviewing how mail-filtering appliances fit into their defenses, Cybersecurity News’ email security gateway guide explains their role in screening messages and attachments. That protective role makes gateway security an important part of email defense.

Barracuda recommends restricting administrative interfaces to trusted internal networks and applying appropriate network access controls. Customers should verify that the latest firmware and every applicable security patch are installed.

Devices several versions behind may need multiple updates. Install missing patches manually, and enable automatic patching where it is disabled.
