cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A suspicious PDF opens normally. The link inside leads to a CAPTCHA page. Nothing obviously malicious appears, yet the real attack is still several steps away. 

For SOC analysts, cases like this can turn a routine phishing alert into a lengthy investigation. Following redirects, examining network activity, checking related infrastructure, and preparing evidence for escalation all take time. 

AI-assisted malware analysis is changing this workflow. By combining automated attack execution, interactive investigation, threat intelligence, and AI-generated reporting, security teams can reach malicious activity faster and spend more time examining what matters. 

Inside an AI-Assisted Investigation: Following the Full Attack Chain 

One of the biggest challenges in phishing analysis is getting beyond the initial lure. An attachment may contain no executable malware, while the actual threat remains hidden behind several browser interactions. 

A recent ANY.RUN sandbox investigation provides a practical example. 

The analysis started with a PDF hosted on the legitimate acrobat.adobe.com platform. Inside the document, an embedded link led to additional stages of the attack, including a CAPTCHA challenge. 

With ANY.RUN’s AI-assisted Automated Interactivity enabled, the sandbox continued through the chain automatically: 

  1. Opened the PDF hosted on Adobe’s platform. 
  2. Followed the URL embedded in the document. 
  3. Navigated the subsequent browser interactions, including the CAPTCHA. 
  4. Reached the Microsoft OAuth phishing flow and captured the resulting activity. 

The important part is what happens during execution. The sandbox continues recording behavioral and network evidence as the attack progresses, allowing analysts to examine suspicious URLs, connections, and other artifacts rather than relying only on the initial document. 

Automation also doesn’t mean losing control. Analysts can interact with the sandbox at any stage, inspect suspicious behavior, or explore another path without starting a separate investigation. 

This combination is especially useful when a phishing campaign depends on user interaction to reveal its malicious content. 

Uncover hidden attack chains faster with AI-assisted automation that handles complex interactions while keeping your analysts in control. Accelerate Threat Analysis with AI 

Beyond the Initial Alert: Finding Related Threat Infrastructure 

Reaching the phishing page confirms the immediate threat, but it doesn’t tell analysts how many other domains, URLs, or previous investigations may be connected to it. 

That requires threat intelligence correlation. 

ANY.RUN’s new Related Threat Context capability addresses this step by showing related sandbox analyses directly alongside suspicious indicators. Analysts can move from an individual finding to previous investigations without rebuilding the search manually. 

In the OAuth phishing investigation, the capability surfaced more than 70 related analyses. 

One domain, slybee[.]com, provided a useful starting point for deeper research. A pivot into ANY.RUN Threat Intelligence Lookup revealed: 

These findings connected the suspicious infrastructure to activity associated with the SkyW4lker phishing campaign. 

For analysts, the value is in what they can do next. The related indicators provide starting points for checking SIEM logs, EDR telemetry, proxy records, and DNS activity for signs that the same infrastructure has appeared elsewhere in the organization. 

A single phishing investigation can therefore support broader threat hunting and detection engineering, rather than ending with an isolated malicious verdict. 

From Raw Evidence to an Actionable Tier 1 Report 

Once malicious activity is confirmed, analysts still have another task: turning the investigation into something the rest of the SOC can use. 

A sandbox session may contain multiple URLs, network connections, behavioral indicators, and threat classifications. Reviewing this information and documenting the findings can take significant time, particularly when several cases are waiting in the queue. 

ANY.RUN’s SOC-ready Tier 1 report helps with this step by combining technical investigation evidence with two AI-generated components: 

  • AI Summary: Explains the observed behavior, key findings, and potential threat impact. 
  • AI Recommendations: Suggests investigation and response steps based on the evidence, including relevant technical checks and MITRE ATT&CK context where applicable. 

In the OAuth phishing case, analysts can use the generated report to understand the observed authentication-related activity, review supporting indicators, and identify what needs further investigation. 

The report does not replace analyst judgment. Recommendations still need to be checked against the sandbox evidence and the organization’s own security telemetry. 

However, it gives Tier 1 a documented starting point and provides Tier 2 with the information needed to continue an investigation without repeating every initial step. 

From AI-Assisted Investigations to Stronger SOC Detection 

Uncovering a phishing attack is valuable, but the intelligence behind it can help protect against future threats, too.

Malicious URLs, IP addresses, domains, and behavioral indicators collected during sandbox investigations can strengthen detection across an organization’s security infrastructure. 

ANY.RUN connects this intelligence to wider SOC operations through its Threat Intelligence Feeds, which deliver fresh, verified indicators collected from real-world malware and phishing investigations. 

Instead of relying on manual indicator collection, security teams can integrate these feeds into existing SIEM, SOAR, and threat intelligence platforms using STIX/TAXII or API/SDK connections. 

Here’s how this helps SOC teams: 

For analysts, this means fewer manual lookups and more context when investigating suspicious activity. For SOC leaders, it means getting more value from existing security investments, improving detection coverage, and reducing the risk of threats reaching corporate systems unnoticed.  

See How AI-Powered Malware Analysis Improves SOC Efficiency and Reduces Costs 

For SOC leaders, improving security performance while keeping costs under control is a constant challenge.

AI-powered malware analysis offers a practical way to handle more investigations with existing resources, reduce repetitive work, and respond to threats before they turn into costly incidents. 

According to customer results reported by ANY.RUN, improved investigation workflows have delivered measurable benefits: 

The Adobe phishing investigation shows how these capabilities work together: automated interactions expose hidden threats, connected intelligence reveals related attack activity, and AI-generated reports help analysts reach decisions faster. 

For organizations looking to improve SOC performance without continuously expanding their teams, AI-assisted analysis offers a way to make better use of existing security investments while reducing the risk and financial impact of cyberattacks. 

Reduce SOC costs, cut investigation time, and handle more threats without increasing headcount with AI-powered malware analysis. Boost SOC Efficiency with AI

articles.description:
North Korean hackers have renewed efforts to steal drone technology while expanding attacks against software developers and the projects they maintain. Activity tracked between April and September 2026 shows Lazarus returning to European defense targets, while DeceptiveDevelopment used stolen developer credentials to spread malicious code through software supply chains. The campaigns share a familiar starting […]

The post North Korean Hackers Target Drone Technology and Software Supply Chains in New Cyberespionage Campaigns appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
North Korean hackers have renewed efforts to steal drone technology while expanding attacks against software developers and the projects they maintain.

Activity tracked between April and September 2026 shows Lazarus returning to European defense targets, while DeceptiveDevelopment used stolen developer credentials to spread malicious code through software supply chains.

The campaigns share a familiar starting point: a convincing job offer that persuades someone to run attacker-controlled software. Their goals then diverge.

Lazarus seeks access to sensitive defense systems and technical knowledge, while DeceptiveDevelopment turns compromised developer accounts into distribution channels, exposing users who never interacted with the original fake recruiter.

ESET researchers identified updated malware across these operations, including MortPusLoader, LightlessTeaR, OmniStealer, and DEV#POPPER RAT.

Their latest APT Activity Report describes changes in delivery, persistence, and command infrastructure. The findings build on earlier European drone industry attacks, but the latest reporting shows renewed targeting and a broader software distribution risk.

North Korean Hackers Target Drone Technology and Software Supply Chains

Operation DreamJob resumed targeting drone technology and related supply chains around June 2026, following a quiet period after activity documented in October 2025.

ESET observed attacks against defense companies, mainly in Europe, including original equipment manufacturers and important suppliers within the unmanned aircraft systems industry.

In one attack against a Central European defense company, an employee received a password-protected ZIP archive containing a BAE Systems-themed job description. The PDF had an incorrect header, and the archive included a trojanized SumatraPDF viewer specifically built to open it. This made the supplied viewer appear necessary for reading the document.

The approach echoes job themed manufacturing attacks, where a document viewer helped deliver malware under a recruitment pretext.

In the latest campaign, Lazarus replaced previously used WinMerge plugins, tracked as BinMergeLoader, with two trojanized Notepad++ plugins collectively named MortPusLoader. Familiar software remained central to making the malicious files look credible.

The main payload was either ScoringMathTea, also called ForestTiger, or LightlessTeaR, a rewritten version of LightlessCan.

LightlessTeaR implements common Windows commands internally instead of launching them through the command line, reducing visible command execution.

Compromised Roundcube Webmail servers belonging to academic and government institutions in South America supported command-and-control communications.

ESET assesses that access to drone designs and manufacturing knowledge could help North Korea develop its own capabilities. Its earlier drone espionage research connected similar targeting with proprietary information theft.

However, the precise information sought in individual intrusions remains uncertain, and the Ukraine war connection is an assessment rather than proof of direct coordination with Russia.

Developer Compromises Expand Into Software Supply Chains

DeceptiveDevelopment widened its reach by stealing Git credentials, SSH keys, and access tokens after developers ran malicious recruitment tasks.

The attackers then used that access to inject code into public and private repositories, often rewriting commit history to hide changes. Earlier fake job interview challenges explain the recruitment setup behind this expanding threat.

Affected artifacts reached npm, the Go module mirror, Packagist, PyPI, and browser extension marketplaces. Most compromised projects were small utilities maintained by individuals.

ESET said this pattern suggested automated propagation rather than carefully selected targeting: each poisoned project could become another entry point for downstream users.

The group also adopted NullReceiver, a blockchain-based method for locating command servers. A loader checks the latest outgoing transaction from a hardcoded Ethereum wallet and extracts the server IP from the recipient address.

As previously covered in blockchain hidden malware servers, operators can change servers through another transaction without updating the malicious package.

ESET also found this lookup mechanism launched through a hidden VS Code task inside a legitimate developer’s compromised repository.

Payloads included OmniStealer, a cross-platform Python tool targeting credentials, wallets, password managers, and developer secrets. Updated DEV#POPPER RAT versions inserted code into VS Code, Cursor, and Discord to execute whenever those applications started.

The attacker needs no credentials, DAG, or scheduler. The bug is tracked as CVE-2026-68982 and is classified as CWE-306, missing authentication for a critical function. The post Critical Apache Airflow RCE Flaw Allows Attackers to Execute Code Without Authentication appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Apache Airflow has a critical remote code execution flaw that lets anyone with write access to the Celery message broker run code on worker nodes.

The attacker needs no credentials, DAG, or scheduler. The bug is tracked as CVE-2026-68982 and is classified as CWE-306, missing authentication for a critical function. It affects Airflow versions before 3.4.0 that run CeleryExecutor.

Airflow gives a worker three ways to receive instructions. The web UI and REST API require credentials. ExecuteTask messages on the broker carry a signed JWT, and the Execution API validates it through supervise_task() before the task runs. ExecuteCallback messages use the same execute_workload Celery task and the same broker, but nothing validates them.

The execute_workload task deserializes any JSON body into a typed object based only on its declared shape. There is no signature, no HMAC, and no broker-side ACL.

In version 3.2.1, execute_callback_workload() reads the path and kwargs values from the message, calls import_module and getattr, and then runs the callable with the attacker’s arguments.

In 3.3.0, this moved into a forked CallbackSubprocess. It builds an httpx. Client with the token but makes no network call and checks nothing, so the callback still runs first.

Because import_module can reach any module in the worker’s environment, the attacker gets full code execution. A message that names os.system with a shell command is enough.

Critical Apache Airflow RCE Flaw

Researcher Or Sahar of Reflectiz confirmed this on Airflow 3.2.1 and 3.3.0 in Docker Compose labs with a Redis broker and a PostgreSQL backend.

The callback path was built for Deadline Alerts, which run a function when a DAG run misses its deadline. The feature is still marked experimental, but that does not limit exposure.

The execute_workload task and its ExecuteCallback handler register on every CeleryExecutor worker as soon as the Celery provider loads. A deployment does not have to use Deadline Alerts to be vulnerable.

The attack also leaves no trace in Airflow. The proof of concept created zero DagRuns and zero TaskInstances, and /api/v2/dags still returned total_entries as 0. A recorded demo went further and dumped the worker’s hostname and every AIRFLOW__* environment variable, including the Fernet key.

Apache rates the flaw as Important and has not published a CVSS score. Reflectiz scored it 9.8 under CVSS v3.1 with the vector AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H.

Reflectiz also reported that 198 of 211 reachable Redis brokers in Airflow and Celery clusters answered without authentication. The flaw echoes CVE-2020-11981, an earlier case where broker access led to code execution on Airflow 1.10.10 and earlier.

Airflow 3.4.0, released November 6, 2026, fixes the flaw. The worker now redeems a single-use token with the Execution API before any callback runs. Apply the upgrade to the Execution API server and every CeleryExecutor worker. No earlier patched release exists.

Until the upgrade is done, turn on Redis AUTH or a RabbitMQ username and password, and block ports 6379 and 5672 from the internet. Since Airflow’s UI will not show this activity, audit broker traffic and Celery worker process logs for unexpected execute_workload messages.

Exposed Redis servers are a common target. Cyber Security News covered how hackers turned more than 3,500 Redis servers into Monero miners, and also reported on Apache Airflow flaws that expose sensitive data.

articles.title: 10 Best Adversarial Exposure Validation (AEV) Platforms in 2026 [Ranked & Scored]
articles.description:
Adversarial exposure validation (AEV) is the category that happened when breach-and-attack simulation tools and autonomous penetration testing stopped pretending to be different markets: both exist to replace “we believe our controls work” with “we attacked ourselves and here is what happened.” Analysts formalized the merger; buyers feel it as one question which platform proves, continuously […]

The post 10 Best Adversarial Exposure Validation (AEV) Platforms in 2026 [Ranked & Scored] appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Adversarial exposure validation (AEV) is the category that happened when breach-and-attack simulation tools and autonomous penetration testing stopped pretending to be different markets: both exist to replace “we believe our controls work” with “we attacked ourselves and here is what happened.”

Analysts formalized the merger; buyers feel it as one question which platform proves, continuously and safely, what an adversary could actually do in my estate this week?

The distinction that still matters inside the category is evidence class.

Simulation platforms run attacker techniques with safe payloads and grade whether controls caught them; exploitation platforms execute the real thing under guardrails and come back holding domain admin.

Both produce truth; they produce different truths, and this ranking scores ten platforms on proof quality, production safety, continuity, and the remediation payoff that justifies the line item. One exclusion to note: Picus Security is not evaluated in this roundup.

Key Takeaways

  • 1 overall: Pentera — proof-grade findings from real exploitation, safely orchestrated.
  • Podium: Pentera, Cymulate (the broadest usable validation sweep), Horizon3.ai (autonomous pentesting at subscription cadence).
  • Evidence classes: exploitation platforms (Pentera, Horizon3.ai, RidgeBot) return proof; simulation platforms (Cymulate, AttackIQ, SafeBreach, SCYTHE) return coverage mature programs run one of each.
  • 2026 theme: AEV results now feed exposure-management prioritization directly validation as the truth filter on the CTEM pipeline rather than a standalone scorecard.

Quick Capability Check

A fast Yes/No pass before the countdown the five questions that sort the field:

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based evaluation; no lab testing, no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data. Criteria: evidence quality (proof versus coverage, and how defensible either is), production-safety engineering, attack-content currency, continuity (always-on versus episodic), and remediation specificity. Weights: evidence quality 25%, safety engineering 20%, content currency 20%, continuity 20%, remediation payoff 15%.

The 2026 AEV Power Rankings

1. Pentera — Best Proof-Grade Validation

Snapshot: Per-scope licensing | Autonomous real exploitation with guardrails | Credential/AD chain depth

Why it earns #1: Pentera ended the argument simulations sometimes lose: its findings arrive as accomplished facts credentials harvested, relays executed, a domain-admin chain documented hop by hop because the platform ran the actual attack under production guardrails.

That evidence class changes remediation politics permanently; nobody files “we obtained domain admin” under accepted risk.

Continuous scheduling turns the annual pentest’s snapshot into a standing capability. Feeding these exploits into a broader cybersecurity risk assessment program ensures leadership views remediation items through an accurate risk lens.

Pros: Unarguable evidence; AD/credential depth; automation scale; remediation chains mapped.

Cons: Change-control culture must bless live exploitation; scope discipline required.

Bottom line: The platform that returns holding the keys.

2. Cymulate — Best Full-Surface Validation Sweep

Snapshot: Module-based SaaS | Email/web/WAF/endpoint/lateral/exfil modules | Exposure-management convergence

Why it ranks here: Cymulate validates more of the estate per analyst-hour than anything else in the field: safe simulations across the email gateway, web gateway, WAF, endpoint stack, lateral movement, and exfiltration paths, runnable weekly by lean teams and scored in language executives accept without translation.

Its convergence into exposure management makes validation the standing truth layer rather than a quarterly report, aligning smoothly with cloud security posture management (CSPM) tools to uncover underlying misconfigurations.

Pros: Surface breadth; lean-team ergonomics; kill-chain scenarios; exposure integration.

Cons: Proof-class evidence belongs to the exploitation lane.

Bottom line: The widest honest sweep in the category.

3. Horizon3.ai — Best Autonomous Pentest Cadence

Snapshot: Subscription (NodeZero)| Self-service autonomous pentesting | Attack-path proof with fix verification

Why it ranks here: Horizon3.ai’s NodeZero made the real pentest a button: autonomous operations that chain misconfigurations, credentials, and exposures exactly as an operator would, documented with proof, then re-run after remediation to verify the fix actually closed the path.

The verify-the-fix loop attack, fix, re-attack is the discipline annual testing never delivered, making it an essential companion to structured incident response playbooks.

Pros: Self-service autonomy; fix-verification loop; attack-path proof; subscription cadence.

Cons: Same live-exploitation governance conversation as its lane.

Bottom line: The pentest that re-runs itself after you patch.

4. AttackIQ — Best Framework-Anchored Validation

Snapshot: Platform subscription | ATT&CK-aligned scenario library | Flexible delivery tiers

Why it ranks here: AttackIQ anchors validation to the MITRE ATT&CK canon: scenarios mapped tightly to the framework, gap reporting that names precisely which techniques slipped past which control, and delivery options from self-serve to fully managed.

For programs that report coverage to boards and regulators in MITRE ATT&CK framework language, the alignment is the product.

Pros: Framework rigor; detection-gap precision; managed options.

Cons: Framework-first lens rewards mature programs most.

Bottom line: Coverage claims, graded against the canon.

5. SafeBreach — Best Attack-Playbook Arsenal

Snapshot: Platform subscription| Thousands of curated attack methods | Rapid headline-threat coverage

Why it ranks here: SafeBreach competes on arsenal: a playbook corpus curated across a decade, headline ransomware TTPs operationalized within days of disclosure, and a breach studio for teams that compose custom attacks.

Depth of method rewards programs with dedicated owners who exploit it; the library is the ultimate tool for verifying continuous endpoint security management posture.

Pros: Playbook depth; new-threat velocity; customization studio.

Cons: Arsenal breadth needs an owner to exploit it.

Bottom line: The deepest safe-attack library on the board.

6. XM Cyber — Best Modeled-Path Validation

Snapshot: SaaS platform | Continuous attack-path computation | Choke-point remediation math

Why it ranks here: XM Cyber validates by graph rather than payload: continuously computing how an attacker would chain exposures from breach points to crown jewels, then ranking the choke-point fixes that sever the most paths at once.

The remediation economics one fix, fifty paths are the argument, and the always-on model makes drift visible the week it opens, strengthening compliance workflows across data security posture management initiatives.

Pros: Path-chaining insight; choke-point ranking; hybrid/cloud graphing.

Cons: Modeled evidence persuades differently than executed proof.

Bottom line: Validates the routes before anyone walks them.

7. SCYTHE — Best Adversary-Emulation Craft

Snapshot: Platform licensing | Emulation authoring with real, controllable payloads | Purple-team workflow

Why it ranks here: SCYTHE serves the teams who write their own adversaries: emulation plans mapped to named actors, real payloads under operator control, and purple-team workflow that turns each campaign into detection improvements.

It multiplies offensive skill already on staff rather than replacing it the craftsman’s platform in an automation market that works hand-in-hand with threat hunting platforms.

Pros: Campaign authoring; payload control; actor-mapped plans.

Cons: Rewards offensive expertise; not push-button validation.

Bottom line: The red team’s force multiplier.

8. Mandiant Validation — Best Frontline-Intel Content

Snapshot: Platform + intel pairing | Verodin lineage | Breach-floor TTPs as test content

Why it ranks here: Google’s Mandiant Validation answers the content-provenance question no rival can: test your controls against what Mandiant’s responders met on breach floors this quarter.

Actor-specific validation with incident-grade sourcing strongest for estates already inside the Google/Mandiant intelligence orbit, where fresh tradecraft flows straight into test content to evaluate existing managed SIEM services.

Pros: Frontline TTP provenance; actor-specific tests; intel fusion.

Cons: Standalone momentum versus the pure-play leaders.

Bottom line: Validate against last month’s real adversaries.

9. IBM (Randori) — Best Outside-In Attack Pipeline

Snapshot: IBM portfolio packaging | Attacker’s-eye recon into continuous red teaming | Temptation-ranked targeting

Why it ranks here: The Randori lineage runs validation from where attackers start: external reconnaissance ranking your assets by adversary temptation, flowing into continuous automated red teaming against what it found.

The recon-to-attack pipeline remains distinctive inside IBM’s portfolio; packaging and roadmap deserve written confirmation in procurement, especially when integrated with enterprise external attack surface management frameworks.

Pros: Attacker’s-eye targeting; recon-to-attack pipeline; continuous model.

Cons: Portfolio-era packaging clarity.

Bottom line: Validation that begins at the adversary’s start line.

10. Ridge Security — Best Value Autonomous Attacker

Snapshot: Platform licensing (RidgeBot) | Automated exploitation with risk scoring | Accessible economics

Why it ranks here: RidgeBot brings the exploitation class down-market: automated attack and exploitation runs with documented proof, risk-scored findings, and economics that put real validation inside budgets the premium platforms ignore.

Ecosystem gravity trails the leaders; the alternative at this spend is validation theater or nothing, complementing standard deployments of vulnerability scanner software.

Pros: Exploitation-class evidence at value pricing; automation simplicity.

Cons: Content depth and ecosystem versus the anchors.

Bottom line: Real attacks, mid-market invoice.

Buying Advice: Match the Evidence Class to the Audience

The architecture question is who must be convinced. Boards and auditors accept coverage scorecards (simulation class); patch-owner standoffs and budget fights end faster with executed proof (exploitation class) which is why mature programs run one of each: a Cymulate/AttackIQ-class sweep for continuous breadth, and a Pentera/Horizon3-class engine for the arguments worth ending.

Structure the pilot as a remediation test, not a demo: same three control sets for every finalist, graded on failures fixed within thirty days using each platform’s guidance.

Gate exploitation-class tools through change control with scope discipline in writing, measure content velocity against headline threats (days from disclosure to runnable test), and wire results into the exposure-management queue so validated gaps age visibly the half-life of a proven finding is the program’s real KPI.

Your BAS stack and CTEM program decide where these results land; your SIEM detections are what half these tests are actually grading.

Full Comparison Table

FAQs

What are the best adversarial exposure validation platforms in 2026?

Pentera leads on proof-grade exploitation, Cymulate on validation breadth, Horizon3.ai on autonomous pentest cadence, with AttackIQ, SafeBreach, XM Cyber, SCYTHE, Mandiant Validation, IBM’s Randori lineage, and Ridge Security completing the field. Picus Security was excluded from this evaluation.

What is adversarial exposure validation?

The category merging breach-and-attack simulation and autonomous penetration testing: platforms that continuously prove by simulation or real execution what an attacker could accomplish against your actual estate.

Simulation or exploitation — which class do we need?

Simulation runs weekly without governance drama and grades control coverage; exploitation produces unarguable proof but needs change-control blessing. Mature programs run one of each for different audiences.

Is it safe to attack production?

Simulation classes are engineered production-safe; exploitation platforms run real techniques under guardrails and deserve explicit change-control governance, scope discipline, and lab-first trials.

How does AEV relate to CTEM?

AEV is the validation stage of the exposure-management cycle the truth filter that separates exploitable exposure from scanner noise before mobilization, supporting enterprise cloud compliance frameworks.

Verdict

Ten platforms, two evidence classes, one conversion: belief into proof.

Pentera and Horizon3.ai and RidgeBot come back holding credentials, Cymulate and AttackIQ and SafeBreach grade the whole surface safely, XM Cyber ranks the routes, SCYTHE arms the purple team, Mandiant tests against last month’s adversaries, Randori starts where attackers start match the evidence to the audience, pilot on fixes shipped, and let the half-life of proven findings tell you whether the program works.

articles.description:
An Android banking malware campaign is using advertisements inside streaming apps to turn everyday phones into tools for financial theft. Mirax, the malware abuses Accessibility Services to watch screens, capture passwords, intercept verification codes, and let criminals operate banking apps directly on infected devices. Thousands of Android phones belonging to retail banking customers across the […]

The post New Mirax Android Malware Uses Accessibility Services to Remotely Control Phones and Steal Bank Funds appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
An Android banking malware campaign is using advertisements inside streaming apps to turn everyday phones into tools for financial theft.

Mirax, the malware abuses Accessibility Services to watch screens, capture passwords, intercept verification codes, and let criminals operate banking apps directly on infected devices.

Thousands of Android phones belonging to retail banking customers across the Middle East, Türkiye, and Africa were confirmed infected between March and September 2026.

Reported fraud cases point to losses reaching millions of US dollars, although the confirmed figures cover only infections and transactions visible to investigators and affected banks.

Researchers from Group-IB identified the campaign in a technical investigation published November 5, noting sharp increases in activity around Eid and late July.

The operation remained active when the report appeared, with its operators changing application names and infrastructure to complicate detection.

New Mirax Android Malware Uses Accessibility Services

Evidence suggests the infection begins with advertisements or video links inside low-reputation streaming apps available through Google Play. Those links direct users to a separate installer outside the official store.

Similar fake streaming app campaigns have used entertainment offers to persuade victims to install remote-control malware and approve dangerous permissions.

One confirmed Mirax installer pretended to be “TikTok 18+,” an imitation unrelated to TikTok or ByteDance. It retrieved the second-stage payload, which disguised itself as Google Play Services.

Its displayed name substituted a Cyrillic “о” for the Latin letter, making the fraudulent system component harder to distinguish at a glance.

The crucial step is persuading victims to enable Accessibility access. Mirax actively guides users toward granting this permission rather than simply displaying a request.

Once enabled, the malware can observe the interface and perform actions on the victim’s behalf, giving operators an interactive route into banking sessions.

Mirax combines that access with keylogging, SMS interception, notification collection, and screen monitoring. It can capture a phone’s unlock PIN, password, or pattern and replay the stolen secret later.

Operators can therefore unlock unattended devices, open banking apps, add beneficiaries, and initiate transfers while the owner is not watching.

This makes the fraud difficult to separate from legitimate activity. Transactions originate from the customer’s actual phone and banking application, rather than an unfamiliar device.

Earlier reporting on Mirax residential proxy capabilities also described how compromised phones can relay traffic, allowing attackers to use victims’ genuine internet addresses.

Investigators documented international transfers and evidence suggesting mule accounts in India helped move stolen funds.

However, tracing remained ongoing, and the report does not establish the final destination of every payment. Its loss estimate is a confirmed baseline, not a complete accounting of the campaign.

Server-Controlled Targets Complicate Detection and Response

Mirax keeps important attack settings outside its Android installation package. Its command-and-control server supplies banking overlay templates and mappings that determine which installed applications to target.

Those overlays imitate legitimate interfaces to collect credentials, while server-side updates let operators change targets without distributing another malware build.

The campaign targeted more than 20 banking and wallet application packages, alongside some global cryptocurrency exchanges. This configurable approach differs from malware carrying every phishing screen inside its installer.

Related Android banking overlay attacks show how convincing imitation interfaces can turn an apparently normal login into credential theft.

Communication uses two persistent WebSocket channels: one for commands and another for stolen data. An HTTP long-polling fallback provides another communication path.

Operators can remotely change hosts, ports, encryption settings, and polling intervals. DNS-over-HTTPS, enabled by default, also reduces visibility into domain lookups through conventional local DNS monitoring.

The malware hides its launcher icon, randomizes package names, and restores activity through Android broadcast receivers after reboots or application restarts.

It can block uninstall screens and security applications, while black overlays or a fake updating screen conceal malicious activity from the victim.

For banks, Group-IB recommends correlating transaction attempts with Accessibility abuse, screen sharing, and remote-control signals rather than relying on file signatures alone.

Suspicious payments should receive priority review and customer verification. Users should reject unexpected Accessibility requests from entertainment apps and avoid installers promoted through untrusted advertisements.

articles.title: CISA Confirms Hackers are Exploiting SSHole, the OpenSSH Vulnerability
articles.description:
CISA has flagged active exploitation of SSHole, an OpenSSH authentication bypass (CVE-2026-123158) that lets remote attackers access certain Linux accounts without a valid password or SSH key. The OpenSSH flaw affects specific server configurations, carries a CVSS score of 8.1, and was added to CISA’s KEV catalog on November 9, 2026, with a November 12 […]

The post CISA Confirms Hackers are Exploiting SSHole, the OpenSSH Vulnerability appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
CISA has flagged active exploitation of SSHole, an OpenSSH authentication bypass (CVE-2026-123158) that lets remote attackers access certain Linux accounts without a valid password or SSH key.

The OpenSSH flaw affects specific server configurations, carries a CVSS score of 8.1, and was added to CISA’s KEV catalog on November 9, 2026, with a November 12 remediation deadline.

The entry requires forensic triage under Binding Operational Directive 26-04 and lists ransomware use as unknown. Organizations should assess exposed systems and follow vendor guidance.

SSHole affects OpenSSH on Linux when the server uses musl libc, a system software library, and checks passwords without PAM, the Linux authentication framework. Alpine Linux is one affected platform. OpenSSH versions before 10.6p2 need the upstream fix or a patched distribution package.

As explained in Cybersecurity News’s earlier OpenSSH analysis, several conditions must exist together. Password authentication must be enabled, the target account’s stored password field must contain *, and another local account must hold a valid SHA-crypt password hash. Simply running an Alpine container does not establish exposure.

The failure occurs when musl’s crypt() function receives an overly long password. For the affected hashing path, input exceeding 256 bytes can make the function return * as an error marker. OpenSSH may compare that marker with the target account’s stored * and accept the login. The documented trigger range is 257 to 1,024 bytes.

Active Exploitation of OpenSSH SSHole Flaw

Accounts with valid password hashes are not bypassed through this mechanism. The risk concerns accounts whose password fields contain the matching marker, even when administrators intended those accounts to use SSH keys. The official CVE record identifies the underlying problem as a password hash interpretation error.

The supplied SANS Internet Storm Center findings describe deliberate attempts using passwords filled with repeated “A” characters.

Researcher Johannes Ullrich recorded 232 long-password requests on November 5 and 713 on November 6. These totals represent suspicious requests, not confirmed breaches or separate attackers.

Cowrie honeypots record only the first 255 password characters, limiting analysis of longer inputs. Ullrich suspected some logins succeeded, but the supplied account does not confirm successful sessions. CISA’s listing provides the broader exploitation warning.

Administrators should install patched packages and restart sshd. OpenSSH 10.6p2 contains the upstream workaround, while distribution fixes may keep older version banners. Where updates must wait, setting PasswordAuthentication no blocks this path; confirm working key access before changing settings.

Investigation should cover successful password logins to accounts without usable passwords, unexpected privilege changes, and newly added authorized keys.

Earlier SSH honeypot research shows why monitoring must include non-interactive commands after login. Updating closes the flaw, but teams must also check whether attackers already used the affected account to run commands, change files, or establish continued access before the fix was applied.

articles.title: Hackers Exploit IBM Aspera Faspex Vulnerability, Granting Admin Access to Any User
articles.description:
IBM has released a security update for a critical IBM Aspera Faspex vulnerability that lets a signed-in user bypass access checks and gain full administrative privileges. Tracked as CVE-2026-123218, the flaw affects versions 5.0.0 through 5.0.19 and carries a CVSS severity score of 9.8. IBM published its security bulletin on November 7, 2026. The supplied […]

The post Hackers Exploit IBM Aspera Faspex Vulnerability, Granting Admin Access to Any User appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
IBM has released a security update for a critical IBM Aspera Faspex vulnerability that lets a signed-in user bypass access checks and gain full administrative privileges.

Tracked as CVE-2026-123218, the flaw affects versions 5.0.0 through 5.0.19 and carries a CVSS severity score of 9.8. IBM published its security bulletin on November 7, 2026.

The supplied CISA catalog entry lists the vulnerability as exploited, with an addition date of November 9 and a remediation deadline of November 12, 2026. It also marks forensic triage as required and ransomware use as unknown.

However, we could not independently retrieve the specific entry during verification. IBM’s bulletin does not describe attack campaigns, victims, or exploitation methods beyond a specially crafted message.

According to IBM’s security bulletin, an authenticated user can craft a specific message that bypasses user authorization. Successful exploitation gives that user full administrative privileges within Faspex.

The advisory does not identify the affected endpoint, message fields, or exact request needed to trigger the flaw. The weakness falls under CWE-863, or incorrect authorization. In simple terms, the software fails to check whether a user has permission to act.

Logging in proves who someone is, but authorization should still prevent a standard account from performing tasks reserved for administrators.

Hackers Exploit IBM Aspera Faspex Vulnerability

IBM’s published details show an important mismatch. Its description says the attacker must already be an authorized user. At the same time, its CVSS vector includes “PR: N,” which means no prior privileges are required.

Until IBM clarifies this difference, the stated signed-in requirement should guide descriptions of the attack rather than claims that anyone can exploit it without an account.

The published score rates potential effects on data privacy, data integrity, and service availability as high. However, the bulletin does not establish that attackers can execute operating system commands or obtain root access. Full Faspex administration and control of the underlying Linux host are different outcomes.

Cyber Security News previously covered a separate IBM Aspera Shares vulnerability involving sessions that remained valid after password changes. That issue affected another Aspera product and should not be confused with this Faspex authorization bypass.

IBM strongly recommends upgrading affected Linux deployments to Aspera Faspex 5.0.19 PL1. Administrators must then verify that the faspex-core container image reports version 5.0.19 with build identifier “1ce4b13” and “Fix Pack: 1.” Checking only the main version number could miss whether the required fix is installed.

IBM lists no workarounds or alternative mitigations. Teams should follow the patch instructions linked in the bulletin and confirm the running container contains the corrected image. A deployment still showing version 5.0.19 without the required fix-pack details should not be treated as patched.

For defenders following vulnerability news, this case highlights why patch verification matters. Confirming the exact fixed build is essential when vulnerable and corrected releases share the same main version number.

ESET Research disclosed the findings on November 10, 2026, describing attacks against government organizations in Kazakhstan and Romania. The malware copies selected emails while allowing normal delivery to continue, […]

The post Turla Hackers Use Cereal Malware Toolset to Exploit Microsoft Exchange Servers for Email Theft appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Russia-aligned hacking group Turla is using a newly documented malware toolset called Cereal to turn compromised Microsoft Exchange servers into email collection systems and command centers.

ESET Research disclosed the findings on November 10, 2026, describing attacks against government organizations in Kazakhstan and Romania.

The malware copies selected emails while allowing normal delivery to continue, helping the attackers collect sensitive information without causing an obvious service failure.

Turla Hackers Attacking Exchange Servers

Researchers first detected the toolset at a Kazakh government organization on November 28, 2025. After improving their detection rules, they identified another compromised government organization in Romania, where activity dated to December 23, 2025.

In Romania, the attackers configured the malware to identify messages involving NATO and European Union addresses, including nato.int and europa.eu. These filters point to targeted intelligence collection rather than broad, random email theft.

ESET attributed Cereal to Turla with high confidence, citing its use alongside a previously attributed Turla component and similarities to older malware. The group has targeted governments and diplomatic organizations for years.

Earlier Cybersecuritynews.com coverage of Turla’s cooperation with Gamaredon described another route to long-term spying, with Gamaredon providing access before Turla deployed its Kazuar backdoor.

The researchers could not determine how the attackers initially entered either organization. Although the Exchange servers were internet-facing, exploitation of a software flaw remains only a possibility.

The findings do not establish a particular vulnerability, phishing campaign, or stolen account as the entry point. That distinction matters because Cereal describes activity after compromise, not a confirmed new method for breaking into Exchange.

Cereal takes its name from serialization, a process for packaging program data so it can later be rebuilt. Its components use this approach to carry encrypted .NET programs, unpack them, and run them in memory.

CerealLoader is the only component stored as a recognizable, unencrypted .NET file. Other components arrive inside encrypted containers, reducing the amount of readable malware available for investigators to examine on disk.

Exchange Becomes the Command Center

According to ESET’s technical white paper, CerealNeuron serves as a passive backdoor. Instead of regularly contacting an outside command server, it waits for incoming requests on the compromised Exchange server.

Observed paths include /owa/sdds/, /AUTODISCOVER/PROXYSERVICE/, and /MICROSOFT-SERVER-ACTIVESYNC/INTEGRATED/API/. Their resemblance to normal Exchange services helps malicious requests blend into traffic that organizations need for everyday email access.

Requests that pass encryption and integrity checks deliver programs for execution. Invalid requests receive redirects to an Exchange error page. ESET observed no dedicated external command infrastructure and could not identify the operators’ incoming IP addresses.

This does not mean the malware has no network activity. Rather, the victim’s server becomes the reachable control point, removing a separate attacker-controlled server that defenders might otherwise identify and block.

CerealRunner packages individual tasks as encrypted .NET programs. Observed commands retrieved mail through Exchange Web Services, queried Active Directory, checked processes and connections, extracted locally stored credentials, and managed files.

A second backdoor, CerealHermit, reads encrypted commands from disk instead of the network. This use of compromised systems also echoes earlier reporting on Turla’s STOCKSTAY operations, although those attacks involved a different backdoor.

The email collection component, CerealBox, runs inside EdgeTransport.exe, which handles Exchange mail flow. Rather than register a new transport agent, it wraps handlers belonging to existing agents in memory.

Its code examines messages before returning control to the original handlers. Mail delivery continues, while Exchange’s configuration does not show a newly installed agent.

ESET describes this approach to hooking the transport pipeline as previously undocumented in malware. Collection follows specific rules. A message must contain a .doc, .docx, or .pdf attachment and match configured sender, recipient, subject, or attachment-name criteria, while avoiding ignore lists.

Selected messages are compressed, encrypted, and stored on disk. Operators then retrieve and delete the staged files using other Cereal commands.

The design separates continuous email monitoring from later data removal, allowing the attackers to choose when they collect the results.

CerealLoader uses native entry points and VTable Fixups to reach malicious .NET code through execution paths that managed-code inspection can miss. Operators also planted loaders in the .NET native image cache and used DLL search-order hijacking.

Together, these techniques show why checking only transport-agent settings or outbound connections would leave important parts of this intrusion unseen during an investigation of compromised Exchange infrastructure and its surrounding Windows systems.

The post Hackers Exploit Trusted Qubole IAM Roles to Access AWS Accounts and Download Entire S3 Buckets appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Hackers abused trusted Qubole integrations to enter customer AWS accounts, steal secrets, and download data from Amazon S3, sometimes taking entire buckets in one session.

The activity ran from October 14 through October 26, 2026, using IAM credentials from an AWS account associated with Qubole rather than exploiting a software vulnerability.

The attackers relied on permissions customers had granted to the data processing platform. Roles created for legitimate business needs remained accessible even when integrations were no longer active.

The case highlights why cloud identity access management requires regular reviews of both permissions and external trust relationships, not simply checks on whether an integration still works.

Researchers from Wiz.io, working with Sentra and Mandiant, investigated the campaign after Sentra detected suspicious activity across customer environments.

Wiz also identified a malicious bootable Linux image hosted on attacker infrastructure, but could not confirm its deployment or use. Its published technical investigation separates that discovery from the confirmed cloud intrusions.

Hackers Exploit Trusted Qubole IAM Roles

Qubole integrations use cross-account IAM roles to operate inside customer environments. A customer creates a role whose trust policy permits the vendor’s AWS account to assume it, typically with an External ID.

AWS Security Token Service then issues temporary credentials limited to that role’s permissions. The attacker followed this legitimate access path. Initial requests came through Mullvad VPN, followed by activity mainly from an OVH-hosted server.

Every role-assumption request attributed to the attacker included an External ID and succeeded. Most compromised roles were otherwise unused, yet their trust policies continued accepting requests.

After gaining access, the attacker mapped storage, compute, databases, identities, and encryption keys. It inspected Lambda function configurations for environment variables, retrieved Secrets Manager values, and read Systems Manager Parameter Store entries.

These locations can hold credentials that extend access beyond the original integration role. The attacker then used TruffleHog to validate discovered credentials across AWS, Microsoft Entra ID, and Okta.

Similar AWS credential validation techniques have appeared in other cloud intrusions, although Wiz found no established connection between this campaign and previously reported activity. TruffleHog itself is a legitimate security tool.

S3 theft followed a repeatable sequence: list available buckets, enumerate objects, inspect object metadata, and download files.

The attacker appeared opportunistic, reading whichever buckets each role could reach rather than pursuing a clearly defined dataset. In some environments, this meant downloading complete buckets during a single session.

Detection, Containment, and Third-Party Trust Hardening

Wiz recommends reviewing CloudTrail records from October 1, 2026, onward across every account holding a Qubole integration role.

Investigators should correlate role assumptions with source networks, principal identities, and subsequent secret or storage access.

Legitimate Qubole traffic observed during the investigation originated from AWS infrastructure, making unexpected external networks especially useful hunting signals.

Logging coverage matters. CloudTrail management events show role assumptions and bucket listings, but not the object reads responsible for data theft.

Sensitive buckets therefore need S3 data events or server access logs. Separately reported rapid AWS account compromises reinforce the importance of investigating credential abuse before attackers expand access.

If an integration role was abused, revoke its active sessions and rotate every accessible secret, parameter, and credential-bearing Lambda variable.

Credential rotation alone does not invalidate temporary sessions already issued. Remove unused integrations, restrict trusted principals and source networks, and reduce permissions to the resources each vendor actually needs.

External IDs should not be treated as passwords: they appear in plaintext logs and may exist in vendor systems or infrastructure code.

Wiz also reported separate customer-owned key abuse during October 8–11, but could not link it to this campaign. Neither the attacker’s identity nor its plans for stolen data were established.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
New York, USA, November 10th, 2026, CyberNewswire

Meet the rest of OffSec as the company brings its hands-on approach to entire cyber teams.

Kali Linux. OSCP. Try Harder. For 20 years, OffSec has set the standard for the tools security practitioners use, the skills they prove, and the mindset they bring to the work.

This month OffSec is marking its 20th anniversary as a global leader in hands-on cybersecurity training and certifications for individuals and enterprise security teams. 

“Our founders built an incredible brand and an incredible product,” said OffSec CEO Ning Wang. “Our mission has stayed the same. We develop critical thinkers, cyber warriors, and problem solvers who are ready to excel in their jobs under stress. Hands-on is the only way we believe you can effectively train someone.”

Built by the People Who Do the Work

OffSec began in 2006 when cybercrime was becoming big business. OffSec grew out of the security community, founded by practitioners who believed the best way to teach cybersecurity was to share what they’d learned through hands-on experience.

That origin story still shapes how OffSec develops cybersecurity practitioners and teams.

Through hands-on training with real systems, learners build practical skills, strengthen their problem-solving abilities, and gain the confidence to tackle challenges when the obvious approach fails.

The Tools Practitioners Use

BackTrack Linux brought penetration testing tools together in one open-source platform. In 2013, OffSec rebuilt it as Kali Linux, a free environment for penetration testing, research, forensics, and reverse engineering. In 2023, Kali Purple extended it to defenders.

The Standard Practitioners Prove Themselves Against

OSCP earned its reputation as the gold standard in penetration testing certifications because candidates must work through live systems, adapt their approach, and document what they accomplish.

Employers trust it as evidence of real capability. For many practitioners, it is a career-defining milestone.

OSCP+ added a renewable credential in 2024. Now, for a limited time, individual practitioners can save 20% off of Learn One annual subscription.

The Research and Practice They Learn From

In 2009, OffSec launched the Exploit Database, a non-profit, public-service archive of public exploits, proof-of-concept (PoC) code, shellcode, and security papers, which it still maintains as a free resource.

It also acquired the open-source training project VulnHub, offers free labs in Proving Grounds Play, and recently added HackTrack. HackTrack offers live weekly training over a 10-week stretch.

The first round of HackTrack focused on OSCP and was offered free to those with a Learn One or Course and Certification Bundle. A new HackTrack focused on OSAI is set to launch soon. 

Along the way, Try Harder became the security community’s shorthand for the persistence and dedication that a career in cybersecurity demands.

In October 2026 at Singapore International Cyber Week, CEO Wang urged her Women in Cyber keynote audience to do hard things early that build confidence and resilience, noting, “If you don’t struggle through something, you will never become really great at it,” she said. 

The Technology Looks Different. The Challenge Feels Familiar

Attackers now use AI to discover and weaponize vulnerabilities at speeds unimaginable 20 years ago.

The time between a vendor patch and a working exploit continues to shrink. Cybersecurity skills gaps remain a growing challenge.

According to ISC2’s 2025 Cybersecurity Workforce Study, 95% of organizations report at least one skills gap, with 59% describing those gaps as critical or significant, up from 44% in 2024.

These findings reinforce the need to move beyond once-a-year training toward continuous, hands-on skill development, an approach rooted in OffSec’s philosophy since day one.

“Frontier AI models are evolving at unbelievable speed. If you don’t keep up, you won’t be able to do the job,” said CEO Wang. “Certification still assesses capability. But you need to constantly upskill your teams so they are ready to defend your organization. It is simply no longer a nice-to-do. It’s a must-do.”

Meet the Rest of Offsec: Training for the Whole Security Team

OffSec has grown from a specialist offensive security provider into a full cybersecurity learning and workforce development portfolio.

Every course teaches the why, the what, and the how so practitioners learn to think through problems they have never seen.

Through Learn Enterprise, OffSec’s hands-on training platform for enterprise security teams, organizations bring that approach to every member of their security team. The platform includes:

  • 14 certifications from foundational to expert level
  • 125+ customizable learning paths
  • 750+ labs
  • 8,000+ hours of content
  • Framework mapping to NICE, DCWF, SCyWF, ECSF, and more
  • Flexible licenses
  • Workforce leadership reporting

In 2026, OffSec added Live Training, which brings its instructors on site to work with security teams in realistic scenarios. OffSec has provided this training to more than two dozen organizations and hundreds of learners. 

OffSec’s AI Training Priorities

CEO Wang calls AI-era learning OffSec’s top priority. “To fight AI you have to use AI,” said CEO Wang. “Your red team and your blue team both need to be AI literate. Next year, we will release new and updated courses that modernize our training for the AI age.”

Preview OffSec’s Learn Enterprise platform, then request a personalized demo to explore how it can support your team’s training goals at: https://www.offsec.com/business/enterprise-solutions/. 

About OffSec

OffSec (formerly Offensive Security) is the world’s leading provider of high-fidelity cybersecurity training and certifications.

Built on a foundation of excellence, integrity, and the relentless “Try Harder” ethos, OffSec empowers individuals and organizations to outsmart evolving cyber threats through rigorous, hands-on learning.

The post Dark Storm Team Expands DDoS-for-Hire Operations, Demands $5,000 to Stop Alleged Amino Attack appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Dark Storm Team is combining political attack claims with a growing cybercrime business, advertising distributed denial-of-service services and demanding money to stop alleged disruption.

A November 6, 2026, investigation documents its Telegram activity, including a $5,000 cryptocurrency demand linked to the Amino social app. The demand dates to October 2025, rather than a newly confirmed incident.

First observed in late 2023, the group gained attention after claiming responsibility for the March 2025 outage affecting X. Its later posts describe attacks against government websites, banks, airports, and online platforms.

However, the available evidence does not independently confirm every attack, its duration, or the damage claimed.

Researchers from StealthMole identified the commercial operation by tracking Telegram channels, account changes, and messages associated with the persona GLITCH.

Their investigation into Dark Storm describes DDoS services and extortion activity, not a newly identified malware family. That distinction matters because the report does not establish which attack software Dark Storm itself deployed.

Dark Storm Team Expands DDoS-for-Hire Operations, Demands $5,000

On October 19, 2025, GLITCH posted that the alleged DDoS activity against Amino would stop in exchange for $5,000 in cryptocurrency.

A formal attack claim followed on October 22, and the group returned to the target in October 2026. The report does not establish whether Amino paid or independently verify the claimed disruption.

The message shows a move beyond selling attacks to customers: the operator publicly used an alleged attack to pressure a target for payment.

This sits within the market illustrated by the NightmareStresser DDoS service takedown, where customers could purchase disruptive traffic without building their own attack infrastructure.

Dark Storm’s frequently reposted price list offered three hours of DDoS activity for $20, eight hours for $50, one day for $100, one week for $350, and one month for $600.

Cryptocurrency was the only advertised payment method. Promotions included an eight-hour service for $25 in late October 2026.

The catalogue extended beyond DDoS. A June 2026 menu advertised access to social media accounts starting at $250 and website database dumps from $300.

Other advertisements listed database dumping from $50, showing that prices varied between menus. Posts also offered payment card data, CCTV access, and paid channel advertising; these advertisements do not prove successful delivery. GLITCH acted as owner, spokesperson, and sales contact across several accounts.

Researchers linked renamed sales handles through a persistent Telegram user ID, allowing them to follow the commercial operation despite changes in its public presentation. This continuity provides stronger evidence of account relationships than matching display names alone.

Telegram Resilience, Alliances, and Limits of the Evidence

Repeated platform bans did not remove Dark Storm’s presence. Replacement channels appeared throughout 2025 and 2026, while backups and allied communities circulated fresh links. In September 2026, Team1914 helped promote a replacement channel.

The pattern adds detail to earlier reporting on pro-Russian hacktivist group alliances involving Dark Storm and other groups.

The relationship with Team1914 included reciprocal promotion and joint attack claims. Dark Storm also regularly forwarded NoName057(16) posts and adopted its campaign tags.

However, researchers distinguished this amplification from a proven operational partnership. Shared targets, forwarded messages, and overlapping hashtags cannot establish that groups share infrastructure or jointly execute attacks.

GLITCH also appeared in a DDoSia Project chat in October 2026 and identified himself as Dark Storm’s owner. Previous reporting on NoName057(16)’s DDoSia attack tool explains its volunteer-driven model, but that appearance does not demonstrate that Dark Storm used the tool.

The report leaves the group’s underlying attack infrastructure unresolved. Many attack posts relied on Check-Host availability reports. These show whether selected probes can reach a website, not why access failed. Geographic restrictions, unrelated outages, or defensive filtering may produce similar results.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Columbus, Ohio, United States, November 10th, 2026, CyberNewswire

Funding Will Scale Finite State’s Autonomous Platform and International Expansion as Manufacturers Face a Surge of AI-Discovered Flaws and New Global Security Mandates

Finite State, a leader in product security and software supply chain risk management, today announced a $27 million Series C funding round led by private funds managed by The O.H.I.O.

Fund, with participation from CIBC Innovation Banking, Energy Impact Partners, Energize Capital, and National Grid Partners to continue its mission to secure the world’s connected devices.

Finite State’s AI-driven product security platform analyzes the software and firmware inside finished devices, giving manufacturers visibility into the products they build and sell, from vehicles and medical devices to industrial equipment, consumer electronics and critical utility infrastructure.

The platform uncovers both known and zero-day vulnerabilities and guides manufacturers in fixing the exploitable ones before attackers strike, making everyday life safer and more secure.

The new capital will expand Finite State’s already global operations, deepen its presence across key international markets, and accelerate development of the platform’s autonomous capabilities.

These investments will enable more manufacturers around the world to uncover the gap between the software they plan to ship and what actually runs in the finished device, and to continuously identify and mitigate security risks across increasingly complex software supply chains.

The funding comes at a turning point for product security. In October, AI-powered research uncovered critical flaws in some of the world’s most widely used software, including a vulnerability in the PHP programming language that underpins much of the web, in a surge security leaders have dubbed the “Vulnpocalypse.”

AI has shrunk the time it takes to find a flaw and turn it into an attack from weeks to days, and sometimes hours.

Connected devices are especially exposed: a single flaw in a shared open-source component can sit inside millions of shipped products that are hard to inventory and slow to patch.

For manufacturers, the urgent question is no longer whether a vulnerability exists. It is which of their products contain it.

In parallel, regulators worldwide now expect connected products to be secure by design, with security built in and demonstrated before a device ships rather than added after it reaches the market.

The EU Cyber Resilience Act, FDA premarket cybersecurity requirements, UNECE R155 and R156 for vehicles, and IEC 62443 for industrial systems all place the burden of proof on the manufacturer, and the cost of falling short includes blocked market access, recalls, and liability.

Meeting that standard is difficult because modern connected products are assembled, not written from scratch.

A single device can contain open source libraries, third-party components, and legacy code from many suppliers, and what ships in the finished firmware often differs from what the source code and bill of materials describe. Manufacturers cannot secure what they cannot see.

“Every connected product—cars, infusion pumps, toys, OT, baby monitors, your home router—runs on third-party code and components, making inspection and security exceptionally challenging,” said Mike Venerable, Founding Partner, The O.H.I.O. Fund.

“Governments worldwide are imposing new regulatory pressures on manufacturers, recognizing how quickly AI-enabled attackers can exploit vulnerabilities. Finite State is solving an incredibly difficult product and technology security challenge by deploying a platform that has earned the trust of investors and customers. We are delighted to support Finite State through this financing and believe the company will be an important solution for connected device security and supply chain risk mitigation.”

“Moments like this separate the companies built for what’s coming from those still catching up,” said Brittany Blanco, Innovation Banking Director II, CIBC Innovation Banking.

“We’re excited to back a team that saw this shift early and is ready to meet it on a global scale.”

Finite State customers span the world’s critical infrastructure and connected device ecosystem—from national power grids and a U.S. national security research laboratory to global automakers, life-saving medical devices, and the connected hardware running inside homes, hospitals, and factories worldwide.

With the IoT security market projected to reach $80.3 billion by 2031,[1] Finite State’s growing international customer base reflects a challenge that increasingly transcends borders: manufacturers must understand exactly what software is inside their products, whether it can be exploited, and what they need to do about it.

Bruce Lin, Senior Manager, Software Department at JET OPTOELECTRONICS CO., LTD., a Tier 1 supplier of automotive electronics and smart cockpit solutions serving global automakers, said: “The depth of Finite State’s binary and firmware analysis, the insight it yields into what’s in a shipped device and not just the build manifest, the direct and transitive dependency visibility, and audit-ready compliance mapped to the regulations we actually face, are all invaluable.

“Finite State founder and CEO Matt Wyckhouse said: “The Vulnpocalypse isn’t a one-month event. It’s the new baseline. AI-equipped attackers can now find a flaw faster than most manufacturers can figure out which of their products contain it. Governments are rightly advancing regulations to protect the public good, leaving security teams to prove that risks they identify are understood and addressed. Finite State delivers the evidence, intelligence, and automation to protect manufacturers, organizations, and consumers. This Series C round will enable our talented team to both drive the next generation of remarkable platform advances and expand our global reach to safeguard both our customers and theirs.”

Among its latest honors, Finite State was named to the 2026 Inc. 5000, an annual ranking of the fastest-growing private companies in America, and chosen as a finalist in SiliconANGLE’s prestigious 2026 TechForward Awards in the Security category.

 About Finite State

Finite State empowers device OEMs to ship securely while enabling engineering teams to move at the speed of AI, immediately transforming product artifacts into audit-ready assurance through a single automated workflow.

Leveraging deep binary analysis and AI-native execution, the platform unifies code, compiled components, and firmware in minutes—connecting security design with deployed software.

By continuously generating SBOMs, VEX, and signed compliance packages, Finite State enables connected device companies across industries such as medical devices and automotive to meet evolving regulations, including the EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA), and deliver continuous compliance at speed.

Learn more at https://finitestate.io/

The team brings deep experience and a robust statewide network to connect leaders and unlock the state’s most promising opportunities.

In its November 10 warning, the exchange named iOS 26.7.1, 27.0.1, and 27.2 as affected, saying seed phrases, private keys, and login details could be exposed. The company said this is an operating system […]

The post Binance Warns iPhone Users of Major iOS Flaw That May Expose Crypto Wallet, Private Keys appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Binance has warned iPhone users about worse_query, an iOS flaw that could let malicious apps read files belonging to other apps. In its November 10 warning, the exchange named iOS 26.7.1, 27.0.1, and 27.2 as affected, saying seed phrases, private keys, and login details could be exposed.

The company said this is an operating system issue, not a flaw unique to Binance. The warning concerns the boundary that normally keeps each app’s private files separate. If an attacker crosses that boundary, sensitive data stored by wallets and other apps could become accessible.

iOS crypto wallet vulnerability

Researcher forcequitOS published worse_query as a developer proof of concept. Its documentation describes a sandbox escape for iOS 26.0 through 26.7.2 and iOS 27.2. A sandbox is the restricted space that limits what an app can access, including files held by other apps.

The project lists access to application data folders, shared App Group folders, and some system locations. It requires an App Group container, a shared storage area linked to an app. The researcher calls it a proof of concept that “isn’t useful by itself,” rather than a complete theft tool.

Cybersecurity News previously covered iOS sandbox escape fixes that addressed similar failures in app isolation. However, those earlier patches do not establish that worse_query is fixed.

For this flaw, the key concern is whether another app’s readable files contain secrets that should remain protected.

The worse_query research repository documents file access, not confirmed cryptocurrency theft. SlowMist security chief 23pds separately warned that untrusted IPA packages could use this access to expose wallet recovery phrases, keystores, or browser cache data stored without encryption. The flaw does not automatically drain wallets.

That distinction matters. Access to a wallet’s files does not necessarily reveal usable private keys. Risk depends on what the wallet saves and how it protects those records.

Related SparkKitty malware coverage shows another exposure route, where attackers searched phone images for recovery phrases rather than breaking app isolation.

Binance recommends deleting apps from untrusted sources, including sideloaded or manually signed IPA files, and updating iOS and installed apps. Anyone who suspects a breach should move funds to a new wallet created on a clean device and reset active login sessions.

Apple’s security release page lists iOS 27.2.1 and iOS 26.7.3 updates released November 9. However, that listing alone does not confirm a worse_query fix. Users should install official updates without treating an update as proof that previously exposed wallet secrets are safe.

The post SAP Security Patch Day – Critical SAP NetWeaver, Dispatcher and Gateway Vulnerabilities Patched appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
SAP’s November 2026 Security Patch Day brings fixes for critical vulnerabilities across SAP NetWeaver, Web Dispatcher, Gateway, and other business applications.

Released on November 10, the update includes 35 new security notes, four GitHub security advisories, and three updates to earlier notes.

Four vulnerabilities carry the maximum CVSS score of 10.0, making them the leading priorities for security teams. The release addresses memory corruption, missing authentication, broken access control, and code injection flaws.

SAP urges customers to review its security support portal and apply relevant corrections promptly. Administrators should check individual notes for affected components, patch requirements, and deployment instructions.

Among the most serious issues is CVE-2026-76964, a memory corruption vulnerability in SAP NetWeaver AS ABAP’s Internet Communication Manager.

According to the published CVE record, the software does not properly validate certain network input. An attacker without credentials could send crafted traffic, trigger memory corruption, and potentially execute arbitrary code, fully compromising the affected system.

SAP Security Patch Day

SAP Security Note 3778530 addresses this vulnerability. Affected releases include KRNL64UC 7.53 and KERNEL versions 7.53, 7.54, 7.77, 7.93, 9.16, 9.18, and 9.20. Its CVSS vector indicates network access, low attack complexity, and no privilege or user interaction requirement.

Another maximum-severity flaw, CVE-2026-89126, affects SAP Web Dispatcher and is covered by Note 3778556. The memory corruption issue spans several kernel, Web Dispatcher, HDB, and runtime components. CVE-2026-89103 addresses broken access control in SAP Gateway and is covered by Note 3798345.

The fourth 10.0-rated issue, CVE-2026-120017, involves missing authentication in the SAML2 Service Provider within SAP NetWeaver AS ABAP and ABAP Platform.

Note 3849308 covers affected SAP_BASIS releases from selected older versions through 922. All four listed vectors indicate that exploitation requires neither credentials nor user interaction.

Three further critical notes carry scores of 9.9. These cover CVE-2026-109803 in NetWeaver Knowledge Management XML Forms, CVE-2026-76965 in the ABAP Application Server, and CVE-2026-109795 in S4CRM. Their listed vectors require low-level privileges, distinguishing them from the four unauthenticated maximum-severity issues.

SAP also patched cross-site request forgery in Web Dispatcher and Internet Communication Manager, rated 9.6, and an XML external entity vulnerability in BusinessObjects Web Intelligence, rated 9.1.

Developers should also review the GitHub advisories. These include improper JWT signature verification in SAP Cloud SDK for Python versions below 0.63.1, path traversal in its Agent Memory module, and a cross-tenant sandbox takeover issue in SAP/astonish.

The release follows October’s SAP security updates, which also addressed critical code injection and access control weaknesses. Earlier September SAP patches covered additional NetWeaver and cloud risks, reinforcing the need to track successive monthly fixes rather than treat each release separately.

Security teams should match installed component versions against the November notes, prioritize reachable systems affected by critical flaws, and test patches before deploying to production.

The supplied bulletin does not report active exploitation. Severity scores describe technical risk, not evidence that attackers have already compromised vulnerable installations.
