cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
France has blamed Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps for a cyberattack that disrupted refrigeration at around 700 supermarket sites.

During the night of October 11–12, 2026, attackers changed cooling controls remotely, causing major food losses and around 20 fires, according to the Paris prosecutor’s office.

Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot confirmed the attribution on November 9, calling it an attack of “unprecedented scale and unprecedented aggression.”

He said France had summoned Iran’s ambassador and would seek European sanctions against those responsible. The affected retailers included Système U, Intermarché, and E.Leclerc.

Hackers Hijacked Refrigeration Systems

Investigators said the attackers reached refrigeration control systems through web interfaces, targeting equipment from Danfoss, followed by Dixell and Copeland.

Once inside, they started abnormal defrost cycles with no time limit. They also disabled sensor safety alerts that should have warned staff when temperatures exceeded set limits.

Defrosting normally removes ice so cooling equipment can work properly. Keeping that function running helps units maintain safe temperatures.

Earlier Cybersecurity News coverage of the supermarket fridge attacks described how remote changes left retailers checking stock and removing chilled and frozen food that could no longer be sold safely.

The attack therefore combined two harmful actions: changing the physical cooling process and removing warnings about the resulting temperature rise.

That distinction matters because the damage was not limited to stolen information or unavailable software. The compromised controls directly affected food storage and created safety risks inside stores.

According to Franceinfo’s report on the investigation, the judicial inquiry targets the leader of Shahid Kaveh, his two deputies, and others yet to be identified. Prosecutors described Shahid Kaveh as an offensive cyber unit linked to the IRGC’s electronic and cyber center.

France’s Anti-Cybercrime Office and domestic intelligence agency, DGSI, investigated the incident. Prosecutors cited an attack pattern associated with the unit, the use of Farsi, and IP addresses linked to devices in Iran.

The inquiry covers organized computer attacks and dangerous damage, aggravated by allegedly serving a foreign power.

The exact entry method remains publicly unconfirmed. Franceinfo’s technical reporting noted a previously disclosed authentication weakness in Danfoss AK-SM 800A systems, but said it had not established its use in this attack.

Separately, Cybersecurity News documented thousands of exposed Danfoss hosts, but that count does not prove each system was compromised.

Operators should remove control interfaces from public internet access, install supported updates, replace default passwords, and restrict remote maintenance through protected connections.

Recovery also requires checking controller settings, defrost schedules, accounts, and alerts. Restoring connectivity without reviewing those settings could leave harmful changes in place.

French officials have also cautioned against linking every refrigeration incident to this group. ANSSI chief Vincent Strubel said similar attacks affecting French blood service sites had not been attributed to the same attacker.

The post Anthropic Launches Claude Mythos 5.2, Scoring 76.3% on Cybersecurity Benchmark to Identify 0-Day Flaws appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Anthropic has launched Claude Mythos 5.2, its latest AI model for cybersecurity engineering, reporting a 76.3% score on CyScenarioBench.

Released on November 9 alongside Claude Fable 5.2, the model is designed to help security teams find, reproduce, and fix software vulnerabilities. Access remains controlled because those same skills could also help attackers.

The result improves on Mythos 5.1’s 61.7%, a gain of 14.6 percentage points. However, Anthropic notes that each laboratory’s CyScenarioBench scores use different tasks.

That limits direct comparisons with competing models, making the improvement over Anthropic’s earlier release more useful than a simple vendor-by-vendor ranking.

Mythos 5.2 also scored 89.6% on Anthropic’s internal CVE Rediscovery evaluation, compared with 78.3% for Mythos 5.1 and 81.3% for Opus 5.5 without safeguards.

The October 2026 test covered 1,829 published vulnerabilities, giving models project code from before each security fix and asking them to independently locate the underlying flaw.

These results need an important distinction. Rediscovering known vulnerabilities is not the same as finding new zero-day flaws unknown to software developers.

The benchmark measures performance against documented issues, rather than proving a specific success rate for unknown bugs. Anthropic says Mythos 5.2 improves vulnerability discovery, reproduction, and repair, but the launch does not establish a 76.3% zero-day detection rate.

The release follows earlier work with Mythos models on vulnerability research and code scanning. Cybersecurity News previously covered Mythos 5’s integration into Claude Security, which gave enterprise customers access to model-powered findings and suggested fixes without unrestricted access to the model itself. That separation remains central to Anthropic’s rollout.

Anthropic reports in its launch announcement that one security company found other tested frontier models missed one in six confirmed bugs identified by Mythos 5.2. Another tester reported fewer exaggerated severity ratings. These are individual testing results, not proof that the model will avoid false alarms across every codebase.

Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 share the same underlying model, but their safeguards differ. Fable includes stronger restrictions for cybersecurity and biology work, while Mythos supports approved research through verification programs.

Both generate output up to 30% faster than their predecessors, with standard pricing of $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens.

The Cyber Verification Program offers Defense, Red Team, and Specialized Access tiers. Individuals can apply for Defense Access, while higher tiers require organizational approval.

Authorized penetration testing and exploit development fall under Red Team Access. Work for customers requires separate approval, and Anthropic’s usage restrictions continue to apply at every tier.

Enterprise customers can also use Mythos 5.2 through Claude Security without joining the verification program. As covered in Claude Security’s continuous scanning update, the service checks repository changes, tracks fixes, and reopens findings when flaws return.

API and MCP connections help teams move findings into existing development and security workflows. Anthropic’s Claude Security documentation keeps human review central. Teams must review and approve proposed patches, especially for critical systems.

Faster discovery can shorten investigations, but finding a flaw is only the beginning. Security teams still need to validate its impact and test the fix.

articles.title: Hackers Steal GitHub Tokens Through Malicious VS Code Extension That Remained Available for 18 Minutes
articles.description:
A poisoned version of the popular Nx Console extension for Visual Studio Code stayed on the official VS Code Marketplace for only about 18 minutes. That was long enough for some developers to install it and hand over their secrets. The theft led to one of the most serious developer-tool breaches of 2026. The extension […]

The post Hackers Steal GitHub Tokens Through Malicious VS Code Extension That Remained Available for 18 Minutes appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A poisoned version of the popular Nx Console extension for Visual Studio Code stayed on the official VS Code Marketplace for only about 18 minutes.

That was long enough for some developers to install it and hand over their secrets. The theft led to one of the most serious developer-tool breaches of 2026.

The extension has more than 2.2 million installs across versions, so even a short window put many machines at risk. The group behind the campaign, TeamPCP, says it took around 3,800 internal repositories from a single GitHub employee’s device.

GitHub called that figure “directionally consistent” with its own investigation. GitHub also said it found no evidence that customer-owned repositories were affected.

Analysts at BlackFog noted the activity in a new report on how TeamPCP turned developer tools into a route for data theft.

The researchers explain that the Nx Console incident was not a one-off. It was the latest step in a campaign that began months earlier with build systems and security tools.

Hackers Steal GitHub Tokens

TeamPCP first appeared at the end of 2025 and is driven by money. Its Telegram channel launched in November 2025 and had close to 700 members by February 2026.

In March 2026, the group got into Aqua Security’s build systems and hid credential-stealing code inside the Trivy vulnerability scanner.

It then used the stolen credentials to hit other tools, including Checkmarx KICS and LiteLLM. Readers can see how this played out when the LiteLLM package was compromised with a backdoor in two versions.

Two months later, on May 18, 2026, the group moved from build pipelines to individual developers. The poisoned Nx Console version reached the marketplace, and it runs directly on a developer’s own computer.

Anything the developer can reach, the malicious code can reach too. That includes source code, cloud keys, and GitHub tokens.

According to BlackFog, the group follows the same pattern each time. It gets into software that already runs, collects every secret within reach, sends the data out, and then uses it.

In the Trivy case, the stealer searched process memory on GitHub-hosted runners for values marked as secrets. On self-hosted runners, it checked more than 50 paths for SSH keys, cloud credentials, and Kubernetes files.

The legitimate scan could keep running, so victims saw nothing odd. Stolen data was locked with AES-256-CBC and an RSA-4096 public key, packed as tpcp.tar.gz, and sent over HTTPS to a lookalike of Aqua’s real domain.

If that upload failed and a strong enough personal access token was available, the payload could create a repository named tpcp-docs in the victim’s own GitHub account and attach the archive to a release.

That fallback is clever because the traffic then appears to come from the victim’s account. Cyber Security News has already covered how the compromised Nx Console extension was pushed using stolen publishing credentials. The Nx team had its own credentials taken during an earlier incident, which made the poisoned release possible.

Why a Short Window Still Causes Long-Term Damage

The 18-minute figure can sound small, but removing a bad package does not remove the access it already gave away. BlackFog says some stolen tokens were used weeks after the first theft.

Credentials taken in March were seen exploring other victim environments later. Stolen GitHub repositories were also listed for sale at a price of at least $50,000.

The group makes money in several ways. It has posted leaked material through ShellForce, offered credentials and source code for sale, and teamed up with ransomware operators such as Vect.

Hijacked servers were also used for cryptomining and proxies. The wider fallout shows up in the Mini Shai-Hulud npm campaign, which pushed npm to reset publishing tokens that bypass two-factor authentication.

Law enforcement has started to respond. In August 2026, Australian authorities charged two alleged principal members, aged 21 and 23.

The US Department of Justice separately announced an indictment against one of them. These allegations remain unproven. Even so, a recent FBI warning about TeamPCP shows how seriously officials take the threat to developer tools.

For defenders, BlackFog offers practical steps. Review third-party actions before using them and pin the full commit SHA in workflows. Give each CI/CD job only the secrets it needs, and use short-lived credentials through OIDC federation where possible.

Consider delaying extension and package updates on developer machines, and commit lock files. Teams can still apply security fixes quickly, but should know the Nx Console case shows how little time a bad update needs.

Teams should also limit public access to Docker APIs, Kubernetes control planes, Ray dashboards, and Redis servers. They should patch apps that use React Server Components against React2Shell (CVE-2025-55182).

If any indicator below turns up, rotate exposed credentials and check logs for signs that they were used. BlackFog also points to outbound traffic as a place to catch trouble.

Data exfiltration appeared in 96% of the attacks in its first-quarter 2026 ransomware analysis, though that figure covers BlackFog’s dataset and not TeamPCP alone.

articles.title: Hackers Use 1,438 Fake FOFA Accounts to Steal OpenAI and DeepSeek API Keys Across the Internet
articles.description:
A threat actor has built an automated system that registers fake accounts on the FOFA search engine, scans the internet for leaked AI keys, and tests them for free use. The operation relies on 1,438 fake FOFA accounts to find exposed OpenAI and DeepSeek API keys on misconfigured servers. The stolen keys power the attacker’s […]

The post Hackers Use 1,438 Fake FOFA Accounts to Steal OpenAI and DeepSeek API Keys Across the Internet appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A threat actor has built an automated system that registers fake accounts on the FOFA search engine, scans the internet for leaked AI keys, and tests them for free use.

The operation relies on 1,438 fake FOFA accounts to find exposed OpenAI and DeepSeek API keys on misconfigured servers. The stolen keys power the attacker’s own AI tools and scripts.

The tool works like a self-running agent. It creates accounts, searches for weak servers, pulls out keys, and checks how much credit each key still has.

Nobody has to operate it by hand. Exposed secrets are already a common problem, and the 28,000 exposed Git repositories found earlier this year included 123 OpenAI keys.

Analysts at VECERT noted the malicious toolset after recovering files from the attacker’s server. They tracked the case as VECERT-TI-2026-1107-B and linked it to a larger campaign they call Operation Ghost-Campus.

In their report on Medium, they say the actor may be based in China. The same server held scripts that target a Shanghai college, which VECERT covered in earlier findings.

Hackers Use 1,438 Fake FOFA Accounts

FOFA is a search engine that lists internet-facing devices and services. Free users get only a small number of searches, so the attacker needed a way around that limit.

VECERT found that the actor runs a private “catch-all” email system on the domain melocc.cc. Its subdomains, including mail, api, pop, imap and smtp, all point to the same server.

This setup lets a script sign up for FOFA, receive the confirmation email, click the activation link, and finish in seconds. Researchers recovered a file named fofa_accounts.csv and control panel screenshots.

These confirm at least 1,438 unique accounts, along with passwords and login tokens ready for API use. Each account is a basic “Registered User” with zero F-points and only 300 web queries. By rotating through all 1,438 tokens, the attacker spreads the searches across accounts.

That allows tens of thousands of free queries a day. The searches look for exposed .env files, Docker settings and poorly secured Git repositories, which often hold secrets.

Scanners that hunt for these files are not new, and the same tactic appeared in the recent fake AI crawler scans that GreyNoise tracked.

When a scan finds a weak server, the agent uses regular expressions to pull out API keys. For OpenAI, it tests keys that start with “sk-proj-” against api.openai.com. It sorts them into working keys, keys with no balance left (a 429 error), and revoked keys (a 401 error).

For DeepSeek, it matches keys with the pattern sk-[a-f0-9]{32} and also checks the money left in the account. One dashboard showed 8 valuable assets, 16 verified credentials and 3 usable DeepSeek keys, with balances of 50.68, 8.52 and 0.80. Those keys came from servers tied to labibiyat.com and nyisu.com.

What the Attacker Does With the Stolen AI Access

The stolen keys supply free computing power. According to VECERT, they run an interactive web terminal called “Pi — AI Coding Assistant,” built on GoTTY. The same AI access supports other scripts on the attacker’s server.

Victims whose keys are taken may see unexpected bills or drained credits, and logs will show their own key in use, not the attacker’s. A recent jailbroken DeepSeek AI agent case shows how much damage cheap, unlimited model access can enable.

The same server also held tools aimed at the Shanghai Publishing and Printing College. VECERT says the data of 5,132 students at the Fengxian campus was collected, including names, phone numbers, national ID numbers, home addresses and campus card balances.

The scraper reportedly refreshes this data every 48 hours. Bots also fake reading activity every 30 seconds to earn school points, adding 10 points for roughly every 11 minutes.

The campaign shows how AI helps attackers scale up simple tricks. Free accounts, public search engines and basic pattern matching were enough to gather keys from servers around the world.

Other credential theft campaigns follow a similar pattern, such as the GhostAction GitHub account compromise that went after OpenAI and cloud keys. Keep API keys out of .env files, public repositories and web-accessible folders.

Revoke and rotate any key that may have been exposed, then check usage logs for odd spikes or unknown locations. Set spending limits on AI accounts, and watch for traffic to the infrastructure listed below.

articles.title: Malicious Ruby Gem Steals 51 Types of Credentials and Plants Backdoors in AI Coding Tools
articles.description:
A fake Ruby package called strutil-core looked like a harmless text helper. In fact, it ran a credential-stealing worm the moment a developer installed it. The worm also wrote backdoors into the settings of AI coding tools. It could even delete a victim’s home folder if they tried to cancel a stolen GitHub token. The […]

The post Malicious Ruby Gem Steals 51 Types of Credentials and Plants Backdoors in AI Coding Tools appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A fake Ruby package called strutil-core looked like a harmless text helper. In fact, it ran a credential-stealing worm the moment a developer installed it.

The worm also wrote backdoors into the settings of AI coding tools. It could even delete a victim’s home folder if they tried to cancel a stolen GitHub token.

The gem was live on RubyGems for only about five hours. Even so, it shows how quickly attackers are moving toward developer laptops, build servers and the AI assistants that now sit on them.

Version 1.0.0 went up on November 1, 2026 from an account named jamnajiea, and it was clean. Less than two hours later the same account pushed version 1.0.1, which carried a 5.48 MB payload.

A sandbox run recorded reads from 51 credential stores, including AWS, npm, PyPI, Docker, Kubernetes, Claude and Codex files. This detail gave the story its headline number.

Researchers at Socket.dev noted that their AI scanner flagged the file 70 seconds after it was published. They found no public projects that depended on the gem.

They also have not confirmed any victims, and they stress that download counters do not show how many people were infected. RubyGems removed both versions within hours.

Malicious Ruby Gem

The gem described itself as “lightweight string manipulation helpers.” In reality, its Ruby code did only one small job. The danger sat in a native extension script named extconf.rb.

RubyGems runs this file during installation, so nobody has to load the gem in an app for the attack to start. On Linux and macOS, the script downloads the Bun JavaScript runtime and quietly runs the bundled payload.

The theft goes well beyond a few password files. The worm looks for cloud keys, package registry tokens, SSH keys, Kubernetes and Vault secrets, password manager data and crypto wallets.

With AWS keys, it reads Secrets Manager and SSM values across 17 regions. The stolen data is encrypted and sent to paleasbest[.]top. If that fails, the worm creates a public GitHub repository, described as “project-utils,” or falls back to GitLab.

On GitHub Actions runners, the payload also reads secrets straight from process memory, using the same trick seen in the 2025 tj-actions compromise.

It even tries to tamper with the StepSecurity Harden-Runner security agent, though StepSecurity says those attempts fail.

Developers who followed an earlier malicious RubyGems campaign targeting developers will see the same goal here: grab keys from the machines that build and ship software.

The code is also built to spread. It contains routines to republish infected packages to RubyGems, npm and PyPI, and to move through SSH. Socket confirmed these routines exist but saw no successful spread from this gem.

The malware skips systems with Russian, Ukrainian, Belarusian and several other regional language settings. It also leaves a trail of odd file names, such as a systemd service called pkg-runtime.

Backdoors Planted in AI Coding Tools

The second half of the story is the AI angle. The worm searches the home folder for settings files used by AI coding tools, such as settings.json, mcp.json and .aider.conf.yml.

It adds a fake MCP server named workspace-tools that runs the malware with Node. It also adds SessionStart hooks, which run code whenever a coding session opens.

If the worm finds working Git credentials, it pushes the same trick into repositories. It writes files such as .claude/settings.json, .cursor/mcp.json, CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md and a VS Code task that runs when a folder opens.

The generated AGENTS.md even tells coding agents to run a setup script before their first command. So a developer who simply opens an infected repo in an AI tool may start the worm again, depending on that tool’s trust settings.

This fits a wider pattern. Attackers have already used a fake Gemini npm package to reach folders used by Cursor, Claude and other AI tools.

More recently, a malicious Claude Code extension in the Cursor marketplace planted an SSH key on developer machines.cybersecuritynews+1

For persistence, the worm installs a Python backdoor, sync.py. Every hour it checks public GitHub commits for a secret marker, msync-3f7a.

It reads a hidden link from the commit message and runs the script found there, but only if the link carries the attacker’s digital signature.

The nastiest piece is a wiper. When the worm steals a GitHub token, it installs a monitor called net-health-checker. Every 45 seconds, the monitor tests the token.

If GitHub answers with a 401 or 403 error, it runs a command that deletes the user’s home folder. In other words, revoking the token, the usual first response step, triggers the damage.

Socket links this build to the testmetest worm, part of the Miasma family that grew out of the public Shai-Hulud toolkit. The sync.py file is identical to the testmetest version.

the Shai-Hulud source has been public since May 2026, shared code does not prove one operator is behind every copy. This fits the pattern in recent supply chain attacks on developers.socket

Anyone who installed strutil-core 1.0.1 should treat the machine and every reachable credential as compromised. Isolate the host first. Then stop and remove net-health-checker and pkg-runtime before revoking the GitHub token.

Rotate all keys from a clean device and rebuild the host. Developers should also check Gemfile.lock files, CI caches and container images, and remove unknown workspace-tools entries from their AI tool settings.

articles.description:
Progress Software has released its November 2026 WS_FTP Server Service Pack to address security weaknesses that could expose credentials, allow access to restricted files, and let remote attackers disrupt file transfers. The company recommends upgrading Windows installations to WS_FTP Server 2025.0.5, also identified as version 10.0.5. The November 9 advisory supplied for this report describes […]

The post Progress WS_FTP Server Fixes 7 Security Flaws Allowing Credential Theft, Path Traversal, and Remote Attacks appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Progress Software has released its November 2026 WS_FTP Server Service Pack to address security weaknesses that could expose credentials, allow access to restricted files, and let remote attackers disrupt file transfers.

The company recommends upgrading Windows installations to WS_FTP Server 2025.0.5, also identified as version 10.0.5. The November 9 advisory supplied for this report describes five high-severity CVEs. Although the requested headline refers to seven vulnerabilities and path traversal, the supplied details do not establish either claim.

Administrators should use the individual CVE descriptions to understand the risks rather than assume every issue allows the same attack.

CVE-2026-115338, rated 8.1, affects the XFT service when connections use unencrypted HTTP. A network attacker could intercept sensitive information or change requests sent to the service.

Until patching is complete, Progress recommends disabling HTTP, requiring HTTPS, invalidating active sessions, and rotating credentials known to have crossed unencrypted connections.

Another flaw, CVE-2026-115340, carries a 7.1 score and concerns temporary files created during file transfers. These files may contain user credentials and session data. Anyone with access could obtain sensitive information. Progress credits researcher Momen Elmady, known as 0xmatrix, with discovering the issue.

Progress WS_FTP Server Fixes Vulnerabilities

Temporary measures include shortening XFT session timeouts where practical and limiting the Ad Hoc Transfer endpoint to trusted networks when public access is unnecessary. These controls reduce exposure but do not replace the update.

CVE-2026-115341, rated 7.7, affects Thin Client Web Transfer. Weak access restrictions could allow an authenticated FTP user to read files outside their intended scope.

Researcher Mateusz Mieczkowski, known as rexnets, received discovery credit. The advisory describes file disclosure, without explaining a confirmed path traversal mechanism.

CVE-2026-115339 has a 7.5 score and allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to exhaust XFT memory because resource limits are insufficient. Administrators can temporarily lower message-size and array-size limits to the minimum needed for normal transfers, with configuration guidance from Progress support.

The fifth issue, CVE-2026-35189, affects OpenSSL certificate processing and also scores 7.5. A certificate containing many relative certificate revocation list distribution points can trigger excessive memory use and denial of service.

Within WS_FTP Server, this risk applies to affected packages containing OpenSSL 3.5.8 when client-certificate requests are enabled. That setting is turned off by default. Progress says releases 2024.0.8 and 2025.0.5 update OpenSSL to 3.5.9. Customers should not replace the bundled library independently.

The broader file-transfer threat remains relevant. Cybersecurity News previously covered active exploitation of Wing FTP Server, a separate product, and millions of internet-facing FTP servers. Neither report establishes exploitation of these WS_FTP flaws.

Progress recommends version 2025.0.5 to resolve all vulnerabilities listed in the supplied notice. The company says workarounds only reduce exposure and that remediation requires the full installer. Organizations should schedule downtime because the upgrade causes a service outage.

Customers should obtain installers through the Progress Community portal and review the vendor’s upgrade guidance. The public release-notes page retrieved for this report still lists 2025.0.4 as its newest entry, so it does not independently confirm the November fixes.

The supplied notice does not report active exploitation. Its documented risks still make patch planning important, especially where web transfer endpoints are reachable from untrusted networks or credentials may have previously traveled over HTTP.

articles.title: Vanderbilt University Shuts Down Campus Devices After BYOD Ransomware Group Claims Network Breach
articles.description:
Vanderbilt University told students, faculty, and staff to shut down university devices and disconnect from campus Wi-Fi on November 9, 2026, while its IT team investigated an active cybersecurity incident. The warning came as the BYOD ransomware group claimed it had locked university databases and stolen sensitive student, employee, and research data. Vanderbilt has not […]

The post Vanderbilt University Shuts Down Campus Devices After BYOD Ransomware Group Claims Network Breach appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Vanderbilt University told students, faculty, and staff to shut down university devices and disconnect from campus Wi-Fi on November 9, 2026, while its IT team investigated an active cybersecurity incident.

The warning came as the BYOD ransomware group claimed it had locked university databases and stolen sensitive student, employee, and research data. Vanderbilt has not confirmed the group’s involvement or its data theft claims.

The Nashville university said the incident could affect devices, internal systems, and cloud services. In its official incident update, Vanderbilt urged users to watch for unexpected pop-ups, missing files, unfamiliar applications, and unusual requests for passwords or login approvals. Its IT team began investigating and working to contain the incident.

BYOD posted a message on its data leak site claiming possession of more than one million Social Security numbers, along with names, email addresses, phone numbers, and student and employee records.

The attackers also claimed access to university research data and control of its domain controller. These claims remain unverified, and Vanderbilt has not announced a confirmed number of affected people.

The note linked to BYOD’s leak site and provided contact details through the Session messaging platform. It claimed that backups were compromised and threatened to release data and cause further disruption unless the university negotiated.

Vanderbilt University Shuts Down Devices After Breach Claim

Local reporting also described files changing to the “.byod” extension and university research becoming inaccessible. Those accounts suggest file encryption, but they do not establish how widely systems were affected.

Vanderbilt has not publicly identified the attackers’ entry point, confirmed which systems were encrypted, or explained whether stolen accounts or a software flaw enabled access.

By 7:15 p.m. on November 9, Vanderbilt said campus Wi-Fi was available again. However, access to most university systems and applications remained restricted.

Its IT team was working with government agencies and other partners. The university planned to operate normally on November 10, with classes, student services, and staff attendance continuing as scheduled.

Faculty facing grant deadlines were directed to seek support from the university’s research office. Students were told to contact instructors about additional guidance and flexibility on coursework deadlines. The update showed that network access had partly returned, while important university applications remained unavailable.

BYOD previously appeared in reporting about an alleged Trump Mobile data breach. Separately, the Stanford University ransomware breach shows how campus incidents can expose sensitive records. Neither report establishes how Vanderbilt was breached.

Vanderbilt instructed anyone seeing suspicious activity not to click links, open attachments, or attempt repairs. Users should shut down the affected device and contact the IT service desk from another device or by phone.

The university’s public notice leaves key questions unanswered, including the full scope of any encryption, whether personal records were stolen, and when restricted systems will return to service.

Apple released iOS 27.2.1 and iPadOS 27.2.1 on November 9, 2026. The update fixes nine security flaws in Bluetooth, AirPlay, Messages, and other parts of the system. It runs on iPhone 11 and later, and on several recent iPad models, including iPad Pro, iPad Air, iPad 9th generation, and iPad mini 6th generation. Apple’s security […]

The post Apple Fixes 9 Security Vulnerabilities in iOS 27.2.1, Including Bluetooth Pairing and iMessage Flaws appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Apple released iOS 27.2.1 and iPadOS 27.2.1 on November 9, 2026. The update fixes nine security flaws in Bluetooth, AirPlay, Messages, and other parts of the system.

It runs on iPhone 11 and later, and on several recent iPad models, including iPad Pro, iPad Air, iPad 9th generation, and iPad mini 6th generation. Apple’s security release page lists the update. Apple does not say any of these flaws were used in real attacks.

Most fixes address how devices pair with each other. Two bugs let someone get around the limit on pairing code guesses. Normally, a device blocks a person who keeps guessing wrong codes. If that limit fails, someone nearby could keep trying until a guess works.

The first, CVE-2026-113964, sits in CoreUtils. Apple says someone in Bluetooth range could skip the limit and pair with a device without the owner doing anything.

An anonymous researcher reported it. A second CoreUtils bug, CVE-2026-113965, could let a malicious Bluetooth device pair on its own, with no user action. Apple found that one itself.

Two more bugs affect AirPlay pairing codes. CVE-2026-113968 lets someone within Bluetooth range bypass the AirPlay limit. CVE-2026-113969 sits in rapportd and lets a person on the same network do the same. Both were fixed by improving how the system tracks its state.

Apple Fixes 9 Security Vulnerabilities

Bluetooth also had a memory bug. CVE-2026-113970 is a use-after-free flaw, which means the system keeps using memory after it has been released. Someone within Bluetooth range could use it to corrupt process memory. Apple fixed it with better memory handling.

The Messages app got two fixes, both reported by anonymous researchers. CVE-2026-113961 could let a remote person join an iMessage group chat and read its messages.

Apple fixed it by adding stronger checks on who can join. CVE-2026-113960 let a person added to a group read messages sent before they joined. Apple removed the code behind that flaw.

iMessage group chats can expose private conversations when access controls fail, although earlier flaws were more severe, including the NICKNAME zero-click exploit used against high-profile targets and fixed in iOS 18.3.

CVE-2026-113963 in App Intents could let an app access sensitive user data. László Várady reported it, and Apple fixed it by adding stronger authorization checks.

CVE-2026-111497 sits in brotli, a data compression tool. A specially crafted file could trigger an out-of-bounds write, meaning data lands outside its intended memory space. That can lead to memory corruption. Apple fixed it with better input checks and did not name a reporter.

Open Settings, tap General, then Software Update, and install iOS 27.2.1 or iPadOS 27.2.1. Apple notes that you can’t roll back an update once it is installed. Turning off Bluetooth and AirPlay when you do not need them also reduces your exposure.

Pairing flaws remind us that attackers don’t always need malware to get in. Sometimes they only need enough guesses. The AirPlay fixes also follow a rough year for the protocol.

Cyber Security News reported on the AirBorne AirPlay flaws, which put billions of devices at risk. Apple tracks each issue by its CVE ID, a shared number system explained on the CVE Program site. Anyone who finds an Apple bug can report it through Apple Product Security.

articles.title: SEGA Confirms Data Breach After Third-Party Email Provider Exposes 2.19 Million Customer Email Addresses
articles.description:

The company disclosed the breach on November 9, 2026, saying the affected records related to promotional emails for SEGA and its group company, SEGA Fave. The SEGA data breach also exposed information linked […]

The post SEGA Confirms Data Breach After Third-Party Email Provider Exposes 2.19 Million Customer Email Addresses appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
SEGA confirmed that attackers exposed 2,196,044 email addresses after gaining unauthorized access to Arara Message, a third-party service used to send newsletters.

The company disclosed the breach on November 9, 2026, saying the affected records related to promotional emails for SEGA and its group company, SEGA Fave.

The SEGA data breach also exposed information linked to newsletter delivery for 92,273 email addresses. SEGA is still checking what those additional details contained. The total represents email addresses, not a confirmed count of individual customers.

According to SEGA’s notice, the leaked data did not include customer names, birth dates, gender, home addresses, phone numbers, credit card details, or login passwords. The company said it had not confirmed any misuse of the exposed information.

Email addresses registered with SEGA Account were not included because that service uses a different email distribution system. This separates the newsletter breach from SEGA’s account platform and avoids suggesting that customer login records were stolen.

The affected newsletters were sent between July 2 and October 28, 2026. They covered CHUNITHM Mate, Ongeki Re: Fresh Act.2, maimai Deluxe MAGiCAL, Sega Lucky Draw, and Tokyo Game Show 2026 announcements.

SEGA contacted Arara on October 29 during a security review and initially received a response stating that no information leak had been confirmed. After Arara’s November 1 announcement, SEGA conducted further checks.

SEGA Confirms Data Breach

Arara notified SEGA on November 3 that email addresses used for its newsletters had leaked. Additional checks between November 5 and November 8 led to an official report.

In its incident update, Arara said attackers exploited a web server vulnerability. It also corrected an earlier timeline, confirming that data theft continued from October 28 until the service was stopped on October 31. That timeline covers the provider’s incident, not a separately confirmed window for SEGA’s records.

The case highlights the risks of storing customer information with outside providers. Similar trust issues feature in Cybersecuritynews.com’s coverage of the EY third-party data breach, where client information was exposed through a service provider’s platform.

SEGA warned that criminals could use the leaked addresses to send messages pretending to represent SEGA, SEGA Fave, Arara, or their products. No such misuse has been confirmed.

Email marketing services can be used for impersonation, as shown in previous MailChimp account abuse. That reporting does not establish a connection to this breach.

Customers should avoid unexpected links and attachments. SEGA said neither it nor SEGA Fave requests passwords or credit card information by email.

SEGA has suspended newsletters sent through Arara pending security checks, plans to file a joint report with Japan’s Personal Information Protection Commission, and will contact affected customers once details are confirmed. Arara’s response notice provides further information.

SEGA also clarified that maintenance affecting Sega Lucky Draw Online follows a separate incident involving SEGA Fave’s arcade network servers. The two events should not be treated as one confirmed breach.

articles.description:
CRQ translates security’s native language severities, maturity tiers, heat maps into the only dialect budgets understand: expected dollars. The 2026 field splits between FAIR-methodology heirs, telemetry-grounded engines that quantify from live estate data, and ratings-lineage platforms monetizing their scoring graphs. The post Top 9 Best Cyber Risk Quantification (CRQ) Tools in 2026 [Ranked & Scored] appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
CRQ translates security’s native language severities, maturity tiers, heat maps into the only dialect budgets understand: expected dollars.

The 2026 field splits between FAIR-methodology heirs, telemetry-grounded engines that quantify from live estate data, and ratings-lineage platforms monetizing their scoring graphs.

One honest count note: our source sheet listed BitSight twice, so we rank nine platforms rather than inflate the field. Safe Security takes 1; BitSight and Balbix complete the podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: Safe Security the FAIR lineage (RiskLens acquisition) fused with live-telemetry quantification.

• Podium: Safe Security (methodology+telemetry), BitSight (ratings-data breadth), Balbix (asset-grounded exposure dollars).

• Honest count: nine, not ten one sheet duplicate (BitSight) consolidated.

• 2026 theme: CRQ left the slide deck insurers, regulators (SEC materiality), and CFOs now consume quantified outputs, so model defensibility matters more than dashboard polish.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based evaluation; no lab testing, no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data.

Criteria: model rigor/defensibility (FAIR alignment, transparent assumptions), data grounding (live telemetry versus questionnaire), decision output quality (board/insurance/materiality use), scenario breadth, integration reach, and accessibility.

Weights: model rigor 25%, data grounding 25%, decision outputs 20%, scenario breadth 15%, integration 15%.

The 2026 CRQ Power Rankings

*Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

1. Safe Security (RiskLens) — Best FAIR-Plus-Telemetry Quantification

Snapshot: Platform subscription | FAIR Institute lineage via RiskLens | Live-signal risk updates

Why it earns 1: Safe Security owns both halves of CRQ’s argument: the RiskLens acquisition brought the canonical FAIR methodology
the open, defensible model regulators and boards can interrogate while SAFE’s telemetry engine grounds loss-event probabilities in live control signals rather than annual questionnaires.

Dollar figures that update when your posture does, on a methodology you can defend in a filing.

Pros: FAIR canon custody; telemetry grounding; materiality-grade defensibility.

Cons: Program maturity required to exploit the depth.

Bottom line: The methodology and the live data, finally in one place.

2. BitSight — Best Ratings-Data-Grounded CRQ

Snapshot: Module atop ratings platform | Decade of external-telemetry loss correlation | Financial quantification module

Why it ranks here: BitSight quantifies from what it has watched for a decade: externally observable security signals across hundreds of thousands of organizations, correlated against real incident history an empirical base most CRQ models envy.

Its quantification module converts that graph into financial exposure, strongest for portfolio, vendor, and insurance lenses where outside-in data is the honest view. (Sheet listed it twice; counted once.)

Pros: Empirical correlation base; portfolio/TPRM lens; insurer currency.

Cons: Outside-in grounding internal control depth needs supplementing.

Bottom line: Quantification backed by the biggest observational dataset in the field.

3. CYE — Best Attack-Path-Driven Financial Exposure

Snapshot: Platform subscription | Attack-path analysis → business impact → financial exposure | Risk-based remediation prioritization

Why it ranks here: CYE connects technical exposure with business impact, using attack-path analysis and risk modeling to show how weaknesses could translate into financial loss.

It helps security teams prioritize remediation based on measurable risk reduction rather than vulnerability severity alone, giving executives a clearer view of where security investment produces the greatest financial benefit.

Pros: Attack-path visibility; financial risk modeling; remediation prioritization; business-impact context.

Cons: Value depends on accurate environment and exposure data; enterprise deployment can require integration effort.

Bottom line: Financial exposure mapped directly to the attack paths that matter most.

4. CyberCube — Best Insurance-Grade Cyber Risk Modeling

Snapshot: Subscription platform | Probabilistic cyber-loss modeling | Insurance, portfolio, and scenario analytics

Why it ranks here: CyberCube brings insurance-grade modeling to cyber risk quantification, using probabilistic scenarios and loss analytics to estimate the financial consequences of cyber events across individual organizations and portfolios.

Its strength is translating technical cyber exposure into loss distributions and decision-ready financial metrics that insurers, brokers, reinsurers, and enterprise risk teams can use for coverage and capital decisions.

Pros: Insurance-grade modeling; probabilistic loss analysis; strong scenario analytics; portfolio-level risk visibility.

Cons: More insurance and portfolio oriented than operational remediation platforms; less focused on asset-level exposure management.

Bottom line: Cyber risk modeled with the financial discipline of the insurance industry.

5. Kovrr — Best Cat-Model-Grade Cyber Quantification

Snapshot: Platform subscription | Catastrophe-modeling heritage | On-demand financial quantification

Why it ranks here: Kovrr brought insurance catastrophe-modeling discipline to enterprise CRQ: frequency/severity modeling built on incident and exposure datasets insurers price with, delivered as on-demand quantifications mapped to frameworks (including materiality assessments for disclosure decisions). Model-first rigor with growing enterprise ergonomics.

Pros: Cat-model rigor; insurer-grade datasets; materiality outputs.

Cons: Brand gravity in enterprise CISO market still building.

Bottom line: The actuarial engine, enterprise-packaged.

6. CyberSaint — Best Compliance-Integrated CRQ

Snapshot: Platform subscription | CyberStrong: controls/compliance + FAIR-based dollars | NIST-mapped automation

Why it ranks here: CyberSaint fuses the compliance posture you already maintain with quantification: control assessments (NIST CSF and kin) feeding FAIR-based loss models, so the same data that answers auditors prices risk.

For programs that live framework-first, it removes CRQ’s double-entry problem one posture dataset, two outputs.

Pros: Compliance-data reuse; framework automation; accessible on-ramp.

Cons: Telemetry-grounding depth versus the live-signal leaders.

Bottom line: Your compliance posture, denominated in dollars.

7. Black Kite — Best Threat-Informed Third-Party CRQ

Snapshot: Platform subscription | Open FAIR-based financial quantification | Threat intelligence + third-party exposure data

Why it ranks here: Black Kite combines third-party cyber risk monitoring with financial risk quantification connecting ransomware activity, vulnerabilities, external exposure, and threat intelligence to probable financial loss.

Its strength is showing organizations which vendors and suppliers represent the greatest financial cyber risk, helping teams prioritize third-party remediation and risk-transfer decisions using threat-informed context.

Pros: Third-party risk depth; FAIR-based quantification; live threat intelligence; financial impact modeling.

Cons: Strongest in external and third-party risk; less suited to deep internal asset-level remediation modeling.

Bottom line: Third-party cyber exposure translated into financial risk with live threat context.

8. X-Analytics — Best Economics-Model Simplicity

Snapshot: Subscription/advisory channels | Patented condition-based economic model | Board/insurer report orientation

Why it ranks here: X-Analytics compresses CRQ into decision-grade simplicity: a condition-based economic model producing exposure, impact-by-category, and improvement-ROI outputs boards digest in one sitting, distributed heavily through advisory and insurance channels.

Less knobs than FAIR shops deliberately which is exactly its fit for programs wanting answers before analysts.

Pros: Decision-speed simplicity; board-report polish; channel reach.

Cons: Model transparency/tunability versus FAIR-canon rivals.

Bottom line: CRQ for boards that want the number, not the seminar.

9. Squalify — Best Insurer-Lineage European CRQ

Snapshot: SaaS subscription | Munich Re-lineage loss data | Top-down quantification for leadership

Why it ranks here: Squalify carries reinsurance DNA loss modeling grounded in Munich Re-lineage cyber claims data into a top-down CRQ product for European enterprises: exposure by loss category, steering decisions for leadership, sovereignty-comfortable delivery.

A young entrant ranked honestly: distinctive data lineage, building ecosystem.

Pros: Reinsurance-grade loss data; European posture; leadership-level outputs.

Cons: Early-stage breadth; integration ecosystem growing.

Bottom line: The reinsurer’s loss tables, productized for the C-suite.

Full Comparison Table

Yes/No Capability Table

Buying Advice: Interrogate the Priors, Then Automate the Pipeline

CRQ’s credibility lives in its assumptions, so procurement starts as peer review: make each vendor decompose one scenario end-to-end where frequency priors come from, how your controls move the severity curve, what the confidence interval honestly is and discard any platform whose answer is “proprietary model” without decomposition.

Ground-truth against your own history: feed finalists two incidents you actually experienced and compare modeled-versus-actual loss; calibration beats precision theater.

Then weight data grounding by decision cadence annual insurance-limit decisions tolerate questionnaire-based models (Axio, Kovrr, X-Analytics lanes), while quarterly budget steering wants live-signal platforms (Safe, Balbix, BitSight).

Wire outputs where decisions happen (board packs, insurance renewals, the exposure-management queue for ROI-ranked fixes), keep the FAIR-portability test in mind as exit insurance, and publish one number consistently expected annual loss with its interval, trending across quarters because a CRQ figure the CFO sees once is a demo, and the same figure tracked for six quarters is a governance instrument.

The honest count here (nine, one sheet duplicate consolidated) is its own lesson: in a category selling rigor, inflation anywhere undermines everything.

FAQs

What are the best cyber risk quantification tools in 2026? Safe Security (with RiskLens’ FAIR lineage) leads, with BitSight’s empirical graph, Balbix’s asset-level dollars, Axio’s insurance scenarios, Kovrr’s cat-modeling, and CyberSaint, ThreatConnect, X-Analytics, and Squalify by decision lens.

Why nine platforms instead of ten? The source sheet listed BitSight twice we consolidated rather than pad a ranking about quantitative honesty.

What is FAIR and does it matter? Factor Analysis of Information Risk the open standard for decomposing cyber loss into measurable factors; FAIR-aligned models are interrogable and portable, which matters when regulators or boards push back.

Questionnaire-based or telemetry-based CRQ? Match to cadence: annual insurance and strategy decisions tolerate assessments; continuous budget and remediation steering needs live control signals updating the model.

How do we validate a CRQ model? Backtest against your own incident history, demand assumption decomposition per scenario, and compare vendor confidence intervals against realized losses over time calibration is the test.

Verdict

Nine platforms, one consolidated duplicate, one discipline: dollars defensible under cross-examination.

Safe Security holding the FAIR canon with live signals, BitSight’s decade of watched reality, Balbix pricing every asset, Axio stress-testing the tower, Kovrr bringing actuarial steel, CyberSaint reusing compliance truth, ThreatConnect weighting by the hunters, X-Analytics and Squalify compressing it for the top floor decompose the priors, backtest the model, track one number for six quarters, and let the interval shrink as the program matures.

The post Top 10 Best GRC Platforms in 2026 [Ranked & Scored] appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
GRC platforms carry security’s least glamorous truth: most risk programs fail on adoption, not analytics the business stops feeding the system, and the risk register quietly becomes fiction.

The 2026 ranking therefore weighs usability and time-to-value as heavily as framework depth, across a field spanning workflow giants, risk-quantification leaders, audit-born challengers, and privacy-lineage platforms.

ServiceNow takes 1; Archer and AuditBoard complete the podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: ServiceNow GRC woven into the workflow platform the business already answers to.

• Podium: ServiceNow (workflow gravity), Archer (deepest risk-program configurability), AuditBoard (adoption-first audit-and-risk).

• Buying split: heavyweight configurability (Archer, MetricStream, IBM OpenPages) versus adoption-speed challengers (AuditBoard, LogicGate) staffing reality should decide, not feature matrices.

• 2026 theme: AI entered the evidence room control-testing automation and AI-drafted risk narratives are now table stakes claims to verify, not differentiators to assume.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based evaluation; no lab testing, no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data.

Criteria: risk/control framework depth, adoption ergonomics (business-user reality), workflow/integration reach, reporting and board-readiness, implementation economics (time-to-value), and ecosystem.

Weights: adoption ergonomics 25%, framework depth 20%, workflow reach 20%, reporting 20%, implementation economics 15%.

The 2026 GRC Power Rankings

*Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

1. ServiceNow — Best Workflow-Native GRC

Snapshot: Module licensing on the Now Platform | IRM/GRC riding enterprise workflow | Continuous control monitoring ties

Why it earns 1: ServiceNow solved GRC’s adoption problem by not asking the business to go anywhere new: risk and compliance workflows ride the same platform that already routes IT tickets, approvals, and assets, so control owners respond in tools they can’t ignore.

CMDB linkage grounds risk in real assets, continuous monitoring feeds evidence automatically, and the result is GRC with the platform gravity to actually run. License math scales with ambition.

Pros: Workflow gravity; asset-grounded risk; automation reach; enterprise adoption rates.

Cons: Platform-committed economics; GRC depth tuned by implementation quality.

Bottom line: Risk management the business can’t quietly abandon.

2. Archer — Best Risk-Program Configurability

Snapshot: Platform + use-case licensing | Deep multi-domain risk architecture | Long-standing program pedigree

Why it ranks here: Archer remains the configurability benchmark: operational, IT, third-party, resilience, and audit domains modeled
to whatever sophistication your program demands, with two decades of complex-program pedigree behind it.

The power is real and so is its tax Archer rewards dedicated administrators and punishes understaffed deployments. Buy it for program depth you’ll actually staff.

Pros: Configurability ceiling; multi-domain depth; mature-program pedigree.

Cons: Admin-staffing prerequisite; implementation weight.

Bottom line: The deepest toolbox, for teams who bring the carpenter.

3. Hyperproof — Best Compliance-Operations and Control Management

Snapshot: Subscription platform | Compliance, risk, and control operations | Automated evidence and framework mapping

Why it ranks here: Hyperproof focuses on making GRC work easier to operate day to day, bringing controls, risks, evidence, compliance frameworks, and audit preparation into one platform with an emphasis on automation and usability.

Its strength is not extreme customization; it is helping security and compliance teams keep evidence current, reduce repetitive work, and manage multiple frameworks without turning the program into an administrative burden.

Pros: Strong control management; automated evidence workflows; multi-framework mapping; approachable user experience; good security-compliance focus.

Cons: Less internal-audit depth than audit-first platforms; highly complex enterprise GRC programs may favor heavier platforms.

Bottom line: The GRC platform for teams that want controls and evidence to stay current without adding operational drag.

4. MetricStream — Best Enterprise GRC Breadth

Snapshot: Platform licensing | BusinessGRC/CyberGRC product families | AI-assist features expanding

Why it ranks here: MetricStream covers the enterprise GRC waterfront operational risk, compliance, cyber risk, third-party, audit
with regulated-industry depth (banking especially) and a platform built for federated, multi-entity programs. It competes in the heavyweight class with Archer: breadth and rigor, bought alongside implementation commitment.

Pros: Domain breadth; regulated-industry fit; federated-program architecture.

Cons: Heavyweight implementation reality.

Bottom line: The waterfront, for institutions sized to swim it.

5. OneTrust — Best Privacy-Lineage GRC

Snapshot: Module subscriptions | Privacy-born, expanded to GRC/TPRM/ethics | Regulatory-intelligence feeds

Why it ranks here: OneTrust rode privacy regulation into the GRC estate: data-mapping and consent machinery that privacy law made mandatory, now surrounded by risk, compliance, ethics, and third-party modules fed by regulatory-change intelligence.

Where privacy obligations anchor the compliance program most consumer-facing enterprises starting from OneTrust’s lineage is the natural architecture.

Pros: Privacy-depth anchor; regulatory-intel feeds; module breadth.

Cons: Classic ERM depth younger than the heavyweights.

Bottom line: GRC built outward from the data-protection core.

6. LogicGate — Best Agile No-Code Risk Platform

Snapshot: Application-based subscriptions | Risk Cloud no-code workflow builder | Mid-enterprise sweet spot

Why it ranks here: LogicGate’s Risk Cloud bets on builders without engineers: no-code workflow design letting risk teams model their own processes custom registers, intake flows, vendor reviews without implementation armies.

Mid-enterprise programs get Archer-flavored flexibility at AuditBoard-flavored speed; extreme scale and depth remain upstream.

Pros: No-code agility; owner-built workflows; sane economics.

Cons: Enterprise-scale ceilings versus heavyweights.

Bottom line: The risk program you can remodel yourself.

7. Diligent — Best Board-to-Risk Connectivity

Snapshot: Suite subscriptions | Board-portal lineage + GRC acquisitions | Governance-to-risk pipeline

Why it ranks here: Diligent owns the top of the reporting chain board portals in most large enterprises and built a GRC suite beneath it, so risk data flows into the governance conversation without reformatting theater.

For programs whose binding constraint is board and committee communication, the connectivity is structural.

Pros: Board-channel ownership; governance integration; acquisition-built breadth.

Cons: Practitioner-depth consistency across acquired modules.

Bottom line: The shortest path from risk register to boardroom.

8. IBM OpenPages — Best AI-Assisted Regulated-Industry GRC

Snapshot: Platform licensing | watsonx-assisted GRC workflows | Financial-services depth

Why it ranks here: OpenPages pairs regulated-industry GRC depth model risk, regulatory compliance, operational risk for banking-grade scrutiny with IBM’s watsonx AI drafting control narratives, mapping regulations, and triaging changes.

For financial institutions already in IBM’s gravity, the AI-assist story is further along than brand perception suggests.

Pros: Regulated-industry rigor; AI-assist maturity; model-risk depth.

Cons: Brand momentum; heavyweight implementation.

Bottom line: Banking-grade GRC with a watsonx pen.

9. Riskonnect — Best Integrated Risk Breadth

Snapshot: Module licensing | Insurable risk + ERM + cyber in one | Claims/insurance lineage

Why it ranks here: Riskonnect integrates the risk families others silo: insurable risk and claims, ERM, compliance, third-party, and cyber in one platform the architecture for CROs who own hazard and digital risk together. Its insurance-lineage depth is distinctive; pure-cyber programs will find specialists sharper per lane.

Pros: Insurable+cyber integration; claims lineage; CRO-shaped breadth.

Cons: Per-lane depth versus specialists.

Bottom line: One register for everything that can go wrong.

10. SAI360 — Best EHS-Adjacent Compliance GRC

Snapshot: Module subscriptions | Compliance/ethics + EHS lineage | Learning-content pairing

Why it ranks here: SAI360 serves programs where compliance means people and operations as much as controls: ethics and compliance workflows paired with environment-health-safety lineage and training content. For manufacturers and healthcare operators consolidating operational compliance, the shape fits; cyber-risk-first buyers look above.

Pros: EHS+compliance integration; training-content pairing; operational-compliance fit.

Cons: Cyber-risk depth versus the field.

Bottom line: Compliance for the physical-world enterprise.

Full Comparison Table

Yes/No Capability Table

Buying Advice: Staff the Platform or Shrink the Platform

GRC failure is predictable: a heavyweight platform bought by a two-person team, eighteen months of implementation, then a risk register nobody updates.

Match class to staffing honestly dedicated GRC administrators justify Archer/MetricStream/OpenPages depth; lean teams succeed with AuditBoard/LogicGate-class adoption speed; ServiceNow shops should price the IRM modules before anything net-new, because workflow gravity beats feature parity.

Pilot with your real control owners, not the risk team: give three business users an actual control attestation and a risk acceptance to complete, and measure clicks, confusion, and completion their experience decides adoption, which decides everything.

Interrogate AI claims with evidence: have the platform draft a control-test narrative from your real evidence and grade it.

Negotiate implementation as part of the deal (fixed-scope first-use-case live in ninety days), demand framework-content currency (the regulations you face, mapped, updated on subscription), and set the program’s honest metric: percentage of controls with current evidence, trending up quarter over quarter. A beautiful register with stale evidence is the category’s signature failure.

FAQs

What are the best GRC platforms in 2026? ServiceNow for workflow-native programs, Archer and MetricStream for heavyweight depth, AuditBoard and LogicGate for adoption speed, OneTrust for privacy-anchored estates, with Diligent, OpenPages, Riskonnect, and SAI360 by shape.

GRC versus IRM versus compliance automation labels or differences? Mostly vendor dialects for overlapping scope; the real axes are configurability-versus-adoption-speed and which risk domains integrate buy against those, not the acronym.

How long should GRC implementation take? First use case live in sixty to ninety days is the modern bar challengers set; multi-quarter timelines deserve explicit justification, not acceptance as normal.

What makes GRC programs fail? Adoption decay: control owners stop responding, evidence goes stale, the register stops reflecting reality which is why business-user ergonomics outweigh analyst features.

Is AI in GRC real? Increasingly AI-drafted control narratives, regulation mapping, and evidence summarization work today, but grade output on your own evidence during the pilot rather than trusting the demo.

Verdict

Ten platforms, one failure mode to design against: the register nobody feeds. ServiceNow’s gravity, Archer’s depth, AuditBoard’s adoption, MetricStream’s waterfront, OneTrust’s privacy anchor, LogicGate’s no-code agility, Diligent’s boardroom pipe, OpenPages’ regulated rigor, Riskonnect’s unified register, SAI360’s operational lane pick the class your staffing can feed, pilot with real control owners, and measure evidence freshness like the program depends on it, because it does.

articles.description:

The operation places decentralized exchange liquidity pools between wallets holding stolen assets and wallets collecting the proceeds, complicating efforts to trace and freeze the money. […]

The post North Korean Hackers Create Fake Meme Coins to Launder Stolen Funds From $6.4 Billion Binance Hack appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
North Korean hackers are creating disposable meme coins to move cryptocurrency stolen in the $6.4 billion Binance hack, using fake trading activity to make criminal proceeds resemble ordinary investment returns.

The operation places decentralized exchange liquidity pools between wallets holding stolen assets and wallets collecting the proceeds, complicating efforts to trace and freeze the money.

The laundering follows the October 29, 2026, theft attributed to TraderTraitor, a North Korean hacking group. Earlier reporting on the FBI’s North Korean attribution connected the Binance attack to an operation previously blamed for major cryptocurrency thefts.

Elliptic’s latest findings show how the operators are moving part of those stolen funds after the initial breach.

Researchers from Elliptic identified the meme coin laundering activity in a November 9 investigation led by co-founder Dr. Tom Robinson.

Their report examines blockchain transactions rather than identifying a new malware family. It documents related techniques on Tron, NEAR, and Solana, with approximately 117,000 NEAR, worth around $430,000, passing through six newly created tokens.

North Korean Hackers Create Fake Meme Coins

The process starts with attackers creating a token through a public launch tool. They then establish a liquidity pool pairing that token with a genuine asset, such as NEAR or a stablecoin.

A liquidity pool holds assets that users can exchange without a traditional buyer and seller matching each trade. One group of attacker-controlled wallets uses stolen cryptocurrency to purchase the new token.

Another group sells tokens into the same pool and withdraws the genuine asset. Because the pool sits between these transactions, funds do not move directly from the buying wallets to the collecting wallets.

The receiving accounts instead appear to have earned proceeds from token trading. Between November 5 and November 7, the operators created six NEAR tokens: FUK, OLCCL, MEILI, MMLI, DABI, and SINU. Each cost approximately 25 NEAR, or $90, to launch.

Their logos copied familiar meme coin imagery, including animals and an Elon Musk-themed banner. Elliptic explicitly stated that nothing suggested Musk had any connection to the tokens. This method builds on earlier laundering after the Bybit theft.

While the earlier Bybit attack investigation described workstation compromise and malicious transaction changes, Elliptic’s research concerns what happened afterward: operators used a worthless Tron token and fresh wallets to move at least $24 million in stolen Bybit assets.

The Binance-linked NEAR tokens followed a consistent pattern. They launched, traded heavily within hours, and were abandoned. None had traded since November 8 when Elliptic published its findings.

Creators of four tokens also withdrew remaining pool liquidity that afternoon, reinforcing the assessment that these were temporary laundering tools rather than genuine trading projects.

Blockchain Evidence and Detection Priorities

Elliptic found that laundering-network wallets accounted for every sale across all six tokens. They also bought every unit of five tokens.

FUK attracted limited outside purchases, but these represented less than 1% of its volume. DABI, MMLI, and SINU each had only one buying wallet and one selling wallet.

Funding relationships provided another link. Five token creators received money from wallets that had already sold an earlier token, just two to thirteen minutes before launching the next one.

Almost the same amount of NEAR entering the scheme later left collecting wallets, often heading into stablecoins or cross-chain bridges.

The activity remains traceable because transactions stay on public blockchains. As previous reporting on Lazarus crypto laundering networks illustrates, connecting wallet movements with other evidence can support investigations and freezes.

Here, the extra swaps create delays rather than erase the trail, buying operators time before services flag their funds. Elliptic advises compliance teams against treating liquidity-pool withdrawals as automatically legitimate.

Newly launched tokens, very few traders, separate buying-only and selling-only wallets, and accounts funded immediately before trading deserve scrutiny. Previously accepted deposits also need renewed screening when investigators identify additional laundering addresses.
