articles.title: Top 10 Best Digital Forensics Tools in 2026 [Ranked & Scored]
articles.description:
Forensics is the security discipline with a courtroom at the end: every tool here is ultimately judged by whether its findings survive cross-examination. The 2026 toolkit spans mobile-extraction giants, disk-and-artifact workhorses, memory-analysis frameworks, and the open-source pillars every lab quietly depends on. Scoring weighs artifact depth, evidentiary rigor, and the economics that decide what a […]

The post Top 10 Best Digital Forensics Tools in 2026 [Ranked & Scored] appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Forensics is the security discipline with a courtroom at the end: every tool here is ultimately judged by whether its findings survive cross-examination.

The 2026 toolkit spans mobile-extraction giants, disk-and-artifact workhorses, memory-analysis frameworks, and the open-source pillars every lab quietly depends on.

Scoring weighs artifact depth, evidentiary rigor, and the economics that decide what a lab can actually license.

Cellebrite takes 1; Magnet Forensics and OpenText EnCase complete the podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: Cellebrite mobile extraction remains the hardest problem, and the deepest answer.

• Podium: Cellebrite (mobile depth), Magnet (cross-source investigation ergonomics), EnCase (courtroom pedigree).

• Open pillars: Autopsy/Sleuth Kit and Volatility rank as infrastructure free, court-tested, and in every serious lab alongside the commercial stack.

• 2026 theme: volume forensics labs drowning in devices buy automation (Magnet’s workflows, AI-assisted review) as urgently as extraction depth.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based evaluation; no lab testing, no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data.

Criteria: artifact/extraction depth, evidentiary defensibility (court track record, hashing/chain-of-custody rigor), analysis ergonomics at caseload volume, platform coverage (mobile, disk, memory, cloud), automation, and licensing economics.

Weights: artifact depth 25%, defensibility 20%, ergonomics 20%, coverage 20%, economics 15%.

The 2026 Digital Forensics Power Rankings

*Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

1. Cellebrite — Best Mobile Extraction Depth

Snapshot: Per-seat/unit licensing tiers | UFED/Premium extraction + Pathfinder analytics | Law-enforcement-grade access research

Why it earns 1: Mobile devices are modern evidence’s center of gravity, and Cellebrite holds the deepest access research in commercial forensics: locked-device extraction capabilities rivals chase, parsing across thousands of app versions, and Pathfinder analytics turning extractions into investigable timelines.

Controversial by the nature of its power, indispensable by the nature of the caseload. Licensing tiers gate the deepest capabilities.

Pros: Extraction-depth leadership; app-parsing breadth; analytics layer.

Cons: Premium tiering; capability-access governance scrutiny comes with the territory.

Bottom line: The phone usually opens this is usually why.

2. Magnet Forensics — Best Cross-Source Investigation Platform

Snapshot: Suite licensing | Axiom across mobile/computer/cloud | Automation (Automate) + AI review

Why it ranks here: Magnet built the examiner’s cockpit: Axiom unifying mobile, disk, and cloud artifacts into one timeline, recovering app data others miss, with Automate orchestrating lab pipelines and AI-assisted review attacking the volume crisis.

The workflow evidence in, story out is the category’s most examiner-loved, and the automation story leads the market’s answer to backlog arithmetic.

Pros: Unified cross-source analysis; artifact-recovery reputation; lab automation.

Cons: Deepest locked-device extraction still pairs with Cellebrite-class tools.

Bottom line: Where the evidence becomes a narrative.

3. OpenText (EnCase) — Best Courtroom-Pedigree Disk Forensics

Snapshot: Per-seat licensing | EnCase Forensic + endpoint investigation line | Decades of precedent

Why it ranks here: EnCase’s E01 format and courtroom history are forensic infrastructure: decades of admissibility precedent, disk-level rigor, and enterprise endpoint-investigation reach under OpenText.

Momentum questions versus younger rivals are fair; when defensibility is the binding constraint, the pedigree still carries weight juries and judges recognize.

Pros: Admissibility track record; disk-forensics depth; enterprise investigation line.

Cons: Ergonomics and innovation pace versus Axiom-era rivals.

Bottom line: The format the courtroom already knows.

4. Exterro (FTK) — Best Lab-Scale Processing Speed

Snapshot: Suite licensing | FTK’s database-driven processing | E-discovery/privacy suite ties

Why it ranks here: FTK’s architecture bet database-backed processing, distributed workers still pays at lab scale: big evidence sets indexed fast, stable under volume, with Exterro’s e-discovery and privacy stack adjacent for the legal-workflow handoff.

The processing-farm choice for labs where throughput is the bottleneck.

Pros: Processing throughput; stability at volume; legal-suite adjacency.

Cons: Examiner-ergonomics race belongs to Magnet-class rivals.

Bottom line: The lab’s heavy press.

5. MOBILedit Forensic — Best Mobile-Forensics Value Challenger

Snapshot: Per-seat licensing | Mobile extraction + app analysis | Cloud, smartwatch, and connected-device evidence

Why it ranks here: MOBILedit Forensic gives investigators a broad mobile-forensics toolkit with device extraction, application-data parsing, deleted-data recovery, cloud evidence collection, and support for connected devices such as smartwatches.

It fits labs that want capable mobile analysis without paying for the highest-end extraction platforms, while still covering many of the evidence sources common in modern investigations.

Pros: Good value; broad mobile-device support; app and cloud analysis; deleted-data recovery; smartwatch evidence support.

Cons: Locked-device access and advanced extraction depth trail the category leaders.

Bottom line: Strong mobile-forensics coverage at a more accessible price point.

6. MSAB — Best Frontline Mobile Extraction Kiosks

Snapshot: XRY licensing + kiosk deployments | Frontline/kiosk extraction model | Chain-of-custody discipline

Why it ranks here: MSAB’s XRY built the decentralized model: kiosks and field units putting controlled extraction at the frontline border posts, precincts with chain-of-custody and audit discipline engineered for non-specialist operators.

For agencies scaling extraction beyond the central lab, the operating model is the product.

Pros: Frontline deployment model; custody discipline; operator simplicity.

Cons: Deep-research extraction race; analytics layer thinner.

Bottom line: Extraction pushed to the edge, auditably.

7. Belkasoft — Best All-in-One Value Suite

Snapshot: Per-seat suite | Evidence Center X across disk/mobile/memory | Accessible economics

Why it ranks here: Belkasoft packs disk, mobile, memory, and cloud artifacts into one suite at a price point that makes small labs and corporate DFIR teams viable: broad artifact support, decent automation, honest capability for the money.

The specialist ceilings above are real; so is the budget math below them.

Pros: Coverage-per-dollar; single-suite simplicity; memory analysis included.

Cons: Depth ceilings versus category leaders per lane.

Bottom line: The whole lab, one SKU, small invoice.

8. Paraben E3 Forensic Platform — Best Broad-Source Forensic Investigation Suite

Snapshot: Commercial licensing | Computer + mobile + cloud + IoT forensics | Unified evidence processing

Why it ranks here: Paraben E3 brings multiple evidence types into one forensic environment, covering computers, mobile devices, cloud sources, memory, email, chat data, IoT, and other digital artifacts.

It gives investigators a broad collection-and-analysis workflow without forcing them to jump between separate specialist tools for every evidence source.

Pros: Broad evidence coverage; computer and mobile forensics; cloud and IoT support; integrated case workflow; flexible acquisition and analysis.

Cons: Less specialized low-level disk analysis than X-Ways; smaller ecosystem than Cellebrite or Magnet Forensics.

Bottom line: One forensic workbench for investigations that span far beyond the hard drive.

9. Autopsy (Sleuth Kit) — Best Open-Source Forensic Platform

Snapshot: Free/open-source; commercial support available | Full GUI platform on Sleuth Kit | Training-ecosystem standard

Why it ranks here: Autopsy is the open pillar: a genuine GUI forensic platform timelines, keyword search, artifact modules, hash sets
free, court-cited, and the training ground half the field learned on.

Budget-constrained labs run real caseloads on it; funded labs keep it for validation and cross-checking commercial findings, which good practice demands anyway.

Pros: Free and court-tested; validation role; training ubiquity.

Cons: Processing speed and polish versus commercial suites.

Bottom line: The lab you can build for the price of hardware.

10. Volatility — Best Memory-Forensics Framework

Snapshot: Open-source framework | The memory-analysis standard | Plugin ecosystem

Why it ranks here: Memory is where modern attacks live fileless malware, injected code, credentials in RAM and Volatility is the discipline’s shared language: the framework court filings cite, plugins extend, and every serious DFIR team scripts against.

It ranks as essential infrastructure: not a product competitor, the capability everyone else’s memory features quietly descend from.

Pros: Memory-analysis standard; plugin depth; community authority.

Cons: Command-line craft; framework, not a workflow product.

Bottom line: RAM’s court reporter.

Full Comparison Table

Yes/No Capability Table

Buying Advice: Equip for the Caseload, Validate in Pairs

Forensic tooling decisions are caseload arithmetic plus evidentiary insurance. Inventory a year of real cases by evidence type most labs discover they’re 70% mobile, which makes the Cellebrite/Oxygen/MSAB tiering decision the budget’s center, with analysis platforms (Magnet/EnCase/FTK) sized to examiner count rather than aspiration.

Never single-source conclusions that matter: dual-tool validation (commercial finding cross-checked in Autopsy, memory claims reproduced in Volatility) is both good science and cross-examination armor, and the open pillars make it nearly free.

Buy automation in proportion to backlog a lab six months behind needs Magnet-Automate-class workflow more than deeper extraction and budget training as seriously as licenses, because an expert on X-Ways outruns a novice on anything.

Keep hash-verified acquisition, write-blocking discipline, and documented chain of custody as process, not product features.

And check jurisdictional procurement rules for extraction capabilities early: access-research tools carry governance obligations that vary by country and agency type.

FAQs

What are the best digital forensics tools in 2026? Cellebrite for mobile extraction, Magnet Axiom for cross-source analysis, EnCase for courtroom pedigree, FTK for lab throughput, with Oxygen, MSAB, Belkasoft, X-Ways, and the open pillars Autopsy and Volatility completing serious labs.

Commercial versus open-source forensics? Both: commercial suites buy depth, support, and speed; Autopsy and Volatility provide validation, training, and court-cited capability dual-tool verification is best practice regardless of budget.

What matters most in mobile forensics? Extraction access (can you get in), parsing currency (are this month’s app versions supported), and custody discipline in that order, because unparsed extractions still beat no extraction.

How do findings stay court-admissible? Hash-verified acquisition, write-blockers, documented chain of custody, validated tools, and examiners who can explain methodology under cross the process certifies the output.

Is memory forensics worth the effort? Increasingly mandatory: fileless tradecraft lives only in RAM capture memory early in response and keep Volatility fluency on the team.

Verdict

Ten tools, one standard of proof. Cellebrite opens the phones, Magnet tells the story, EnCase carries the precedent, FTK presses the volume, Oxygen and MSAB and Belkasoft stretch the budget, X-Ways rewards mastery, Autopsy and Volatility keep the science honest and free size to the caseload, validate in pairs, train past the license, and remember the tool is only as admissible as the process around it.

The post Top 10 Best GenAI SOC Copilots in 2026 [Ranked & Scored] appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
The SOC copilot market split into two species while nobody was renaming it: assistants that summarize, draft, and answer questions inside a human’s workflow, and agents that autonomously work tier-1 queues end-to-end under policy guardrails.

The 2026 ranking covers both suite copilots riding platform gravity and pure-play AI analysts selling triage as the product scored on the only currency that matters: verified analyst-hours returned without new risk.

Microsoft Security Copilot takes 1; CrowdStrike Charlotte AI and Dropzone AI complete the podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: Microsoft Security Copilot the widest deployed surface and deepest estate integration in the category.

• Podium: Security Copilot (estate reach), Charlotte AI (telemetry-grounded answers), Dropzone (pure-play autonomous triage).

• Species split: assistants (suite copilots) accelerate humans; agents (Dropzone, Prophet, Radiant, Simbian) replace tier-1 toil buy for different problems.

• 2026 theme: audit trails became the differentiator the credible products show their reasoning, cite their evidence, and accept human override at every step.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based evaluation; no lab testing, no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data. Criteria: investigation/triage quality, grounding (telemetry-cited answers, not hallucinated narrative), guardrails and auditability, workflow integration, autonomy maturity, and pricing accessibility. Weights: triage quality 25%, grounding 20%, guardrails/audit 20%, integration 20%, autonomy 15%.

The 2026 GenAI SOC Copilot Power Rankings

*Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

1. Microsoft (Security Copilot) — Best Estate-Integrated Copilot

Snapshot: Consumption (SCU-based) | Embedded across Defender/Sentinel/Entra/Intune | Promptbooks + agents roadmap

Why it earns 1: Security Copilot wins on surface area: embedded where Microsoft-estate analysts already live, summarizing incidents in Defender, drafting KQL in Sentinel, explaining risky sign-ins in Entra, with promptbooks templating repeatable investigations and agentic capabilities expanding under governance controls.

Consumption pricing demands discipline, but no rival touches as many consoles the analyst already has open.

Pros: Estate embedding; cross-product context; promptbook repeatability; governance tooling.

Cons: SCU consumption needs budget governance; value concentrates in Microsoft estates.

Bottom line: The copilot that’s already inside your consoles meter it wisely.

2. CrowdStrike (Charlotte AI) — Best Telemetry-Grounded Copilot

Snapshot: Falcon module | Answers grounded in Falcon telemetry + intel | Agentic triage expansion

Why it ranks here: Charlotte’s answers come with receipts: natural-language questions resolved against Falcon’s live telemetry and adversary intel, not model memory “show me unmanaged assets touched by this actor’s tradecraft” returns estate truth.

Agentic expansion moves it from answering to acting through the same platform guardrails. Grounding quality is the moat.

Pros: Telemetry-cited answers; adversary-intel fusion; platform-native action path.

Cons: Falcon-estate coupling.

Bottom line: The copilot least likely to make things up.

3. Dropzone AI — Best Autonomous Tier-1 Analyst

Snapshot: Per-alert/subscription | End-to-end alert investigation autonomously | Evidence-documented verdicts

Why it ranks here: Dropzone sells the agent species honestly: every alert investigated end-to-end context gathered across your stack, hypotheses tested, verdict written with evidence trail no playbook authoring required. Human analysts review conclusions instead of raw queues.

The pure-play reference for AI-as-tier-1, with the audit transparency that makes delegation defensible.

Pros: True autonomous triage; evidence-trail verdicts; no-playbook onboarding.

Cons: Pure-play scale versus suite gravity; verify stack-connector depth.

Bottom line: Tier-1 toil, retired with receipts.

4. Google (Gemini in Security) — Best Retention-Scale AI Investigation

Snapshot: SecOps-included tiers | Gemini across SecOps + Mandiant intel | Year-scale hot-data interrogation

Why it ranks here: Gemini’s SOC edge is what it can reach: natural-language investigation across SecOps’ months-to-a-year of hot retention, Mandiant intel woven into answers, searches and rules drafted conversationally.

Asking “has this actor’s infrastructure ever touched us?” against a year of data is a different question than against thirty days retention makes the AI smarter.

Pros: Retention-scale reach; Mandiant-grounded context; conversational rule drafting.

Cons: SecOps-coupled; assistant-species more than agent.

Bottom line: An AI with a year of memory to interrogate.

5. Palo Alto (Cortex Copilot) — Best Platform-Automation Copilot

Snapshot: Cortex/XSIAM-bundled | Copilot across XSIAM workflows | Automation-fabric leverage

Why it ranks here: Cortex Copilot rides the XSIAM thesis: AI assistance fused to an automation fabric that already executes investigation summaries flowing into playbook actions, queries drafted into a platform built to respond.

Where suite rivals assist analysis, Palo Alto’s bet couples assistance to actuation. Value concentrates inside the Cortex commitment.

Pros: Automation-coupled assistance; XSIAM-scale context; action proximity.

Cons: Platform-commitment prerequisite.

Bottom line: The copilot wired to the machinery.

6. SentinelOne (Purple AI) — Best Hunt-Acceleration Copilot

Snapshot: Singularity module | Natural-language hunting over Singularity data lake | Investigation summarization

Why it ranks here: Purple AI’s sweet spot is the hunt: plain-English questions compiled against the Singularity lake, hypotheses iterated at conversation speed, findings summarized into shareable investigations.

It makes mid-skill analysts hunt like seniors the skill-leverage pitch, delivered inside SentinelOne estates.

Pros: Hunt ergonomics; skill leverage; lake-scale queries.

Cons: Estate-coupled; agent autonomy younger than pure-plays.

Bottom line: Senior-analyst questions from mid-tier keyboards.

7. Intezer AI SOC — Best Forensic-Depth Autonomous SOC

Snapshot: Subscription | Agentic AI + deterministic forensics | Alert investigation + response workflows

Why it ranks here: Intezer AI SOC investigates alerts across endpoint, identity, cloud, phishing, network, and other security telemetry, gathering evidence and applying forensic analysis before reaching a verdict.

It combines autonomous investigation with response workflows and human approval controls, giving SOC teams a way to reduce tier-1 workload without handing over unrestricted remediation authority.

Pros: Deep forensic investigation; automated triage; cross-stack integrations; evidence-backed verdicts; human approval for response.

Cons: Enterprise-focused deployment; full value depends on strong telemetry and integration coverage.

Bottom line: Autonomous investigation backed by forensic evidence, with humans still controlling the response.

8. Prophet Security — Best Investigation-Depth AI Agent

Snapshot: Subscription | Agentic investigation emphasis | Transparent reasoning chains

Why it ranks here: Prophet’s agent leans into investigative depth: multi-step reasoning across identity, endpoint, and cloud signal, with the chain of logic exposed for review the “show your work” species of AI analyst. Young-category caveats apply; the reasoning-transparency bar it sets is where the whole field is heading.

Pros: Reasoning transparency; multi-signal investigation; depth emphasis.

Cons: Early-stage scale; validate against your alert mix.

Bottom line: The agent that argues its case.

9. Splunk AI Assistant — Best SPL-Fluency Copilot

Snapshot: Splunk-bundled features | Natural language → SPL | ES workflow assistance

Why it ranks here: Splunk’s assistant attacks its own moat’s tax: SPL fluency, translated plain English becoming working queries, searches explained back in prose, detection drafting accelerated.

For the enormous Splunk-skilled-shortage reality, it’s leverage on the estate you already run rather than a new species of automation.

Pros: SPL democratization; estate-native; onboarding acceleration.

Cons: Assistant-species scope; Splunk-coupled.

Bottom line: The query language, finally conversational.

10. Simbian — Best Multi-Agent SOC Ambition

Snapshot: Subscription| Multiple specialized AI agents across SOC functions | Autonomy-spectrum controls

Why it ranks here: Simbian’s thesis is the full org chart:specialized agents for triage, hunting, intel, and GRC working as a coordinated AI team under human command. The ambition outruns the category’s maturity which is the honest ranking logic but the multi-agent architecture sketches where SOC staffing economics are headed. Pilot with eyes open.

Pros: Multi-agent architecture; function breadth; autonomy controls.

Cons: Ambition-to-maturity gap; early-adopter posture required.

Bottom line: The org-chart-of-agents bet, early edition.

Full Comparison Table

Yes/No Capability Table

Buying Advice: Demand the Hallucination Audit

AI SOC purchases should be run like analyst hiring: a structured tryout on your real work. Feed each candidate thirty days of your actual alert history including your known false positives and two or three past true incidents and grade verdict accuracy against what your humans concluded, time-to-verdict, and crucially the hallucination rate: answers asserting things the telemetry doesn’t support.

Any product that can’t expose its evidence chain for that audit fails procurement regardless of demo polish.

Match species to problem drowning tier-1 queues want agents (Dropzone/Radiant/Prophet-class), skill-shortage pain wants suite assistants already in your consoles, and suite estates should exhaust their bundled copilot before buying pure-play.

Govern consumption pricing (the Security Copilot SCU lesson: meter before the bill teaches you), write data-handling terms for what leaves your tenant, and keep autonomy earned: analysis-autonomous first, action-autonomous per playbook only after the agent’s false-positive record beats your tier-1’s. Publish hours-returned monthly the metric that justifies the category or kills the renewal.

FAQs

What are the best GenAI SOC copilots in 2026? Microsoft Security Copilot for estate reach, Charlotte AI for grounded answers, Dropzone for autonomous triage, Gemini for retention-scale investigation, with Cortex Copilot, Purple AI, Radiant, Prophet, Splunk AI Assistant, and Simbian by species and stack.

Assistant versus agent which do we need? Assistants multiply analyst speed inside consoles; agents work queues autonomously. Skill shortage → assistant; volume drowning → agent; most mature SOCs end up with one of each.

How do we test for hallucination? Replay historical alerts with known ground truth and count unsupported assertions demand evidence-citation for every claim, and reject products that can’t show the chain.

Will AI replace SOC analysts? It’s replacing tier-1 toil triage, enrichment, documentation and moving humans to judgment, hunting, and engineering; staffing shifts rather than disappears.

What guardrails matter most? Evidence-cited reasoning, human approval gates per action class, full audit logs, tenant-boundary data terms, and autonomy granted per playbook on measured performance.

Verdict

Ten copilots, two species, one procurement rule: audition on your own alerts and count the hallucinations.

Security Copilot across the estate, Charlotte grounded in Falcon truth, Dropzone retiring tier-1, Gemini interrogating a year of memory, Cortex wired to automation, Purple AI leveling the hunt, Radiant and Prophet showing their work, Splunk translating its own language, Simbian sketching the agent org chart ground every answer, gate every action, meter every token, and publish the hours you got back.

articles.title: RevStealer Uses 100+ Domains and Hijacked YouTube Channels to Spread Credential-Stealing Malware
articles.description:

The post RevStealer Uses 100+ Domains and Hijacked YouTube Channels to Spread Credential-Stealing Malware appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A credential-stealing malware called RevStealer is now spread through more than 100 linked domains, hijacked YouTube channels, and fake AI tools.

It targets gamers, content creators, and people who want free software. The goal is simple: steal saved passwords, cookies, game accounts, and crypto wallets, then disappear.

The campaign is built around things people search for, such as game cheats, account tools, and free versions of paid AI apps. Victims download what looks like a useful file, and a multi-stage infection starts in the background.

The operators appear to be financially motivated, and no nation-state link has been confirmed. The malware has been tracked by several security firms, including Elastic Security Labs and Morphisec.

Researchers from Akatsuki Legion also noted the malware in a new report published on November 9, 2026. They tied the distribution network to the same sites and hosting that others had seen.

One lure is a trojanized Electron app posing as Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5, which matches the earlier report on the fake Claude Opus 5 desktop app.

RevStealer Uses 100+ Domains and Hijacked YouTube Channels

Akatsuki Legion found four main hubs: elitecheatsx[.]live, elitemods[.]shop, satano[.]xyz, and cheatseller[.]com. These sites share the same image files, which points to a common owner.

By matching these file hashes and shared IP addresses, the team found about 100 more related domains. One hash links to around 70 domains, and another links to about 30. The researchers say not every domain is confirmed to spread RevStealer.

Some may be connected to other activity, and one cluster looks related to the REMCOS RAT. The lures cover a wide range of games and tools, including Minecraft, Roblox, Fortnite, Valorant, and Counter-Strike 2.

Other bait includes Discord Nitro generators, Spotify and Canva premium tools, free VPNs, and fake ChatGPT, Grok, DeepSeek, and Gemini unlockers. Pirated copies of Slack, qBittorrent, and SteelSeries GG are also used.

The group also takes over existing YouTube channels. It posts AI-generated videos about game cheats and puts download links in the descriptions.

This is an old trick, and earlier reports on hijacking popular YouTube channels show how a trusted channel makes a risky link look safe.

After the download, the file runs through several stages. The first stage is packed with VMProtect, a tool that makes code hard to read. It uses Windows tools like WMI and PowerShell and injects code into other processes.

The next stage runs only in memory, so it leaves little on disk. A decoy file is also dropped to distract analysts.

Evasion & Data Theft

Before it does any harm, RevStealer checks whether it is being watched. It runs ten tests, covering memory size, CPU cores, hostname, username, graphics adapter, uptime, and sleep timing.

A virtual graphics adapter counts double. If the score reaches seven, the malware quits. It also quits if the system language is Russian, Ukrainian, or a Central Asian language, which suggests the operators want to avoid local police attention.

If the machine passes, the malware decrypts its AES-256-CBC payload and saves it in a randomly named folder under AppData.

It tries to add that folder to Microsoft Defender’s exclusion list. It then uses 14 indirect syscall wrappers and FNV-1a API hashing to avoid security hooks.

The theft is broad. It takes passwords, cookies, and history from Chrome, Edge, Brave, Firefox, Opera, and Vivaldi. It can bypass Chrome’s App-Bound Encryption using hardware breakpoints.

It also goes after 225 Chromium password-manager extensions, 51 standalone wallet and password apps, and VPN and 2FA tools. Steam, Roblox, Battle.net, EA Desktop, and Minecraft files are also taken, along with screenshots and clipboard data.

The data is sent over HTTPS port 443 as encrypted records. If the main server is down, the malware reads a backup address from a Polygon smart contract, a method known as EtherHiding.

Similar cases appear in reports on how attackers hide malware on Polygon. Because blockchain data cannot be removed, this backup is hard to shut down.

RevStealer does not stay on the system, and it deletes itself after the theft. The report also says the operator can push ransomware through the same channel, and a LockAppHost module can run the XMRig coin miner.

Defenders should watch for Defender exclusion changes, new executables in AppData, and non-browser programs contacting Polygon RPC servers. Users should avoid cheats and cracked software, as shown in cases where gaming channels and SEO tricks lead to malware.

In a November 9, 2026 update, the company said attackers reached its development machines through a third-party cloud provider, expanding the impact beyond the exposed credentials reported in October. The findings change the picture presented in […]

The post Hackers Breach Fireworks AI Through Third-Party Cloud Provider to Steal Customer Data appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Fireworks AI has disclosed a wider security breach involving customer account details, billing records, datasets, and incomplete model weights. In a November 9, 2026 update, the company said attackers reached its development machines through a third-party cloud provider, expanding the impact beyond the exposed credentials reported in October.

The findings change the picture presented in its first disclosure. Fireworks initially reported unauthorized access to secrets used in evaluation jobs across a limited number of accounts. Its latest investigation confirms access to additional customer information, including portions of unfinished models and datasets belonging to certain customers.

Fireworks AI Data Breach

The newly disclosed attack path began on October 23, when a cloud provider hosting Fireworks research and development machines experienced a security incident. On October 24, an unauthorized party used that opening to access Fireworks development machines and run an unauthorized workload, causing further customer data exposure.

Fireworks said it detected the activity that day, took immediate response measures, and closed known critical vulnerabilities. The company has not named the cloud provider or disclosed specific vulnerabilities. It reported no further detected successful access by the attacker on its customer platform as of October 25.

The earlier incident began on October 6, when Fireworks detected misuse of internal credentials. Attackers accessed environment variables used by evaluation jobs, potentially capturing API keys and tokens. Fireworks began customer notifications on October 7 and later revoked affected keys, employee credentials, and service-account tokens.

According to the updated security bulletin, the affected internal application exposed resource identifiers, names, descriptions, and creation times. Billing information included billing and shipping addresses, invoices, payment history, balances, and credit usage. Fireworks does not store payment card numbers and said those numbers were unaffected.

For certain customers, attackers accessed a subset of incomplete model weights and datasets. The disclosure does not establish theft of complete production models. Fireworks also reported no detected impact to Inference, Training SDK, or Nexus, which operate with zero data retention by default. Its investigation remains ongoing.

Fireworks said evidence points to a financially motivated cybercriminal group seeking to sell unauthorized access to large language models through illicit routing gateways, known as LLMJacking. Cybersecurity News previously covered LLMHijacking attacks and large cloud bills, explaining how stolen cloud credentials enable resale of paid AI services.

The company has notified law enforcement and brought in Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 for forensic support. Its response includes replacing credentials, reducing elevated permissions, isolating affected systems, and tightening storage access. Related reporting on cloud credential theft using autonomous AI agents highlights the broader risk around compromised cloud accounts.

Fireworks has disabled self-service dataset uploads and downloads for Batch Inference and dataset-based training during the investigation. Training SDK remains available, while Fireworks Lab-based training runs in an isolated environment with added network and storage protection. The company is directly notifying customers whose data was affected.

Its original customer guidance advises affected users to replace revoked Fireworks keys and rotate exposed third-party credentials with their issuing providers. Deleting a stored secret does not invalidate the underlying credential. Customers should also review access logs, unfamiliar users, API keys, training jobs, and datasets for unauthorized activity.

articles.title: Google Chrome 0-Day Vulnerability in the Wild to Execute Malicious Code Remotely
articles.description:
Google has fixed a Chrome zero-day that attackers are already using. The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-125350, and it lets a remote attacker run malicious code in the browser. Google’s Stable channel update moves Chrome to version 157.0.8103.50/.51 for Windows and Mac and 157.0.8103.50 for Linux. The rollout will reach users over the coming days […]

The post Google Chrome 0-Day Vulnerability in the Wild to Execute Malicious Code Remotely appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Google has fixed a Chrome zero-day that attackers are already using. The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-125350, and it lets a remote attacker run malicious code in the browser.

Google’s Stable channel update moves Chrome to version 157.0.8103.50/.51 for Windows and Mac and 157.0.8103.50 for Linux. The rollout will reach users over the coming days and weeks. The Chrome Security team explains that bug details stay locked until most users have the fix.

CVE-2026-125350 is a high-severity use-after-free bug in Chrome’s XML component. Google says it is aware that an exploit for this flaw exists in the wild. An anonymous researcher reported it on November 6, 2026, only three days before the patch shipped.

Google has not said who is using the exploit or how many people were targeted. A use-after-free flaw happens when a program keeps using memory after it has been released. Attackers can sometimes use this to crash the browser or run their own code, often through a booby-trapped web page.

Eight More Flaws Fixed in the Same Update

The release carries nine security fixes in total, and seven of them are rated High. Google’s list includes an uninitialized resource in WebGL (CVE-2026-125345), incorrect authorization in FileSystem (CVE-2026-125347), a buffer overflow in Compositing (CVE-2026-125343), an out-of-bounds write in GPU (CVE-2026-125348), and type confusion in V8 (CVE-2026-125344).

A second use-after-free in XML, CVE-2026-125346, came from Arni Hardarson of Neonix Security. Two Medium flaws were also fixed. These are CVE-2026-125349 and CVE-2026-125342, and both are uninitialized resource bugs in the GPU. Vo Duc Thang reported the second one. Google’s own team found most of the rest. The full issue tracker list will open up once most users are updated.

Browsers read untrusted content all day, so memory bugs in parts like XML are a favorite target. A victim may only need to open a bad link. Attackers can send that link through phishing emails, ads, or hacked sites.

We saw the same pattern when Google patched an earlier Chrome zero-day in June, which also allowed remote code execution through a crafted page. The newest fix also reaches enterprise users. The Extended Stable channel gets the same zero-day patch in version 156.0.8078.96.

This patch arrives just days after Chrome 157 launched. That release fixed 213 security issues, including seven rated Critical, as our earlier report on the Chrome 157 update covered.

Google says many of its security bugs are caught by tools such as AddressSanitizer, MemorySanitizer, Control Flow Integrity and libFuzzer. These tools help find memory errors before they reach the stable channel. Zero-days like this one show that some still slip through. You can read the full list of code changes in this build.

Chrome downloads updates in the background, but the fix only works after a restart. Open the menu, choose Help, then About Google Chrome, and select Relaunch when it appears. Linux users should update through their package manager.

People who use Chromium-based browsers should watch for vendor patches, because they often share the same engine code.

articles.title: Terminal2Shell: 55-Year-Old ‘Zero-Day’ Dating Back to 1971 Claims to Affect Billions of Devices
articles.description:
Terminal2Shell claims a critical flaw dating back to 1971 affects more than two billion devices, allowing anyone who opens a terminal to gain an interactive shell. However, the website is satire, not a confirmed vulnerability disclosure. Its “exploit” describes normal terminal use, making it a joke about security marketing rather than a newly discovered threat. […]

The post Terminal2Shell: 55-Year-Old ‘Zero-Day’ Dating Back to 1971 Claims to Affect Billions of Devices appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Terminal2Shell claims a critical flaw dating back to 1971 affects more than two billion devices, allowing anyone who opens a terminal to gain an interactive shell.

However, the website is satire, not a confirmed vulnerability disclosure. Its “exploit” describes normal terminal use, making it a joke about security marketing rather than a newly discovered threat.

The page calls the issue “TermGeddon,” lists its CVE as pending, and claims a CVSS score of 11.0 out of 10. That score is an immediate warning sign because the official CVSS scale stops at 10.0. Claims about billions of affected devices should therefore not be treated as verified findings.

Terminal2Shell 55-Year-Old ‘Zero-Day’

The supposed attack requires local access, a keyboard, and the ability to open a terminal. It then gives the person the permissions of the account already signed in.

Nothing in this description demonstrates an authentication bypass, remote compromise, or access to another user’s account. The claimed attack simply starts with access the person already has.

This distinction matters. A shell provides a way to enter commands. A security flaw must do more than show that commands run when an authorized user types them. Terminal2Shell presents expected behavior as a critical discovery, using alarming labels and a branded website to make an ordinary feature sound dangerous.

For readers, the useful question is not whether a demonstration opens a shell. It is who controls that shell, what access they needed beforehand, and whether the attack crosses a security boundary. Terminal2Shell’s own description fails that test because the user already has the access being “obtained.”

How Real Shell Exploits Differ

The Terminal2Shell website contrasts sharply with Able2Shell. N-able took hosted N-central servers offline after reports of 33 alleged vulnerabilities and published exploit code.

Huntress identified four exploit chains, including three leading to remote code execution. Unlike opening your own terminal, these chains involve attackers gaining control through weaknesses in management software.

Plex2Shell shows why that difference matters. Attackers reportedly used a chain of Plex flaws to install cryptocurrency miners shortly after exploit code became public. The reported fixed release is Plex Media Server 1.43.3.10861. Users should check their installed version rather than assume an exposed server remains safe because it works normally.

PHP2Shell involved another important distinction: gaining an initial foothold is not always the final step. Researchers reported attackers combining it with a Linux kernel flaw to obtain root access on 25 servers. Updating an application alone would not address a separate weakness in the underlying operating system.

HTTP2Shell and Node2Shell concern a Brotli decoding flaw, not ordinary command entry. Reported effects differ across affected software, including crashes and demonstrated code execution. Node.js users should check the fixed releases listed in the coverage: 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1. A shared component does not mean every affected product has an identical attack path.

WP2Shell reportedly allows attackers to create WordPress administrator accounts and install web shells without signing in. That missing login requirement marks a real security boundary being crossed. The coverage identifies WordPress 6.8.6, 6.9.5, and 7.0.2 as fixed releases.

Terminal2Shell needs no emergency patch based on its stated behavior. Its practical lesson is to separate dramatic branding from evidence: identify the affected product, required access, demonstrated impact, and available fix before treating a claim as an incident.

articles.title: N-able Takes N-central Servers Offline Worldwide After 33 0-Day Vulnerabilities and Able2Shell Exploits
articles.description:
N-able took its hosted N-central environments offline on November 9, 2026, after an independent researcher published details of 33 alleged zero-day vulnerabilities and exploit code. The company also told customers running N-central on their own servers to take them offline until further notice, creating an outage for users of its remote monitoring and management platform. […]

The post N-able Takes N-central Servers Offline Worldwide After 33 0-Day Vulnerabilities and Able2Shell Exploits appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
N-able took its hosted N-central environments offline on November 9, 2026, after an independent researcher published details of 33 alleged zero-day vulnerabilities and exploit code.

The company also told customers running N-central on their own servers to take them offline until further notice, creating an outage for users of its remote monitoring and management platform.

The shutdown covers hosted services across the Americas, Europe, and Asia-Pacific. N-able said the move was a precaution while its teams worked on a hotfix. As of November 9 at 15:15 UTC, the company said it had not seen active exploitation. Customers were told not to restore servers until N-able confirms they can safely return online.

The public release, called Able2Shell, contains technical writeups and proof-of-concept code. Huntress reported that the 33 disclosed issues can form four separate exploit chains.

Three lead to remote code execution, allowing commands to run on a vulnerable server. The fourth enables privilege escalation to root, the most powerful account on the underlying operating system.

The research targets N-central Appliance 2026.4.0.31, with earlier versions also potentially affected. However, the full scope remains unconfirmed.

Censys noted that N-able had not published an affected-version list, fixed versions, CVE identifiers, or severity scores for these newly disclosed issues as of November 9. The reported count should therefore remain distinct from a vendor-validated vulnerability list.

N-central gives managed service providers a central place to monitor devices, install patches, run scripts, and support customer systems. That access makes a server compromise especially serious. Earlier N-central authentication bypass attacks showed how attackers could use the platform’s Take Control feature to reach managed devices. Those previous incidents are separate from Able2Shell.

Able2Shell Exploit Chains Allow Server Takeover

According to Field Effect’s analysis, the disclosure includes both authenticated and unauthenticated weaknesses. Claimed impacts include command execution, credential exposure, administrator account creation, configuration changes, and audit record manipulation.

One published Python proof of concept describes an XML External Entity, or XXE, flaw that can be chained into remote code execution without a login.

An XXE flaw occurs when an application processes unsafe references inside XML data. In this case, researchers describe it as an entry point into a broader server takeover chain. However, the public release should not be treated as proof that every claimed issue works across every installation. Censys cautioned that N-able’s notice did not confirm the individual mechanisms or impacts.

The incident follows earlier N-central security problems, including an actively exploited remote code execution vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-86218. That flaw received a September hotfix.

It is not an Able2Shell identifier, and installing an earlier security update does not establish protection against this new disclosure. Customers need guidance specific to the current incident.

Some management functions remain available despite the classic N-central outage. N-able’s notice directs eligible customers to its separate application portal using N-able Login.

The application documentation describes asset views, patch management, vulnerability management, scripts, policies, and tags. Availability depends on permissions, licensing, and configuration. Take Control through this portal currently supports Windows devices, not macOS.

For defenders, Huntress recommends reviewing login and authentication activity from November 8 onward. Teams should investigate unexpected administrator accounts, unusual remote access sessions, and newly deployed scripts.

Suspicious activity should trigger an incident response review that includes customer networks managed through the affected server, rather than stopping at the N-central appliance itself.

Recovery should follow N-able’s instructions, not simply the appearance of an update. Huntress noted that live hotfixes may not change the displayed version number. Administrators should keep servers offline, confirm that the required fix has been applied, and wait for explicit clearance before restoring access to production management services.

The post N-able Takes N-central Servers Offline Worldwide After 33 0-Day Vulnerabilities and Able2Shell Exploits appeared first on Cyber Security News.

articles.title: New Abe Office Malware Bypasses Chrome App-Bound Encryption to Steal Browser Passwords and Cookies
articles.description:
A new remote-access trojan called Abe Office can steal browser passwords and cookies, even from Chrome’s App-Bound Encryption. It poses as an office helper tool and carries a valid code-signing certificate. Researchers at Rogue Authority broke its weak protections and watched the operator at work in a sandbox. Abe Office malware The file is named […]

The post New Abe Office Malware Bypasses Chrome App-Bound Encryption to Steal Browser Passwords and Cookies appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A new remote-access trojan called Abe Office can steal browser passwords and cookies, even from Chrome’s App-Bound Encryption. It poses as an office helper tool and carries a valid code-signing certificate.

Researchers at Rogue Authority broke its weak protections and watched the operator at work in a sandbox.

Abe Office malware

The file is named AbeAgent.exe and calls itself the “Abe Office workstation helper.” No such product exists. The file is signed through SSL.com in the name of a private person, Kimberley Hankinson, in Pennsylvania. The certificate became valid on 26 October 2026 and the file was signed on 4 November.

A signature only shows who sealed a file and that nobody changed it afterward. It does not prove the file is safe. A brand-new certificate in a person’s name, used at once to sign a “company” product, is a pattern researchers see again and again in signed malware. The certificate has been reported to the CA and added to the CertGraveyard.

The name “Abe” most likely stands for App-Bound Encryption, the Chrome feature the malware is built to beat.

On first run, the program copies itself to the user’s profile folder and restarts from there. It removes the Mark of the Web tag, which is the hidden label Windows uses to warn about downloaded files.

It then adds a Run key named “Abe Office Sync” and a scheduled task, both starting it with the switch –autostart. It also tries to add a firewall rule called “Abe Office Agent.”

Three encrypted add-ons are written to disk. One is the main RAT, one runs the hidden desktop, and one is a small helper that runs inside the browser. Before loading them, the starter asks its server for a key. The goal is to hide the add-ons from anyone who has only the file.

According to technical research published by Rogue Authority, the lock does not hold. The file contains a default password, AbeOffice-ChangeMe, which can be used to work out every key. Researchers decrypted all three add-ons this way. The key sent by the live server matched the one they had computed offline.

The same password protects the network traffic. The AES key is just a hash of that password, so the whole captured conversation could be read. This is good news for defenders, since anyone holding a sample can unpack the kit.

The hidden desktop add-on creates an invisible Windows desktop and starts browsers on it. It first copies the victim’s Chrome and Edge profiles to C:\ProgramData\AbeOffice\SystemCache. In the sandbox it copied 287 profile files. A browser opened from those copies is already signed in to email, banking and shopping sites.

This lets the operator act as the victim without a password, and from the victim’s own PC. That helps get past “new device” checks. Hidden-desktop tools like this are growing in number, as shown by our earlier report on Shadow hVNC, which also steals cookies and reuses live sessions.

In a multi-day sandbox run, the operator connected three times over about a day and a half. The operator listed the browsers, opened Chrome and Edge on the hidden desktop, and went straight to the saved-password pages. The sandbox held no saved passwords, so nothing was taken.

Google added App-Bound Encryption in Chrome 127 in July 2024. A Windows service with system rights checks which app is asking before it gives up the key. Google said malware would now need system rights or code injection, which are noisier actions. Google’s security blog explains the design.

Abe Office takes the second route. It starts a browser off-screen at position -32000,-32000 and injects its helper DLL. The helper asks the browser’s own elevation service to decrypt the key. Because the request comes from the real browser, the service agrees.

The key is saved to C:\ProgramData\AbeOffice\abe_job\key.dat. The code also holds backup routes, including a browser extension named “Abe Crypto Bridge.”

Other stealers use similar tricks. SpyCloud found that families such as Lumma and Vidar claimed bypasses soon after launch. Phemedrone used Chrome’s remote debugging port. Our earlier story on infostealers bypassing Chrome’s cookie protection covers Elastic’s findings on these methods. A recent Marsalek malware report shows the same DLL injection idea.

The command server at 2.26.230[.]54 also hosts the operator’s control panel. Shodan data showed its Windows computer name matched the one that drove the hidden browsers. Its port 80 served an “Abe Update” page listing the kit’s files.

A second server, 87.199.195[.]141, served the same page. VirusTotal links 133 files to the two servers, first seen between mid-September and early November.

They include 10 other AbeAgent.exe files, 61 launcher-bootstrap-stub.exe files and 49 app.zip packages. Only this build uses a certificate from a real CA, so it may be the newest step. The delivery method is still unknown.

If you ran this file, treat your browser sessions as stolen. From a clean device, sign out of all sessions, change passwords for key accounts starting with email, and turn on two-factor authentication. Then clean or reinstall the PC.

Defenders should look for the AbeOffice folders, the “Abe Office Sync” Run value and any process started with –autostart. They should block outbound traffic to both servers on port 9090.

They should also flag browsers launched with –window-position=-32000,-32000 or with local remote debugging, and non-browser programs reading Login Data, Cookies and Local State files. A sign-in from the victim’s own PC should not be trusted by default either.

The post New Abe Office Malware Bypasses Chrome App-Bound Encryption to Steal Browser Passwords and Cookies appeared first on Cyber Security News.

articles.title: Notepad++ 8.9.9 Released With Fixes for 6 Vulnerabilities Allowing Plugin Command Execution
articles.description:
Notepad++ released version 8.9.9 on November 6, 2026, fixing six security flaws across Windows message handling, protected file saving, clipboard operations, and MIME Tools decoding. The update addresses flaws including conditional plugin command execution, memory exposure, and buffer overflow. The release notes list no assigned CVE identifiers for these issues. The command execution issue involves […]

The post Notepad++ 8.9.9 Released With Fixes for 6 Vulnerabilities Allowing Plugin Command Execution appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Notepad++ released version 8.9.9 on November 6, 2026, fixing six security flaws across Windows message handling, protected file saving, clipboard operations, and MIME Tools decoding.

The update addresses flaws including conditional plugin command execution, memory exposure, and buffer overflow. The release notes list no assigned CVE identifiers for these issues.

The command execution issue involves WM_COPYDATA, a Windows message used to exchange data between applications. In Notepad++ 8.9.8, the sender checks whether a window handle supplied by the caller is trusted rather than proving which process sent the message. A local attacker could nominate a separate, legitimate Notepad++ window to pass those checks.

This could let an attacker pass plugin commands into an elevated editor. However, the demonstrated attack required the optional NppExec plugin to be installed and initialized, an already elevated target, and a second Notepad++ instance running from the same executable path. It is local privilege escalation under specific conditions, not network-based remote code execution.

The release separately lists a WM_COPYDATA sender authentication bypass and the plugin command execution flaw. Both highlight the danger of trusting caller-controlled message data across privilege levels.

The update follows earlier Notepad++ code execution fixes involving configuration files, although those earlier vulnerabilities have different causes.

Another flaw affects saves that require User Account Control approval. Notepad++ wrote document contents into a temporary file, closed it, and passed its path to an elevated helper.

A malicious process running as the same user could replace those contents before the helper copied them into the protected file selected by the user. User approval remained necessary.

Memory Flaws and Plugin Risks

The heap disclosure advisory describes an unchecked clipboard length in Paste Binary. A local process could supply a small text buffer alongside a larger claimed size, causing Notepad++ to copy adjacent process memory into a document. Testing recovered heap data beyond the supplied buffer.

The NPPM_MENUCOMMAND flaw used unchecked indexes when selecting stored commands. Testing showed out-of-bounds data reaching ShellExecute and blocking the interface, but attacker control over the resulting command was not demonstrated.

Separately, MIME Tools versions through 3.1 contain SAML Decode buffer overflows. Crafted input could crash the editor or potentially execute code when decoded. MIME Tools 3.2 fixes that issue.

Earlier Notepad++ plugin abuse involved replaced plugin files, a different attack path from these newly patched flaws. Users should install version 8.9.9 through the official download page and verify MIME Tools is updated.

The release also improves Find in Files performance, refreshes Scintilla and Lexilla, adds dialog font controls, and fixes clipboard history errors and memory leaks.

articles.title: GhostAction Hackers Compromise 500+ GitHub Accounts to Steal AWS, OpenAI, and Cloud Credentials
articles.description:
A new wave of the GhostAction campaign has hit more than 500 GitHub accounts. The attackers use those accounts to plant a fake security workflow in tens of thousands of repositories, and the workflow steals cloud, AI, and publishing keys. Security firm Socket reports that the accounts added the malicious file starting October 7, 2026, […]

The post GhostAction Hackers Compromise 500+ GitHub Accounts to Steal AWS, OpenAI, and Cloud Credentials appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A new wave of the GhostAction campaign has hit more than 500 GitHub accounts. The attackers use those accounts to plant a fake security workflow in tens of thousands of repositories, and the workflow steals cloud, AI, and publishing keys.

Security firm Socket reports that the accounts added the malicious file starting October 7, 2026, and that some of the repositories belong to large organizations.

GhostAction GitHub account compromise

Socket studied a burst on October 8, 2026. Two hijacked accounts, henrywoo and kitao, pushed a file named security-audit.yml into 346 repositories.

The commit messages were “Add security audit workflow” and “Update security audit workflow.” Despite the name, the file does no security work. It collects secrets and sends them in plain text to the IP address 193.32.204[.]199.

The list of targets includes uber/athenadriver, which is owned by Uber, and kitao/pyxel, a popular Python game engine with more than 18,000 stars. The henrywoo account has write access to the Uber project because he is its original author.

This shows why one stolen maintainer account is so costly. The damage reaches every repository the account can edit, not just the owner’s own projects.

The attackers first get a working login for a maintainer account. Socket did not see how they did this. Next, they scan each repository for the secret names its workflows already use, and they write those names into the fake file.

Last, they commit the file straight to the default branch, where it runs on the next push. The same file went into hundreds of repositories within minutes, so Socket believes a tool did the work and not a person.

The timing supports that view. The henrywoo changes landed in a window of about 16 minutes, and the kitao changes landed in a four-minute window. Even repositories that had sat idle for a decade got the file.

You can read how this campaign grew in our earlier GhostAction coverage of the 772-repository wave, which tracked the same weak spot in GitHub Actions.

According to technical research published by Socket, earlier GhostAction waves only took secrets stored in GitHub Actions. GitGuardian first described that style in September 2025, when 327 users and 817 repositories lost 3,325 secrets.

The new version keeps that trick and adds a search through the repository files and the full git history.

This matters because many developers delete a key from the latest file and think the problem is gone. The old commit still holds the key.

The workflow uses a setting called fetch-depth: 0, which pulls every branch and tag so the script can read the whole past of the project.

The script looks for 13 types of keys. These include AWS access keys and session tokens, plus OpenAI, Anthropic, and OpenRouter API keys. It also looks for GitHub and GitLab tokens, Google and Firebase keys, Slack tokens, and SendGrid keys.

One detail shows the AWS focus. An AWS key ID alone cannot log in to anything. The secret half usually sits a line or two away in an .env file or a Terraform file.

So the script also copies two lines above and below each key ID. That lets the attacker rebuild a full, usable AWS key pair.

Stolen publishing tokens are just as risky. For Pyxel, the named secrets were tokens for PyPI and crates.io plus a GitHub personal access token. With those, an attacker could push a bad update of a package that many people trust.

As of October 9, 2026, the file was still on the default branch of the repositories Socket checked. The workflow had also run successfully, which means data could already have left.

Socket saw no bad package versions on PyPI or crates.io at the time of writing, but that does not prove the stolen keys went unused.

Forks add more risk. Socket counted 279 forks under the henrywoo name that carry the file, and Actions can run it on later pushes if they are enabled.

Machine learning projects such as henrywoo/pyllama and henrywoo/chatllama stand out, since their users often hold AWS and AI keys.

The campaign has kept growing. OpenSourceMalware counted 790 repositories with the workflow through October 9, 2026, which our team covered in a report on 790 hijacked GitHub repositories. AI tools can make exposed keys even more dangerous.

Microsoft says attackers used an AI framework called ARTEX to find GitHub secrets and reach Azure Key Vault in about five minutes, as shown in our ARTEX AI report.

Start by opening .github/workflows/security-audit.yml and checking which secret names it lists. Rotate every secret named there.

For a GitHub personal access token, revoke it and make a new one. Then review the Actions run history and treat every finished run as a successful theft.

Next, scan the full git history with git log -p –all and rotate every key you find, even if it no longer shows in the current files. For AWS keys, check CloudTrail for new IAM users, new access keys, and use in odd regions.

Treat the maintainer account as fully compromised. Revoke all sessions, tokens, OAuth grants, and SSH keys. Turn on phishing-resistant multi-factor login, then search the organization audit log for new workflow files.

Block 193.32.204[.]199 in egress logs, including self-hosted runners. Finally, turn on GitHub secret scanning with push protection and require approval for workflow runs from outside contributors.

The post GhostAction Hackers Compromise 500+ GitHub Accounts to Steal AWS, OpenAI, and Cloud Credentials appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Attackers using Anubis ransomware broke into a U.S. organization in October 2026. They used a new custom backdoor called Lindnor and dropped at least 13 tools built to switch off security software.

Symantec’s Protection Bulletin says the encryption payload was blocked before it could run.

Anubis ransomware Lindnor backdoor

Symantec tracks the developer of Anubis as Hawkmoth. The group runs a ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) operation that appeared in December 2024 as a rebrand of the Sphinx ransomware. The payload looks mostly unchanged from Sphinx, and only the branding is new.

Because Hawkmoth lets affiliates carry out the attacks, the methods can change from one break-in to the next. Researchers at Barracuda have described the group’s mix of wiping, leaking and extortion. The group has claimed about 96 victims in the past 12 months, and 52% of them are in the United States.

The group is also persistent. In a July 2026 case, Symantec saw the attackers use four different tools to steal data: Megasync, WinSCP, Filezilla and S3browser. Using that many tools of one type in a single attack is unusual.

According to technical research published by Symantec, investigators did not learn how the attackers first got in. The first warning sign was the Lindnor backdoor, which sat on two machines. Those were the only two Microsoft SQL Servers among the affected systems.

The attackers named the backdoor healthcontroller64.exe on one machine and placed it in a folder made to look like a Chrome component directory. On the other machine it was svchelper.exe in a VMware folder. Both copies ran as a service.

Lindnor sends the process ID, Windows version, file path, computer name, user name, domain and logon server to its command-and-control server. It has a main server and a backup, and both use port 443, which blends in with normal web traffic.

Custom backdoors are rare in ransomware cases, since most crews use public or built-in tools. Symantec also saw Lindnor on two other unrelated networks, but no ransomware appeared there.

Within about an hour, the attackers dropped at least 13 executables meant to shut down security products. They leaned on a method called Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver (BYOVD) and brought five signed but flawed drivers to get kernel-level control.

Two of the tools, gbbsym.exe and symgooq.exe, pretended to be Symantec software. Eleven of the 13 had not been published before, though all the drivers were already known.

Symantec blocked every dropped file except huntreagent.exe and s1.exe. Those two have the same size but different hashes, so they may be two builds of one tool. The pattern looks like trial and error, with the attackers trying one tool after another until something worked.

BYOVD works because Windows trusts signed drivers. Symantec’s Lights Out whitepaper says hundreds of vulnerable drivers are in circulation and that BYOVD tools now come bundled with RaaS kits.

Our earlier report on EDR killer tactics beyond vulnerable drivers shows how common these tools have become.

The attackers installed the real AnyDesk remote tool, then created a new local user and added it to a local group. They also ran safemode.exe, which sets AnyDesk to keep working when Windows starts in Safe Mode with Networking.

This matters because most security software does not fully run in Safe Mode. That gives attackers a quiet window to load drivers and turn off protection. The trick is not new, but it is rarely seen.

The Anubis encryptor was named iservice.exe. It adds the .anubis extension to files and leaves ransom notes called restore files.txt and restore files.html. The notes say data was stolen and will be published if talks fail.

Anubis also has an optional wiper mode that empties file contents. Our earlier coverage of Anubis wipe mode explains why paying may not bring files back. In this case, Symantec blocked the payload before encryption began.

The attackers came ready for security tools to get in their way, but the last step still failed. Symantec says few ransomware crews build their own backdoors.

Defenders should watch for the file names and hashes Symantec listed, including the domains msrcontrib[.]com and cfgsync-relay.eastus.cloudapp.azure[.]com. The key Lindnor hash is fc200686175559f4544a5de826905f09a68476d889690a3be40ac32356790cb8.

Teams should also block known vulnerable drivers, limit admin rights and alert on new services that mimic Chrome or VMware files.

Watch SQL Servers closely, because both Lindnor infections were found there. Finally, review any AnyDesk install and any odd Safe Mode registry change.

articles.title: Jailbroken DeepSeek AI Agent Breaches European Telecom and Accesses Millions of Patient Records
articles.description:
A jailbroken DeepSeek AI agent spent more than two weeks breaking into a European telecom provider and 13 companies hosted on its systems. It reportedly reached millions of healthcare records along the way. Researchers at Malbear Labs call the campaign “Operation Snowball.” They found it after a routine sweep turned up an open directory holding […]

The post Jailbroken DeepSeek AI Agent Breaches European Telecom and Accesses Millions of Patient Records appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A jailbroken DeepSeek AI agent spent more than two weeks breaking into a European telecom provider and 13 companies hosted on its systems. It reportedly reached millions of healthcare records along the way.

Researchers at Malbear Labs call the campaign “Operation Snowball.” They found it after a routine sweep turned up an open directory holding the attacker’s full workspace.

Jailbroken DeepSeek AI agent Breach

According to technical research published by Malbear Labs, the open directory needed no password. Inside were about 70 session transcripts, scan results for hundreds of hosts, stolen credentials and database dumps. Everything the operator typed and every report the agents wrote back was in Chinese.

The researchers did not publish the server’s IP address, which protects the victims. They also warn that the operator’s language does not prove nationality or any link to a government.

The setup was a custom agent framework built on DeepSeek Flash, a model with a one-million-token context window. That window let the main agent keep every host, password and failed attempt in memory for days. A human attacker has to re-read notes after each break. This agent did not.

DeepSeek normally refuses to write webshells or guess passwords. The operator got around this with a 78,000-character system prompt. It began with a public jailbreak template called “Little Code Sauce,” which spread through a plugin community on a Chinese forum.

The operator removed its roleplay tricks and added about 400 lines of attack instructions. The prompt told the model that a refusal was a malfunction and gave it a list of refusal phrases to avoid in English and Chinese.

This matches what other teams have seen. Palo Alto’s Unit 42 reported that a hacker named BUGSTER used a jailbroken DeepSeek V4 with the Hermes Agent framework.

That actor stole more than 5,200 records from an Indian university, and the jailbreak was only a simple system-prompt override. You can read our earlier coverage of that case for the full timeline.

The agent ran tasks from scouting to data theft with very little help. It scanned networks, tested passwords, deployed webshells and moved between systems. When defenses blocked it, it changed course.

Reports say it wrote its own replacement tunneling tool and rebuilt an exploit chain against a locked-down Liferay server.

The operator’s messages were very short. One was “Go on,” and another told the agent to close up the latest high-risk hole. The agent chose the target, the flaw and the method. A person running this does not need to understand the techniques.

The harness also scored every break-in, like a game. A pivot into a separate internal network segment earned far more points than a single server shell. Security tools such as firewall consoles also scored high.

At the time of recovery the total was 3,725 points. The scoring shows the operator cared most about the systems that watch and divide a network.

The most worrying finding involves healthcare data. Default login details reportedly gave the agent full database admin access to a TrakCare system running on an old Oracle 9i database.

That exposed millions of records across patient, vaccination and appointment tables. The agent also pulled thousands of rows of subscriber billing and device data and took cryptographic keys from the telecom.

One caution applies. A summary of the report notes that these outcomes were not independently verified in the material available. Treat the exact scale as the researchers’ claim for now.

Even so, the root cause is basic, because an unchanged default password opened the door.

This campaign is not a one-off. CrowdStrike reported that the China-linked group VAPOR PANDA ran the ARTEX framework, mostly on DeepSeek, against more than 200 organizations in at least 14 countries over 11 days starting October 17.

It confirmed access at nine organizations, where the group planted the BLOODALCHEMY backdoor. Telecom providers in the US, Belgium and the Philippines were also hit.

Speed is a big change here. CrowdStrike’s Adam Meyers said human intruders usually run up to 40 commands an hour, while ARTEX activity passed 1,500. Our own report on how ARTEX automates enterprise attacks explains the framework in more detail.

Because no human sits at the keyboard, hunting for working-hours patterns or slow, careful sessions will not help. The agent’s activity is loud and repetitive, so watch endpoint and network logs for fast scanning, bursts of failed logins and unusual tunnels.

Start with the basics:

  • Change every default password, especially on old database systems.
  • Keep internal network segments truly separate.
  • Place endpoint sensors on servers that seem unreachable from the internet.
  • Keep an eye on open directories and exposed storage.

The lesson is simple. AI did not invent new weaknesses. It found the old ones faster than any team can patch them.

The post Jailbroken DeepSeek AI Agent Breaches European Telecom and Accesses Millions of Patient Records appeared first on Cyber Security News.

articles.title: Hackers Used Default admin:admin Credentials to Exploit ForgeRock RCE and Remotely Unlock Cars
articles.description:
Researchers used default admin:admin credentials as part of a vulnerability chain that let them run code on two automakers’ production ForgeRock servers and remotely unlock connected cars. Found in early 2026 and disclosed on November 7, the flaws also exposed vehicle locations and supported remote engine commands. The findings came from controlled security research, not […]

The post Hackers Used Default admin:admin Credentials to Exploit ForgeRock RCE and Remotely Unlock Cars appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Researchers used default admin:admin credentials as part of a vulnerability chain that let them run code on two automakers’ production ForgeRock servers and remotely unlock connected cars.

Found in early 2026 and disclosed on November 7, the flaws also exposed vehicle locations and supported remote engine commands.

The findings came from controlled security research, not a reported criminal campaign. Both unnamed automakers fixed the issue within about two hours of receiving the report and rotated affected credentials. Their identity systems served multiple regions, but the researchers tested the complete account takeover and vehicle access chain only with US accounts and vehicles.

ForgeRock Attack Chain

The investigation began with the Android apps used by vehicle owners. Both apps relied on ForgeRock Access Management for login sessions and OpenIDM for customer records. Tracing an email validation request led the researchers toward administrative services, including the Apache Felix Web Console running alongside OpenIDM.

A web application firewall blocked direct requests to those services. However, specially encoded paths made requests appear to target static files while Jetty, the backend web server, interpreted them as console requests. This mismatch in URL handling exposed the hidden management interface, where the documented default username and password still worked.

Access to Felix’s ConfigMgr interface allowed the researchers to create an OpenIDM scheduled task that ran Groovy code. They used it to install a small Java component inside the running service, giving them a controlled command endpoint. This confirmed remote code execution within the production identity process rather than inside the cars themselves.

From Server Access to Vehicle Commands

According to the researchers’ technical report, server access exposed administrative credentials that allowed local requests to customer records. The team changed a test account’s email and password, received its verification codes, and completed the normal login process. They then exchanged the session for tokens accepted by the vehicle APIs.

Those tokens exposed the account’s vehicles, location, status, and supported remote controls. With the owner beside the test vehicle, Shah confirmed unlocking, engine start, engine stop, and locking.

Restoring the original email did not cancel the new tokens. The findings follow earlier Kia remote access research and Subaru STARLINK security flaws.

Ping Identity’s production hardening guide already advises removing or protecting the Felix console and changing its default credentials. It also warns that console authentication is separate from IDM authentication. The case shows why blocking administrative URLs at a firewall cannot replace securing the service behind it, especially when that service controls customer identity and access to connected vehicles.

articles.description:
