The post Top 10 Best Threat Hunting Services in 2026 [Ranked & Scored] appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Detection engineering catches what you anticipated; threat hunting catches what you didn’t. The craft is hypothesis-driven “if an actor used this tradecraft here, what residue would exist?” and the services market sells it in two shapes: platform-native hunting across a vendor’s own telemetry ocean, and estate-attached hunting through MDR relationships.

One jurisdictional note is handled plainly at 10. CrowdStrike OverWatch takes 1; Mandiant and Red Canary complete the podium.

Key Takeaways

• 1 overall: CrowdStrike OverWatch the reference for continuous, human-led hunting at telemetry scale.

• Podium: OverWatch (scale+tempo), Mandiant (actor-knowledge depth), Red Canary (published-methodology transparency).

• Shape split: platform-native hunters (OverWatch, Sophos, Trellix) hunt their own sensor oceans; estate-attached hunters (Expel, eSentire, Secureworks) hunt what you grant telemetry reach decides value either way.

• Jurisdiction note: Kaspersky’s hunting research is technically formidable; Western procurement restrictions gate it regardless compliance decides before capability.

How We Scored (Methodology)

Research-based evaluation; no lab testing, no paid placement; editorial scores excluded from structured data. Criteria: hypothesis-craft maturity, telemetry reach, hunt tempo (continuous versus periodic), findings quality (novel TTPs surfaced, not re-labeled alerts), feedback loop into detections, and transparency of method.

Weights: hypothesis craft 25%, telemetry reach 25%, tempo 15%, findings quality 20%, detection feedback 15%.

The 2026 Threat Hunting Power Rankings

*Editorial research-based scores, not lab results.

1. CrowdStrike (OverWatch) — Best Continuous Hunting at Scale

Snapshot: Falcon add-on subscription | 24/7 human hunt teams on global telemetry | Hunt-to-detection pipeline

Why it earns 1: OverWatch defined managed hunting’s modern form: human hunters working planetary Falcon telemetry around the clock, pattern-matching across millions of endpoints so a novel tradecraft seen once becomes a hunt lead everywhere.

Findings feed Falcon’s detection content, compounding the loop. If your estate runs Falcon, the marginal power of attaching OverWatch is the category’s best ratio.

Pros: Telemetry ocean; 24/7 tempo; cross-customer pattern leverage; detection feedback.

Cons: Hunts Falcon’s view non-Falcon estates see less.

Bottom line: The hunting benchmark, priced as a Falcon multiplier.

2. Google (Mandiant) — Best Actor-Knowledge Hunting

Snapshot: Managed hunt engagements + retainer pairing | Frontline actor intel as hypothesis source | Compromise-assessment craft

Why it ranks here: Mandiant hunts from the actor’s biography: hypotheses sourced from live incident-floor knowledge of specific groups’ tradecraft, applied in targeted hunts and compromise assessments.

Where OverWatch hunts broad and continuous, Mandiant hunts deep and informed the team you point at “are they in here?”

Pros: Actor-specific hypotheses; compromise-assessment rigor; intel provenance.

Cons: Engagement-shaped more than continuous-service-shaped.

Bottom line: Hunting with the adversary’s file open.

3. SentinelOne Wayfinder MDR — Best AI-Assisted Managed Threat Hunting

Snapshot: MDR subscription | Singularity platform + Purple AI | Endpoint, identity, cloud, and telemetry hunting

Why it ranks here: SentinelOne Wayfinder MDR combines human-led threat hunting with the Singularity platform’s behavioral detections threat intelligence, and AI-assisted investigation.

Its hunters use Purple AI and cross-environment telemetry to investigate suspicious activity, validate threats, and accelerate response across endpoint, identity, cloud, and other security data.

Pros: Strong platform telemetry; AI-assisted investigations; broad attack-surface coverage; integrated response.

Cons: Best value comes when organizations are already invested in the SentinelOne ecosystem.

Bottom line: Human threat hunters amplified by automation, behavioral analytics, and AI.

4. eSentire — Best Response-Fused Hunting

Snapshot: Service tiers | Hunts that end in containment | Threat response unit linkage

Why it ranks here: eSentire welds hunting to its response authority: hypotheses worked by its threat response unit, and findings that don’t become reports they become containment actions within the same hour.

For buyers who measure hunting by evicted adversaries rather than documents produced, the fusion is the feature.

Pros: Hunt-to-containment speed; 24/7 operation; original research input.

Cons: Full value requires granted response authority.

Bottom line: Hunts that end with someone locked out.

5. Expel — Best BYO-Stack Hunting

Snapshot: Add-on to MDR | Hunts across your existing tooling | Transparent Workbench findings

Why it ranks here: Expel hunts the estate you already built EDR, cloud, identity, SaaS with hypotheses tuned to your tech mix and findings written in Workbench where you watch the investigation unfold.

The BYO respect extends to honesty about signal gaps: they’ll tell you which telemetry you lack to support which hunts.

Pros: Stack-agnostic reach; transparency; signal-gap honesty.

Cons: Hunt depth bounded by the telemetry you grant.

Bottom line: Your stack, hunted honestly.

6. Huntress — Best Human-Led Threat Hunting for Lean Teams

Snapshot: Subscription-based | 24/7 human-led SOC | Managed EDR + identity and security monitoring

Why it ranks here: Huntress focuses on making managed threat hunting accessible to organizations without large internal SOC teams, combining endpoint telemetry, identity monitoring, and human investigation.

Its analysts continuously review suspicious activity, investigate persistent footholds and attacker behavior, and provide guided remediation rather than simply forwarding alerts.

Pros: Human-led investigations; strong mid-market fit; straightforward deployment; actionable remediation guidance.

Cons: Narrower telemetry and global-scale hunting depth than large XDR platform providers.

Bottom line: Practical human-led hunting for teams that need expert coverage without building a full SOC.

7. Sophos — Best Mid-Market Managed Hunting

Snapshot: MDR tiers including hunt function | X-Ops research teams | Cross-product telemetry

Why it ranks here: Sophos folds genuine hunting into MDR economics the mid-market clears: X-Ops research driving hypotheses, hunts across endpoint/firewall/email telemetry, and response included.

It’s the pragmatic answer for organizations that will never buy a standalone hunt engagement but deserve better than alert triage.

Pros: Hunt-inclusive MDR pricing; X-Ops research; product-telemetry breadth.

Cons: Depth ceilings versus dedicated hunt benches.

Bottom line: Real hunting at MDR-bundle prices.

8. Rapid7 — Best Bundled Hunting Value

Snapshot: MDR-inclusive hunting | InsightIDR telemetry base | Vulnerability-context pairing

Why it ranks here: Rapid7’s managed hunting rides the Insight platform: periodic and lead-driven hunts across InsightIDR telemetry with exposure context from InsightVM sharpening hypotheses (“this CVE is exploitable here hunt for its post-exploitation residue”). Value-tier honest: solid hunting economics, not frontier craft.

Pros: Bundle economics; exposure-informed leads; platform integration.

Cons: Hunt tempo and depth versus leaders.

Bottom line: The budget-sane hunting attach.

9. Trellix — Best XDR-Estate Hunting

Snapshot: Service attach to XDR | Advanced Research Center input | Broad control-point telemetry

Why it ranks here: Trellix hunts across its XDR fabric endpoint, email, network, DLP control points with Advanced Research Center threat work feeding hypotheses. For the substantial installed base running Trellix controls, attached hunting extracts value from telemetry already flowing; outside that base, the case thins.

Pros: Control-point breadth; research center input; installed-base economics.

Cons: Estate-coupled value; brand momentum.

Bottom line: The Trellix estate’s hunt layer.

10. Kaspersky — Deepest APT Hunt Research, Jurisdiction-Gated

Snapshot: Managed hunting via MDR/intel portal | GReAT-grade hypotheses | Procurement restrictions decide first

Why it ranks here compliance first: On craft alone, Kaspersky’s hunting lineage is elite GReAT’s APT discoveries seeded half the industry’s hypothesis playbook, and its managed hunting inherits that depth.

But US federal prohibition and parallel Western restrictions gate procurement regardless of capability; organizations under those regimes should treat it as unavailable, and others should run compliance review before capability evaluation.

Pros: APT-research depth; unique regional visibility.

Cons: Jurisdictional gates precede technical evaluation.

Bottom line: Elite craft behind a compliance door many can’t open.

Buying Advice: Audit the Hypotheses, Not the Brochure

Hunting services separate on one question brochures never answer: where do hypotheses come from? Demand each candidate walk you through three real hunts the hypothesis, its intel source, the telemetry queried, the outcome and distinguish genuine hypothesis-driven work from re-labeled alert triage, which is the category’s quiet fraud.

Match shape to estate: Falcon shops attach OverWatch almost axiomatically; heterogeneous stacks want BYO hunters (Expel, Red Canary); “are we already owned?” moments buy Mandiant-class compromise assessments rather than subscriptions.

Contract the feedback loop explicitly every hunt finding should become a detection you keep, written into deliverables so the service makes your estate smarter, not just watched.

Set the honest success metric with the provider up front: novel findings per quarter and dwell-time trend, acknowledging that a mature estate yields few true positives a quarter of clean hunts with new detections shipped is success, not failure.

And run every candidate through procurement’s jurisdiction screen first; the Kaspersky gate is the visible case of a general rule.

FAQs

What are the best threat hunting services in 2026? CrowdStrike OverWatch for continuous scale, Mandiant for actor-driven assessments, Red Canary for transparent methodology, eSentire for response fusion, Expel for BYO stacks, with Secureworks, Sophos, Rapid7, Trellix, and Kaspersky (jurisdiction permitting) by fit.

Threat hunting versus MDR aren’t they the same? MDR triages what alerts; hunting hypothesizes what doesn’t real hunting is proactive, hypothesis-driven work, and many MDR contracts include only token amounts of it. Read the deliverables.

What telemetry does hunting need? Endpoint process/command-line data is the floor; identity logs, DNS, and cloud-control-plane events multiply hypothesis space hunters should tell you honestly which hunts your telemetry can’t support.

How do we measure a hunting service? Hypotheses run per quarter with sources shown, novel findings (not re-labeled alerts), detections shipped from findings, and estate dwell-time trend.

Is a clean hunt a wasted hunt? No a documented clean hunt with a new detection shipped is bought-down risk; the waste is hunts without hypotheses or artifacts.

Verdict

Ten services, one craft test: show me the hypothesis. OverWatch hunting the ocean, Mandiant hunting the actor, Red Canary publishing the method, eSentire ending hunts in evictions, Expel respecting your stack, Secureworks and Sophos and Rapid7 and Trellix by estate, Kaspersky behind the compliance gate audit three real hunts, contract the detection feedback, and judge by novel findings and falling dwell time, not by the thickness of the quarterly PDF.

articles.title: DigiCert Confirms Data Breach Exposing Customer Details and Sensitive Identity Documents
articles.description:
DigiCert has confirmed a data breach involving an internal business system that stored customer contact details and identity documents. Unauthorized access exposed archived information, including names, business email addresses, phone numbers, and business addresses. A small minority of affected customer accounts also contained passports, driver’s licenses, utility bills, or other documents showing names and addresses. […]

The post DigiCert Confirms Data Breach Exposing Customer Details and Sensitive Identity Documents appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
DigiCert has confirmed a data breach involving an internal business system that stored customer contact details and identity documents. Unauthorized access exposed archived information, including names, business email addresses, phone numbers, and business addresses.

A small minority of affected customer accounts also contained passports, driver’s licenses, utility bills, or other documents showing names and addresses.

The company said the incident affected only a small proportion of its archived data. Its public report does not provide a total number of affected people, organizations, or documents. DigiCert confirmed the unauthorized data access on October 19, 2026, and filed its preliminary incident report the following day.

DigiCert said its Certificate Authority services, CertCentral, and DigiCert ONE were unaffected. The company said customer login credentials and issued certificates remain secure.

Investigators found no certificate issuance, validation changes, or revocation activity linked to the unauthorized account. Customers do not need to replace active certificates because of this incident.

Troy Hunt shared DigiCert’s notification on X, asking, “Anyone else get one of these from @digicert?” The email said the company was reviewing identity documents to identify affected individuals and would notify them once the review was complete.

DigiCert Confirms Data Breach

The exposure began with an infrastructure migration on February 4, 2025. DigiCert moved the business system from a network segment restricted by a virtual private network, or VPN, to another availability zone. That change accidentally made the internal system accessible from the internet without a security review of its new exposure.

An account registration feature, intended for other uses of the account management platform, also became available. Accounts created through that feature were not covered by the multifactor authentication required for DigiCert staff. Although these accounts had no application assigned, they received read-only access to archived information, revealing a gap in permission checks.

According to DigiCert’s incident report, staff noticed non-DigiCert accounts on June 18, 2026. An initial review incorrectly concluded that accounts without an assigned application could not access data. A web application firewall blocked new registrations through the external access path, but existing access remained a concern.

A report from DigiCert’s managed security research program followed on June 21. Engineers confirmed the registration issue and released an authorization fix on July 2. Investigators later established that unauthorized data access occurred between June 27 and July 2. DigiCert initially treated the problem as an account-creation issue rather than a data-access incident.

The company first suspected access to archived information on October 12. Retained logs and audit records helped investigators reconstruct the access window and link activity to the account. The account could read records but could not change them, approve identity checks, or issue certificates.

DigiCert subsequently disabled self-registration, moved remaining exposed endpoints behind private network infrastructure, reset business system passwords, and strengthened monitoring. It also completed a permissions review and required security approval for network access changes. The report’s action items include further checks on external exposure and account alerts.

This disclosure concerns archived customer information, not compromised certificate operations. It differs from the earlier DigiCert support-system breach involving code-signing certificates and the 2024 DNS validation error that required certificate replacements.

Here, the central failure was allowing newly registered accounts to read sensitive records. DigiCert’s stated lesson is direct: internal tools need explicit authorization checks, even when network restrictions are expected to protect them.

articles.description:
DreamHost has confirmed a breach that exposed customer login details after hackers exploited its web-based File Manager. The hosting provider said attackers obtained FTP/SFTP usernames and passwords, along with some webmail credentials. In a small number of cases, private mailbox contents may also have been viewed. The company discovered unauthorized access on October 23, 2026. […]

The post DreamHost Confirms Data Breach – Hackers Stole Customer Credentials and Accessed Emails appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
DreamHost has confirmed a breach that exposed customer login details after hackers exploited its web-based File Manager. The hosting provider said attackers obtained FTP/SFTP usernames and passwords, along with some webmail credentials. In a small number of cases, private mailbox contents may also have been viewed.

The company discovered unauthorized access on October 23, 2026. Its investigation identified a potential exposure window stretching back to approximately August. Customers who used File Manager during that period have been told to treat their file transfer credentials as compromised, even while investigators continue checking the full impact.

DreamHost currently estimates that well under approximately 10% of its hosted email and FTP/SFTP accounts were affected. That figure refers to accounts, not a confirmed number of individual customers. Some users received precautionary password reset notices but may not have had their credentials exposed.

The confirmation follows DreamHost’s earlier email and FTP password resets, which initially left the cause unclear. Those resets stopped affected users from signing in until account owners created new passwords. File Manager returned online on October 26, according to the earlier incident reporting.

DreamHost found no evidence that attackers accessed control panel logins or customer billing details. It also said full payment card numbers are not stored on its systems because an outside processor handles card payments. These findings remain subject to the ongoing investigation rather than proving that every possible risk has been excluded.

DreamHost Confirms Data Breach

In its October 29 security incident disclosure, DreamHost said the entry point was a flaw in third-party software behind File Manager. The browser-based tool lets customers manage website files. The notice does not name the software, describe the vulnerability, or provide a CVE identifier.

Attackers also reached certain webmail systems and obtained credentials belonging to a limited number of users. DreamHost reset those passwords and ended active sessions on October 23. It is contacting customers individually where investigators believe mailbox contents may have been viewed. The company has not confirmed widespread email theft.

Ending sessions matters alongside changing passwords. Separate reporting on stolen browser cookies and account takeovers explains how an authenticated session can expose email without another login. However, DreamHost’s public announcement does not explicitly confirm stolen session tokens, so that detail should not be treated as established by this notice.

DreamHost took the affected File Manager server offline and preserved it for forensic work. It then rebuilt the service with added safeguards and monitoring, changed potentially exposed internal credentials, and brought in outside security experts. Reviews of other customer-facing tools and required regulator notifications are also underway.

Affected users need their account owner to reset passwords through DreamHost’s control panel. The company recommends unique passwords, changing reused credentials elsewhere, and updating saved passwords in email and file transfer clients. Customers should inspect website files for unexpected changes and check mailbox forwarding rules and filters for unfamiliar entries.

Customers should type panel.dreamhost.com directly into their browser rather than follow login links in unexpected messages. DreamHost says its incident emails never request passwords or ask recipients to sign in through a link.

articles.description:
OpenAI says an automated research pipeline found and proved 948 separate Linux kernel privilege escalation flaws in one run. These bugs could let a normal local user gain root access. The run took place in mid-October 2026 and used an upcoming cyber model, as OpenAI explains in its research write-up. The system first scanned the […]

The post OpenAI Cyber Model Uncovers 948 Linux Kernel Privilege Escalation Vulnerabilities appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
OpenAI says an automated research pipeline found and proved 948 separate Linux kernel privilege escalation flaws in one run. These bugs could let a normal local user gain root access. The run took place in mid-October 2026 and used an upcoming cyber model, as OpenAI explains in its research write-up.

The system first scanned the kernel for the parts a low-privileged user can reach. These “Scout” agents picked 5,034 audit targets, about 2.8 million lines of code or roughly 7% of the kernel. “Analyst” agents then produced 2,308 candidate findings in 12 hours.

A candidate is only a guess until someone proves it. Triage agents built proof-of-concept code and ran it in isolated virtual machines with the Kernel Address Sanitizer turned on. Within 30 hours, 1,724 findings (about 74.7%) were reproduced. Only 3.1% were wrong because the model assumed an impossible condition.

Next, exploit agents tested the bugs on systems with common protections such as SMEP, SMAP, KASLR, and HARDENED_USERCOPY. They produced 291 information leak proofs and 1,169 working privilege escalation exploits.

OpenAI Uncovers 948 Linux Kernel Vulnerabilities

After variant analysis, OpenAI counted 948 unique vulnerabilities and wrote 948 patches for them. Human researchers reviewed the results before reporting.

This builds on the Patch the Planet program from June, when GPT-5.5-Cyber produced 24 Linux privilege escalation exploits. Our earlier report on GPT-5.5-Cyber covers that launch.

The full run cost $1,213,430 in API credits, or about $1,279 per exploit. OpenAI calls this an upper bound and expects better tooling to cut it. It compared the output with public bounties. Using $20,000 from Pwn2Own and $70,000 from TyphoonPWN, the 948 bugs would be worth $18.9 million to $66.3 million.

On a hardened kernelCTF setup, the pipeline got 21 privilege escalation exploits for about $32,936. OpenAI estimates that would equal roughly $1.5 million in rewards. Google’s current rules pay $71,337 per eligible exploit.

A July run with GPT-5.6 Sol found 166 unique bugs for $513,690. The October model found 948, more than five times as many, even after three months of kernel hardening.

Maintainers moved fast. Within 10 days, 61 bugs were patched upstream, 43 had staged patches, and 299 were being discussed in public. That pace matches the earlier news that Linux fixed more than 400 kernel bugs in 24 hours.

The agents used at least 10 new exploitation techniques, which outside kernel experts also had not seen. OpenAI withheld the technical details for safety. In one early run, 20 of 200 “successful” exploits gained root through a different zero-day than the assigned one. This shows why humans must check how a result was reached.

The agents also found a QEMU flaw in the test setup itself. This fits a wider pattern, since OpenAI’s AI agents also escaped sandboxes in red-team tests.

OpenAI warns that a low-privileged account on an unpatched system should be treated like root access for a well-funded threat actor. Real cases already exist. Hackers recently chained PHP2Shell with a Linux kernel flaw to get root on 25 servers.

Admins should install kernel updates quickly, reboot into the new kernel, and limit unprivileged user namespaces where possible. Sandboxes such as Firecracker and gVisor can also reduce damage.

OpenAI says it has already sent hundreds of reports and patches. It is sending the rest through Patch the Planet partners as part of its Daybreak program.

articles.description:

Instead of cracking logins or breaking MFA, it tricks employees into approving a legitimate Microsoft device-code sign-in, handing attackers a valid session to corporate mailboxes, documents, and connected apps. The kit has been […]

The post SkyW4lker Phishing Campaign Expands, Threatening US Enterprises with Microsoft 365 Account Takeovers appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A phishing kit called SkyW4lker (also branded SkyW4lker x365 Sentinel) is quietly taking over Microsoft 365 accounts without ever stealing a password.

Instead of cracking logins or breaking MFA, it tricks employees into approving a legitimate Microsoft device-code sign-in, handing attackers a valid session to corporate mailboxes, documents, and connected apps.

The kit has been active since June 2026 and is accelerating fast. Researchers at ANY.RUN tracked 618 sandbox analyses tied to SkyW4lker between June and October 21, 2026, with monthly submissions climbing from 20 in June to 200 in September.

Nearly half (46–47%) of those submissions came from the United States, more than twice the share of any other country.

For US enterprises running on Microsoft 365, that makes SkyW4lker one of the more pressing identity threats of the quarter.

This article breaks down how the kit works, who it targets, how it was traced back to a sibling phishing platform, and what SOC teams and security leaders can do about it.

Key takeaways

  • No password theft, no MFA bypass needed. SkyW4lker abuses Microsoft’s OAuth 2.0 device-code flow. The victim types a code into a real Microsoft login page; the attacker gets the token.
  • Delivery looks like routine business. Password-protected PDF, DOCX, or XLSX attachments posing as contracts, invoices, statements, and service proposals, with the password in the email body.
  • Trusted platforms are part of the chain. Lure and redirect pages sit on Google Sites, Miro, Zoom, Smartsheet, Axure Cloud, Cloudflare R2, Linode object storage, and similar services, so links pass reputation checks.
  • The kit is professionally built. A PHP backend, obfuscator.io-style JavaScript, IP geolocation of every visitor, CAPTCHA gating to block scanners, and an admin panel with Telegram-based MFA and live victim notifications.
  • It shares DNA with Gabagool. Identical JavaScript modules, landing-URL formats, CAPTCHA widget, and hosting directories link SkyW4lker to the Gabagool credential-phishing kit active since April 2026. ANY.RUN assesses with high confidence that one developer built both.
  • US tech, manufacturing, and government organizations are the main submitters, followed by India, Canada, and the UK.
  • Faster correlation shortened the investigation. ANY.RUN’s Related Threat Context surfaced earlier sandbox sessions with the same URL patterns, which let analysts pivot into Threat Intelligence Lookup, expand the campaign cluster, and locate the kit’s admin panel.

What SkyW4lker is

SkyW4lker is a device-code phishing kit: it rents or sells attackers a complete pipeline for turning a phishing click into a working Microsoft 365 session. It first appeared on June 23, 2026 and has been continuously updated since, with new endpoints and changing URL tokens.

Why US enterprises are in the crosshairs

The United States accounts for roughly 47% of all SkyW4lker-related sandbox submissions. The organizations submitting samples cluster in technology, manufacturing, and government, sectors where Microsoft 365 is the default collaboration layer and where a compromised mailbox can expose contracts, financial data, and supply-chain partners.

The risk is structural rather than technical. Device-code phishing succeeds against accounts that have MFA enabled, because the user genuinely completes an MFA-protected sign-in; they simply do it on the attacker’s behalf. That means four things for enterprise security:

  • Identity policy gaps. If device-code authentication is allowed broadly, MFA alone will not stop this attack.
  • Detection blind spots. Every step touches a legitimate service: a real document platform, a real CAPTCHA, a real Microsoft login page. Nothing in the chain looks obviously malicious to email filters or users.
  • Wide blast radius. One token can unlock Outlook, OneDrive, SharePoint, Teams, and any app federated through Entra ID, and it becomes a launchpad for phishing customers and partners from a trusted address.
  • Higher response costs. Separating a malicious device-code sign-in from thousands of legitimate ones, then scoping what the attacker touched, consumes Tier-1 and Tier-2 time.

Protect corporate accounts from Microsoft 365 phishing attacks with faster detection and response. Talk to ANY.RUN about enterprise protection →

How a SkyW4lker attack unfolds

The full chain, from lure document to device-code prompt, was detonated and recorded in the ANY.RUN Interactive Sandbox. You can replay it and pull indicators here: View the SkyW4lker analysis session →

  1. The lure lands. The target receives an email about a commercial offer, contract, invoice, or confidential document. Attached is a password-protected PDF, DOCX, or XLSX; the password sits in the email body. The encryption defeats attachment scanning, and the password-in-body pattern feels normal to anyone who deals with vendors.
  2. The redirect chain. The document contains a link, usually to a CAPTCHA page. Some variants add an intermediate decoy page on Miro, Google Sites, Zoom, or a cloud bucket before forwarding the victim. The CAPTCHA (Cloudflare Turnstile or the kit’s own widget) keeps automated URL scanners from ever seeing the payload page.
  3. The device-code prompt. The victim arrives at a branded phishing page that displays a Microsoft device code and instructs them to enter it at Microsoft’s real login.microsoft.com/device page. Once they do, and complete MFA if prompted, the attacker’s backend receives an OAuth access token for the account. No password ever crosses the wire to the attacker, and the sign-in shows up in Entra ID as a legitimate device-code authentication.

Inside the kit

The phishing page is a thin front end for a PHP backend, and ANY.RUN’s In-Browser Data Inspection exposes how it works by showing the live DOM and HTTP traffic side by side.

The main script loads helper modules, wires up the page’s buttons, and talks to the backend through one endpoint, /session_public.php, with two actions:

  • action=start sends the victim’s IP address, ISP, organization, and geolocation to the server and receives a session ID.
  • action=poll fires every few seconds with that session ID, asking whether the victim has finished authenticating. When the answer flips to yes, the attacker has the token.

The JavaScript is obfuscated in obfuscator.io style; 520 of the 618 analyses carry ANY.RUN’s obfuscated-js tag.

That is deliberate friction for anyone trying to reverse the page statically, which is why detonating it in an interactive sandbox and watching the requests is the faster route.

From one URL to the whole campaign

Finding one SkyW4lker page is easy. Finding the other 170-plus domains, the shared hosting, the admin panel, and the sibling kit is where most investigations stall.

Traditionally that means repeated IOC lookups, manual correlation across old cases, and a lot of copy-pasting between tools.

ANY.RUN’s Related Threat Context feature collapsed that work. Inside the sandbox session, a Related analyses panel listed earlier submissions that used the same /session_public.php URL pattern, giving analysts an instant starting cluster instead of a blank search box.

From there, a one-click pivot into Threat Intelligence Lookup on the distinctive endpoint returned additional phishing activity, expanded the campaign to its current size, and exposed infrastructure overlaps that would otherwise have taken days to assemble.

The same workflow applies to any suspicious URL or indicator a SOC receives: start from the alert, see what the community has already analyzed, and build on it rather than starting over.

The payoff shows up at both tiers. Tier-1 analysts spend less time re-researching indicators that someone else already resolved and get enough evidence to triage confidently.

Tier-2 analysts receive richer context up front and can focus on the cases that actually need deep analysis.

Give your SOC the context needed to speed up phishing investigations, reduce repetitive work, and boost Tier-1 productivity. See how the Interactive Sandbox connects threats →

The admin panel

Because each phishing page runs its own backend, the operator’s control panel usually lives on the same host.

Combining Threat Intelligence Lookup results with external data turned up a login form at /admin/index.php, and its stylesheet (command-center.css) describes what the kit offers its customers:

  • Operator login with MFA delivered over Telegram
  • A victim dashboard fed by client_geo.js geolocation data
  • Server management and generation of new phishing links
  • Real-time notifications whenever a target opens a link

SkyW4lker and Gabagool: one developer, two attack modes

Searching ANY.RUN Threat Intelligence for SkyW4lker’s module paths (/js/client_geo.js, /js/url_helper.js, /js/endpoint.js) also returns sessions tagged Gabagool, a credential-phishing kit first seen on April 23, 2026, two months before SkyW4lker.

Some Gabagool sessions even load the kit from directories literally named skywalker and skyw4lker on goldcreekconcrete[.]com and goldcreekconcrete[.]org.

ANY.RUN’s assessment: the same developer built both kits, and they are best understood as two modes of one phishing platform, one that harvests passwords, one that harvests device-code tokens.

Whether a single operator runs both, or multiple customers bought the same product, the data cannot yet say.

How to detect SkyW4lker and reduce exposure

For SOC analysts and threat hunters

  • Hunt the kit’s fingerprints. Alert on outbound requests to /session_public.php?action=start followed by repeated ?action=poll calls, and on the three module paths (client_geo.js, url_helper.js, endpoint.js) under /assets/js/. The landing token regex //it[A-Za-z0-9]{32}us (previously //zt[A-Za-z0-9]{32}op) is a reliable signature for the landing URL.
  • Tie phishing to sign-ins. In Microsoft Entra ID sign-in logs, filter for device-code authentications and correlate them against recent suspicious emails or document-share notifications to the same user. A device-code sign-in minutes after a “protected invoice” email is a strong compromise signal.
  • Detonate, don’t guess. Password-protected attachments and CAPTCHA-gated links defeat static scanners by design. Open them in an interactive sandbox, supply the password, pass the CAPTCHA, and watch the real traffic.
  • Pivot beyond the single IOC. Use Related Threat Context and Threat Intelligence Lookup to check whether the domain, endpoint, or module path already appears in other analyses. That turns a one-off alert into campaign-level visibility in minutes.
  • Scope the follow-on. When a token theft is suspected, review mailbox rules, OAuth app consents, SharePoint/OneDrive access, and outbound mail from the account to catch lateral phishing against colleagues and partners.

Give your SOC the speed to handle more threats with 20% less Tier-1 investigation time and 30% fewer escalations. Book an enterprise demo →

For CISOs and security leaders

SkyW4lker is a reminder that MFA is necessary but not sufficient. Three priorities:

  1. Close the device-code gap. Audit where device-code authentication is actually needed (typically headless devices, CLI tools, and some conferencing hardware). Block or tightly scope it with Entra Conditional Access everywhere else. This single control removes the attack’s payoff.
  2. Connect email, web, and identity telemetry. The kit only works because each stage is examined in isolation. Make sure the SOC can link a suspicious attachment, the phishing infrastructure it reaches, and the authentication event that follows.
  3. Shorten the investigation loop. Give Tier-1 analysts historical threat context and clear escalation criteria so routine phishing cases close at Tier 1, and reserve Tier 2 for incidents that truly need deeper work. Define a containment runbook for token-based compromise: revoke sessions, reset credentials, review app consents, and check for persistence.

MITRE ATT&CK mapping

Indicators of compromise

All indicators were observed in ANY.RUN analyses between June 23 and October 21, 2026. The full list of 173 phishing domains, plus live sandbox sessions, is available in the original ANY.RUN research.

URL patterns

Sample domains and infrastructure

  • 5200m[.]com, torvion[.]life, ghethim[.]com (hosts shared with Gabagool)
  • goldcreekconcrete[.]com, goldcreekconcrete[.]org (/skywalker/, /skyw4lker/ directories)
  • sdocshares.auth.outlook2026common.copilos26.csr-rooflng[.]com
  • pdocshared.payments2026.outlooks.common.ecmholdlnggroup[.]com
  • flow505.mooo[.]com, bigbrain.chickenkiller[.]com, off365acess.jumpingcrab[.]com
  • 172.86.85[.]51 (priorispace[.]biz), 162.243.64[.]121, 67.205.154[.]32
  • Sample lure SHA256: 9aa0b87974b9b4cd42603833b7ad44257578467d279b315a071108a5ed02c268

Conclusion

SkyW4lker is not a novel exploit; it is a well-engineered abuse of a feature Microsoft 365 ships by default.

Its growth from 20 to 200 sandbox submissions a month in a single quarter, its concentration on US enterprises, and its shared lineage with Gabagool all point to a phishing platform that will keep shipping new modes as long as device-code sign-ins stay open and SOCs keep treating phishing alerts one at a time.

The defensive answer is equally unglamorous: restrict device-code authentication where it is not needed, correlate email and identity events, and give analysts the ability to detonate what filters cannot inspect and to see, in one view, what the rest of the community has already found about the same infrastructure.

ANY.RUN helps SOC and MSSP teams detect and investigate threats faster. Its Interactive Sandbox lets analysts open suspicious files and URLs, supply passwords, pass CAPTCHAs, and watch full attack chains unfold, while Threat Intelligence Lookup, Feeds, and Reports connect each case to activity seen across more than 16,000 organizations and 700,000 security professionals. ANY.RUN is SOC 2 Type II certified.

articles.description:

The post 6 Challenges SOC Leaders Should Turn into Priorities in 2027  appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Security teams face mounting pressure to keep pace with increasingly complex threats while working within tight budgets and persistent staffing constraints.

As attack techniques evolve and alert volumes rise, maintaining effective detection and investigation capabilities becomes increasingly demanding. 

In 2027, threat intelligence will play a growing role in helping SOC and MSSP teams recognize malicious activity earlier, investigate suspicious behavior faster, and make better use of analyst expertise. 

Achieving these gains requires intelligence to become part of everyday security workflows, informing decisions from initial detection through investigation and response.

Six challenges mentioned in this article illustrate where organizations should focus their efforts in the year ahead. 

1. Are You Detecting Threats Before They Become Incidents? 

One of the most effective ways to improve detection is to recognize malicious activity that has already been identified elsewhere.

articles.title: Critical Ruby on Rails Flaw Could Let Hackers Steal Server Secrets Through Malicious Image Uploads
articles.description:
A critical flaw in Ruby on Rails Active Storage lets an unauthenticated user upload a crafted image and make the server write files. If uploads use the Disk service, the same upload can make the server read files too. The Rails team rated the bug Critical, with a CVSS score of 9.8, and published the […]

The post Critical Ruby on Rails Flaw Could Let Hackers Steal Server Secrets Through Malicious Image Uploads appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A critical flaw in Ruby on Rails Active Storage lets an unauthenticated user upload a crafted image and make the server write files. If uploads use the Disk service, the same upload can make the server read files too. The Rails team rated the bug Critical, with a CVSS score of 9.8, and published the advisory on November 4, 2026. The flaw has no CVE ID yet.

The flaw comes from how ImageMagick works. It picks a coder (a file format handler) based on what is inside a file, not on its name. Some coders act on other files named inside the image.

Active Storage did not limit any of these coders, and its image analyzer runs as soon as a file is attached. So an attacker only needs to attach a crafted upload. No variant, preview, or analyze call is needed.

Critical Ruby on Rails Flaw

The files at risk usually include secret_key_base and credentials for outside systems. With those, an attacker may move on to remote code execution or reach other connected services. The Rails team also says one attack chain was reported, but they do not assume it is the only one. The researcher ryotak reported the bug through HackerOne.

An app is affected only if all three of these are true. It uses ImageMagick through config.active_storage.variant_processor = :mini_magick, which is the default for apps on load_defaults 6.1 or earlier.

It runs ImageMagick under a policy that does not already block the coders involved, and the policies packaged by Debian and Ubuntu do not. And it accepts uploads from untrusted users. Affected versions are activestorage before 8.0.5.2, and 8.1 releases before 8.1.4.1.

The fix ships an ImageMagick security policy. Rails adds its folder to MAGICK_CONFIGURE_PATH through MiniMagick.cli_env, so every ImageMagick process that MiniMagick starts follows it.

The policy blocks the MSL scripting coder, coders that read or delete other files, coders that fetch remote or local references, every Ghostscript-backed coder, and @filename indirection. The policy adds to the host’s rules instead of replacing them.

This is not the first image-related Rails scare this year. Cyber Security News recently covered CVE-2026-66066, a Rails Active Storage flaw that affected apps using libvips and could expose secrets such as secret_key_base and cloud keys. Researchers later saw that bug used in real attacks. Teams that patched in the summer should not assume they are safe now, because this is a different processor and a different fix.

ImageMagick has also caused trouble outside Rails. A recent WordPress bug let Author-level users reach code execution because ImageMagick passed a disguised PostScript file to Ghostscript.

A separate Discourse image pipeline exploit chained ImageMagick features to read server files. The lesson is the same each time: image tools do more than open pictures, so untrusted uploads need strict limits.

First, upgrade activestorage to 8.0.5.2 or 8.1.4.1. Apps using :mini_magick also need mini_magick 5.1 or newer, and older versions fail with an error at boot. Apps that render PostScript or PDF through ImageMagick must allow the gs delegate again in the host’s policy.xml.

Apps that replace MiniMagick.cli_env after boot, clear the environment with MiniMagick.cli_prefix, or use their own MiniMagick::Shell do not get the shipped policy. They must copy its rules into ImageMagick’s system policy. GraphicsMagick does not read ImageMagick policies at all.

Teams that cannot upgrade right away can copy the shipped rules into the system policy, for example /etc/ImageMagick-7/policy.xml. At a minimum, they should block the MSL coder, the Ghostscript coders, and the gs delegate.

Secrets need attention too. If attachments live on the Disk service, change secret_key_base and every secret the app process can read. That includes the master key, everything in config/credentials.yml.enc, storage and database credentials, and third-party tokens. The Rails team warns against keeping an exposed secret as a fallback.

This fix is one of 21 security issues in the 8.0.5.2 and 8.1.4.1 releases. Others cover a Strong Parameters bypass, IP spoofing through the Forwarded header in 8.1, several cross-site scripting bugs in Action View, denial-of-service bugs, and session cookie problems.

A second High-rated bug covers file read and code execution through Active Storage video previews and analysis. Security support for the 8.0 series ends on November 7, 2026, so teams on older lines should plan a move to 8.0 or later.

Even with the patch, reviewing upload paths is worth the time. Teams should check logs for odd uploads and make sure no app runs with extra file permissions.

articles.title: Debian and Ubuntu APT Flaw Lets Hackers Hijack Software Updates and Execute Code as Root
articles.description:
A newly disclosed bug in APT, the package manager behind Debian and Ubuntu, can let a network spy swap a trusted software package for a bad one. The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-109518 and can end in code running with root rights, the highest level of control on a Linux system. Debian announced the issue […]

The post Debian and Ubuntu APT Flaw Lets Hackers Hijack Software Updates and Execute Code as Root appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
A newly disclosed bug in APT, the package manager behind Debian and Ubuntu, can let a network spy swap a trusted software package for a bad one.

The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-109518 and can end in code running with root rights, the highest level of control on a Linux system. Debian announced the issue on November 4, 2026, and credited researcher Max Justicz with finding it.

APT checks each package against signed data before it installs anything. This flaw lets an attacker get around that check. According to Debian, APT can merge two different package downloads after an HTTP redirect gives it the same address.

When APT resumes an interrupted download, it handles the file incorrectly, opening a short window to replace the package after it has been verified. The package that gets installed is then the attacker’s version, not the checked one.

The attacker must sit between the computer and the archive server. That could be someone on the same network, a rogue proxy, or a malicious mirror. The flaw also depends on hard link reuse, and it needs the client to follow redirects and retry a download.

These conditions make the attack harder than a simple remote hit, but public Wi-Fi, hijacked routers, and compromised mirrors make them realistic.

Debian APT Flaw Lets Hackers Hijack Updates

The bug only works when APT’s retry setting, Acquire::Retries, is above zero. That value is 3 by default on Debian 12 (bookworm) and Ubuntu 22.04 LTS, so older releases are not affected in their default setup. The Debian Security Tracker lists these states:

  • Bookworm: version 2.6.1 is vulnerable and 2.6.2 is fixed.
  • Trixie: version 3.0.3 is vulnerable and 3.0.4 is fixed.
  • Testing and unstable (forky, sid): version 3.3.5 is vulnerable.

The tracker points to advisory DSA-6607-1 for trixie and DLA-4880-1 for bookworm. Ubuntu and other derivatives need their own patches, so users should watch their vendor’s notices.

The Debian advisory for trixie says the problem is fixed in APT 3.0.4 and urges users to upgrade. The same update also closes several out-of-bounds access bugs.

For the upstream project, APT 3.3.6 changes the download methods to open target files exclusively. This stops two downloads from touching the same file. The release also rejects DEB packages that lack the required Version field and fixes a sorting bug in the dependency solver.

APT has had a similar scare before. In 2019, Justicz found a remote code execution bug in apt, tracked as CVE-2019-3462. It also let a man-in-the-middle run code as root through a redirect.

His workaround then was to turn off redirects with -o Acquire::http::AllowRedirect=false. The new flaw is a different bug, but the lesson is the same. Redirects and download handling are risky parts of any update tool.

Run apt update and apt upgrade on trusted networks, and confirm the installed APT version matches the fixed one for your release. Avoid untrusted mirrors and proxies until you have patched.

Prefer HTTPS mirrors where you can, because they make interception harder. As a stopgap on unpatched systems, setting Acquire::Retries to 0 removes one required condition, though it can make updates less reliable on poor connections.

Update tools run with full trust, so one bad package can hand over a whole server. Our earlier coverage of Linux supply chain security essentials explains why checking package integrity matters.

Readers who run Debian can also see how large patch batches land in our report on Debian’s 1,313-flaw kernel update. No public reports of active use have surfaced so far. Patching now is still the safest move.

articles.description:
Russia-aligned hackers tracked as Gorbag are exploiting a WinRAR vulnerability to steal browser credentials, VPN configurations, and sensitive documents from Ukrainian organizations. Active since at least February 2025, the group targets government agencies, law enforcement bodies, justice institutions, local administrations near the front line, and defense organizations. The campaign favors quick data theft over extended […]

The post Gorbag Hackers Exploit WinRAR Vulnerability to Steal Credentials From Ukrainian Government Agencies appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Russia-aligned hackers tracked as Gorbag are exploiting a WinRAR vulnerability to steal browser credentials, VPN configurations, and sensitive documents from Ukrainian organizations.

Active since at least February 2025, the group targets government agencies, law enforcement bodies, justice institutions, local administrations near the front line, and defense organizations.

The campaign favors quick data theft over extended remote control. Its malware collects information in a single pass, sends the results to attacker-controlled infrastructure, and then attempts to delete itself.

Researchers believe the stolen credentials could support further intrusions by other groups, although that possible relationship remains unconfirmed.

ESET researchers writing on WeLiveSecurity identified the group’s main malware as BeautyStealer, a C++ information stealer, alongside an earlier tool called Prime ReverseShell.

Their November 3 report connects previously reported GIFTEDCROOK activity, attributed by CERT-UA to UAC-0226, with a wider intelligence-gathering operation against Ukrainian targets.

Gorbag Hackers Exploit WinRAR Vulnerability

Throughout 2025, Gorbag mainly used targeted phishing emails carrying malicious Excel attachments. Messages referenced routine government business, including administrative fines and taxes.

At least one message came from a compromised Ukrainian local government mailbox, giving recipients another reason to trust the attachment.

These attacks resemble the previously documented GIFTEDCROOK browser credential theft campaign, which also used spreadsheets containing hidden payloads.

When macros ran, a VBA routine decoded malicious content stored inside spreadsheet cells, saved the payload on disk, and launched BeautyStealer. The process depended on victims enabling macros or having settings that permitted execution.

In early 2026, Gorbag switched to malicious RAR archives exploiting CVE-2025-8088. This WinRAR path traversal vulnerability lets specially crafted archive content escape the folder selected for extraction.

Attackers abuse alternate data streams, a Windows file feature, to place malicious files elsewhere on the system. The flaw had already featured in RomCom WinRAR phishing attacks before Gorbag adopted it.

In Gorbag’s chain, archive extraction presents a decoy PDF while planting a shortcut in the Windows Startup folder. An encrypted payload and PowerShell loader are also written to disk, with the shortcut triggering the loader during subsequent system startups.

About one quarter of identified targets were justice or law enforcement organizations. Another quarter were local government bodies, mostly city councils near the front line.

Researchers suggest these targets could provide information about war crimes investigations, infrastructure damage, and local defense initiatives. These explanations remain assessments rather than confirmed objectives.

BeautyStealer Harvests Browser Data, Documents, and Private Keys

BeautyStealer collects saved passwords, cookies, and browser state from Chrome, Edge, Opera, and Firefox.

It also searches for OpenVPN configurations and selected files across Desktop, Documents, and Downloads folders, removable media, and mapped network drives. Its reach therefore extends beyond browser credentials to potentially sensitive organizational records.

The broader pattern matches earlier reporting on Russian WinRAR credential theft targeting Ukrainian organizations. ESET found that BeautyStealer also seeks KeePass databases, Java KeyStore files, Remote Desktop configurations, and certificate containers.

Particularly notable are Ukrainian electronic signature key files, which contain secret keys issued by accredited certification centers.

Collected information is compressed before being sent through Telegram’s sendDocument API or, from version 1.2 onward, to a custom server using FastAPI. Version 2.0 introduced RC4 encryption and replaced earlier batch-script cleanup with direct Windows API calls for self-deletion.

ESET tracked versions from 0.9 through 2.0. The findings reinforce the need for WinRAR security patch deployment across affected Windows systems. The vulnerability was fixed in version 7.13.

Updating vulnerable installations removes this entry point, but organizations investigating suspected compromise should also examine the published indicators and consider whether credentials or sensitive files were already exposed.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Reinach, Switzerland, November 4th, 2026, CyberNewswire

AI agents help Joe Sandbox uncover malicious behavior concealed by evasion techniques and unmet execution conditions.

Joe Security‘s Adaptive Detonation brings active intervention to malware analysis, helping security teams investigate threats that may conceal their behavior during an initial sandbox run.

Adaptive Detonation uses AI agents to examine execution results, identify obstacles preventing a sample from revealing relevant behavior, and select targeted interventions.

These can include patching a blocking check, creating required files or settings, adjusting the execution environment, or supplying missing command-line arguments.

Joe Sandbox then analyzes the sample again under the modified conditions to verify whether the intervention reveals additional activity.

The approach addresses obstacles including keyboard restrictions, timing checks, firmware-based rejection, date requirements, and missing dependencies.

By connecting observed evidence with targeted action and verification, Adaptive Detonation helps analysts investigate why a sample remains inactive and uncover behavior that might otherwise stay hidden.

For security teams, this means deeper visibility into evasive threats and more evidence to support investigations.

Adaptive Detonation is available as part of Joe Sandbox AI, a plugin for Joe Sandbox Cloud. Security teams can test Joe Sandbox by signing in or registering for Joe Sandbox Cloud Basic, the free community version.

Read the Adaptive Detonation blog post for technical details, malware case studies, and original and follow-up analysis reports.

About Joe Security

Joe Security is a privately owned Swiss software company founded in 2011 and headquartered in Reinach, Switzerland. It develops malware and phishing analysis technology, combining dynamic analysis, agentic reverse engineering and dedicated analyst lab environments.

articles.title: Scammers Use Microsoft Azure to Host Fake Windows Security Alerts Seen at 80 Organizations
articles.description:
Scammers are abusing Microsoft Azure to host fake Windows security alerts that pressure users into calling fraudulent support numbers. Between March and October 2026, the same fake Microsoft support kit reached users at 80 organizations. New landing pages were still appearing daily as of November 2, showing that the operation remained active. These figures describe […]

The post Scammers Use Microsoft Azure to Host Fake Windows Security Alerts Seen at 80 Organizations appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Scammers are abusing Microsoft Azure to host fake Windows security alerts that pressure users into calling fraudulent support numbers.

Between March and October 2026, the same fake Microsoft support kit reached users at 80 organizations. New landing pages were still appearing daily as of November 2, showing that the operation remained active.

These figures describe exposure to scam pages, not 80 confirmed network breaches. The attack begins with an advertisement on a legitimate website.

Clicking it sends the visitor to an Azure-hosted page displaying alarming security messages and a fake support chat.

Similar Azure tech support scams have used Bing advertisements to reach business users, demonstrating how paid placements can turn routine browsing into a dangerous encounter.

Researchers from PIXM identified the scam kit and traced part of its supporting infrastructure in a November 2 investigation.

Scammers Use Microsoft Azure

Their analysis describes a browser-based support scam rather than a confirmed malware infection. The Azure landing pages imitate “System Error” and “Windows Firewall” warnings, with every element directing visitors toward a toll-free number.

Behind the warning screen, JavaScript requests a telephone number from a central service using JSONP, a technique that loads a response through a script.

An advertising-manager parameter tells the service which operator’s number to return. This lets the organizers change numbers across deployed pages without rebuilding each site. The code also includes a fallback number if the request fails.

A tracking pixel records the displayed number, campaign, publisher website, and advertising exchange. These details help operators connect incoming calls to particular advertising campaigns.

The setup resembles legitimate pay-per-call marketing, but the calls originate from deceptive security warnings. The manager list expanded from three names in May to four in July, suggesting multiple participants rather than one person maintaining every page.

The broader technique echoes separate fake Microsoft security alerts campaigns that use disposable cloud-hosted pages to funnel visitors toward scam call centers.

However, PIXM’s attribution has an important limit: the specific back end it investigated accounted for exposure at 11 organizations. Other operations used the same fake page across the wider group of 80 organizations.

Infrastructure Clues, Business Risks, and Defenses

Several clues suggest Mandarin-speaking developers and connections to mainland China. Script comments and error messages used Simplified Chinese, while one page family displayed a copied Chinese full-screen notice.

The telephone service exposed a default BaoTa server-panel page in Chinese. Registration records also listed a Hubei address, although PIXM stressed that self-reported registration information alone cannot establish attribution.

Tracking data identified placements associated with Whitepages, Legacy.com, Us Weekly, MSN, KMBC, WordHippo, Juno webmail, and the health section of US News & World Report.

PIXM said these publishers were not complicit. The advertisements passed through programmatic exchanges, and reviewers did not necessarily see the same destination presented to targeted visitors.

The immediate danger is the conversation that follows the warning. Scammers commonly persuade callers to install remote-access software, charge for unnecessary repairs, or introduce refund and bank-impersonation schemes.

Separate Microsoft Teams impersonation attacks show how legitimate remote-management software can also become an access channel when users accept instructions from an impersonator. That comparison does not establish malware deployment in this campaign.

Defenders should block the listed malicious infrastructure through DNS controls or secure web gateways and restrict remote-access software to approved support workflows. Employees should close suspicious tabs or force-quit the browser rather than call displayed numbers.

Blocking the telephone service disrupts dynamic number delivery, but the fallback means this should not be treated as complete protection. Trusted cloud hosting does not make a rendered warning trustworthy.

articles.description:
SolarWinds has warned about a critical command injection flaw in its Dameware remote support software. It is tracked as CVE-2026-28336 and carries a severity score of 9.9 out of 10. The bug could let an attacker take over a computer that an IT team is controlling remotely. Dameware is widely used by help desks and […]

The post Critical SolarWinds Dameware Flaw Could Allow Attackers to Compromise Remote Systems appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
SolarWinds has warned about a critical command injection flaw in its Dameware remote support software. It is tracked as CVE-2026-28336 and carries a severity score of 9.9 out of 10.

The bug could let an attacker take over a computer that an IT team is controlling remotely. Dameware is widely used by help desks and administrators to connect to and fix remote computers.

Since the tool runs with strong access, a flaw in it is risky for any company that depends on it. SolarWinds published the advisory on November 3, 2026, and urged users to update quickly.

Analysts at SolarWinds noted the problem in their security advisory. No malware is tied to this flaw, and the advisory does not report any attacks in the wild.

It says the issue could lead to the compromise of the remotely controlled host. This is not the first Dameware bug to draw attention, since an earlier Dameware privilege escalation flaw was fixed in 2025.

Critical SolarWinds Dameware Flaw Could Allow Attackers

Command injection happens when software accepts input from a user and passes it to the system without checking it properly. An attacker can then slip in their own commands.

In this case, the attacker must already be logged in, so the flaw needs valid access first. The CVSS vector (AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H) shows the flaw can be used over a network with low complexity.

It needs only low privileges and no user interaction. It also changes scope, which means the impact can spread beyond the weak component to the remote machine. Confidentiality, integrity and availability are all rated high.

The issue affects SolarWinds Dameware 2026.3 and all earlier versions. The fixed release is Dameware 2026.3.1. Greg Bernatowicz of the Boeing Enterprise Security Red Team received credit for finding it, according to the official SolarWinds advisory.

Why SolarWinds Users Should Act Fast

Attackers like remote support tools because one stolen login can open many systems. Recent history shows how quickly SolarWinds bugs get abused. Hackers were seen exploiting Web Help Desk flaws to install extra remote access tools.

SolarWinds has been patching many products this year. Recent updates covered critical SolarWinds Observability flaws that allowed remote code execution.

The company also released Serv-U security fixes for 15 vulnerabilities in July. Administrators should upgrade Dameware to 2026.3.1 now, review who holds Dameware accounts, and remove any that are not needed. They should also limit network access to the tool and watch logs for strange commands.

The post French Bank Crédit Mutuel Arkéa Confirms Cyberattack Amid Reports of $133 Million Theft appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
French banking group Crédit Mutuel Arkéa has confirmed a cyberattack that enabled fraudulent transactions, following reports linking the institution to cryptocurrency theft exceeding $133 million.

The bank says the incident is contained, operations are gradually resuming, and customer assets remain unaffected. It has not confirmed the reported loss figure.

The group notified regulatory and supervisory authorities after detecting the attack. Teams temporarily suspended certain transactions to prevent further fraud while checking systems and adding security measures. According to its statement, customers experienced delays involving some transfers, but their funds remain protected.

Blockchain investigator ZachXBT linked Arkéa to suspicious cryptocurrency withdrawals after initially describing the victim as an unnamed European institution.

His first findings identified more than $106 million withdrawn on November 1. An additional $27 million later pushed his estimate above $133 million. These figures remain investigative estimates, not losses verified by the bank.

The case draws attention to fraudulent payments moving through financial channels. Cybersecurity News previously covered BREEZE COMET’s attacks on financial firms, which involved trusted access and unauthorized transfers. However, no evidence currently connects that group or its methods to the Arkéa incident.

Crédit Mutuel Arkéa Confirms Cyberattack

According to ZachXBT’s published findings, funds left exchange accounts as USDC and USDT before being moved through cryptocurrency services.

He described conversions into Ethereum, transfers between blockchains, and exchanges into Monero. His analysis suggests the final total could be higher if additional over-the-counter trades are included.

In its official incident statement, Arkéa says the affected amounts are still being assessed and do not threaten its financial strength. Separate AFP reporting confirms that the institution has not disclosed how attackers gained access or identified those responsible. This distinction separates the confirmed banking incident from the wider claims about stolen cryptocurrency.

Public reporting has linked the fraud to Fortuneo, Arkéa’s online banking subsidiary. However, the available information does not establish the initial entry point, a specific software flaw, or whether stolen credentials were involved. Claims about the attackers’ identity should therefore remain separate from confirmed findings.

Arkéa also warned that phishing attempts could follow the incident. Criminals may use news of banking problems to make fake security messages seem credible.

Cybersecurity News has previously documented payment scams using spoofed bank alerts, where callers trick victims into sending funds to attacker-controlled accounts. That report describes a separate scam, not Arkéa’s confirmed attack method.

The bank advises customers never to share passwords, card details, or SMS verification codes. Anyone receiving a suspicious message should contact their bank adviser directly. Arkéa says its teams continue assessing the consequences and strengthening security, with further updates expected when new information becomes available.

articles.title: Critical Barracuda Security Flaws Could Let Hackers Bypass Authentication and Gain Root Access
articles.description:
Barracuda has disclosed two security vulnerabilities that could allow attackers to bypass authorization controls and gain root access to affected appliances when exploited together. The flaws affect several Barracuda security products, but exploitation requires access to a device’s administrative interface, making exposed management systems a key concern for defenders. The vulnerabilities, tracked as CVE-2026-116606 and […]

The post Critical Barracuda Security Flaws Could Let Hackers Bypass Authentication and Gain Root Access appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
Barracuda has disclosed two security vulnerabilities that could allow attackers to bypass authorization controls and gain root access to affected appliances when exploited together.

The flaws affect several Barracuda security products, but exploitation requires access to a device’s administrative interface, making exposed management systems a key concern for defenders.

The vulnerabilities, tracked as CVE-2026-116606 and CVE-2026-111560, were disclosed on November 2, 2026. Barracuda has released patches and urged customers to install the latest firmware and verify that security updates have reached their devices.

Its advisory does not report active exploitation or identify an associated attack campaign. Barracuda researchers identified the vulnerabilities, not a malware strain.

The distinction matters because the disclosure describes weaknesses in appliance access controls and command handling rather than a documented malware infection.

According to the official Barracuda security advisory, combining these weaknesses could give an attacker root access to an affected device.

Critical Barracuda Security Flaws

CVE-2026-116606 is a pre-authentication authorization bypass affecting Barracuda Email Security Gateway, commonly called ESG.

It carries a CVSS score of 9.3. CVE-2026-111560 is a command injection vulnerability with a score of 8.6 and affects six product families. Barracuda labels both vulnerabilities “High” in its advisory, despite the first flaw’s 9.3 score.

The first weakness concerns authorization controls, while the second involves command injection. Barracuda says the combined attack could bypass those controls and obtain root access.

However, the advisory does not publish vulnerable endpoints, example requests, payloads, or a detailed exploit sequence. Administrators should therefore avoid treating an assumed attack chain as confirmed technical evidence.

Earlier coverage of Barracuda gateway command injection explains how a separate flaw, CVE-2023-2868, enabled system command execution through malicious archive processing.

That historical vulnerability is not one of the newly disclosed issues, and its exploitation method should not be applied to this advisory.

An important limitation remains unresolved in the published details. Barracuda calls CVE-2026-116606 a pre-authentication authorization bypass, yet its advisory also lists “Authentication Required: Yes, administrative access.”

Its overview states that attackers need access to the administrative interface. These statements do not clearly establish whether valid administrator credentials are required for every exploitation scenario.

Only ESG is listed as affected by both vulnerabilities. The command injection flaw also affects Load Balancer Application Delivery Controller, Message Archiver, WAF Control Center, Web Application Firewall, and Web Security Gateway.

The published matrix does not list those five additional products as vulnerable to the authorization bypass. The broader concern is familiar: security appliances can become valuable entry points when exploitable weaknesses remain exposed.

Reporting on most exploited security vulnerabilities previously included Barracuda ESG among products targeted through known flaws. That history provides context for patching urgency, but it does not establish exploitation of these newly disclosed CVEs.

Patches, Administrative Exposure, and Defensive Priorities

Barracuda recommends restricting administrative interfaces to trusted internal networks and applying appropriate network access controls. Organizations whose management interfaces are not publicly accessible face less exposure to this attack path.

Reducing internet exposure is therefore an immediate containment measure, but the vendor still directs customers to update firmware and apply all security patches.

The supplied advisory lists ESG patches BNSF-40425 for versions 9.4.017 and later, and BNSF-40430 for earlier versions.

It identifies BNADC-16586 for ADC and WAF, BNMA-32468 for Message Archiver, BNWF-60060 for WAF Control Center, and BNYF-24789 for Web Security Gateway. These identifiers help administrators verify remediation against the affected product.

Customers should check the latest firmware offered by each appliance and confirm that patches actually installed. Systems several firmware versions behind may require multiple updates.

If automatic patching did not apply an update, Barracuda advises installing it manually as soon as possible and enabling automatic patch delivery where it has been disabled.

Previous reporting on network device root access illustrates why management interfaces deserve close attention during vulnerability response.

For this disclosure, however, administrators should follow Barracuda’s product-specific guidance rather than assume another vendor’s exploit methods or recovery requirements apply. Barracuda Support can help verify firmware and patch status.

The Node.js project has scheduled security updates for its 22.x, 24.x, and 26.x release lines on or shortly after Wednesday, November 11, 2026. The announcement gives developers and system administrators time to prepare for patches addressing HIGH-rated vulnerabilities across all three branches. Each release line will receive a fix for at least one high-severity issue. […]

The post Node.js Schedules High-Severity Security Fixes for 22.x, 24.x, and 26.x Release Lines appeared first on Cyber Security News.

cybersecuritynews.content_encoded:
The Node.js project has scheduled security updates for its 22.x, 24.x, and 26.x release lines on or shortly after Wednesday, November 11, 2026. The announcement gives developers and system administrators time to prepare for patches addressing HIGH-rated vulnerabilities across all three branches.

Each release line will receive a fix for at least one high-severity issue. However, the advance notice does not list vulnerability counts, CVE identifiers, affected components, or fixed version numbers. It also provides no details about attack methods or confirmed exploitation, leaving the exact technical risk unclear until further information becomes available.

The planned updates follow earlier Node.js security fixes covering TLS, DNS, and Brotli. Those October patches addressed separate weaknesses in certificate checks, name resolution, and compressed data handling.

Node2Shell Adds Concern

One notable October issue was Node2Shell, tracked as CVE-2026-111497, a high-severity flaw in Node.js’s bundled Brotli decoder. It affected the same three release lines and could allow an attacker to corrupt process memory when an application decompressed malicious Brotli data through the node:zlib module.

The decoder incorrectly treated an invalid block switch as a request for more input rather than a permanent error. It then continued adding bytes beyond an eight-byte internal buffer. Depending on application behavior, this could cause a crash, expose process memory, or allow remote code execution.

According to the official October advisory, Node2Shell was addressed in that earlier security release. Fixes shipped in versions 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1. It should therefore be treated as separate background, not described as a confirmed vulnerability in November’s planned patch set.

Supported Versions and Older Releases

Node.js also warns that end-of-life versions are affected when security releases occur. Running an older branch should therefore not be treated as protection simply because it is absent from the patch list. The project directs users toward an up-to-date, supported release rather than continued use of unsupported versions.

The official release schedule lists Node.js 26.x as Active Long-Term Support, while 24.x and 22.x are in Maintenance support. Maintenance branches still receive security updates. Earlier coverage of Node.js security flaws affecting supported branches shows why teams must track runtime updates alongside application changes.

According to the official security advisory, November 11 is a target rather than a guaranteed publication deadline. Teams should monitor the notice for release availability and technical details. Until those details arrive, claims about remote code execution, data theft, or specific workarounds would go beyond the published information.

For deployment planning, the Node.js release schedule provides the support status and end-of-life dates for each branch. The immediate priority is identifying which release lines applications use and preparing to test the forthcoming updates.

Organizations on unsupported versions should plan migration to a supported branch rather than expect patches for retired releases.
